  <div class="lesson-main">

    <div class="lesson-objectives">
      <h2>After this lesson, you will be able to:</h2>
      <ul>
        <li><span>Explain why data is compressed and what redundancy has to do with it</span></li>
        <li><span>Compare lossless and lossy compression and state exactly what each guarantees</span></li>
        <li><span>Work a run-length encoding example by hand and show why it is lossless</span></li>
        <li><span>Reason about the size-versus-quality trade-off and pick the right method for a use case</span></li>
        <li><span>Explain why fewer bits does not automatically mean less information</span></li>
        <li><span>Describe how data-format and compression choices appear in your Create Task written response</span></li>
      </ul>
    </div>
    <div class="score-impact">📈 <span><strong>Exam weight:</strong> Big Idea 2 (Data) is 17 to 22 percent of the AP CSP exam, and compression is one of its most reliably tested ideas. Expect MCQs that ask you to choose lossless versus lossy for a scenario, judge whether the exact original can be recovered, and reason about how much a file will shrink. These are quick points once the distinctions are automatic.</span>
</div>
    <div class="hook-box">
      <div class="hook-label">💡 Think about this first</div>
      <p>A single minute of raw, uncompressed audio is over 10 megabytes, yet a three-minute song streams to your phone in seconds. A photo straight off a camera sensor is enormous, yet it fits in a text message. Nothing about the original recording changed; the file just got dramatically smaller on the way to you. Compression is the reason almost everything on the internet is fast enough to use, and the key question this lesson answers is: when is it safe to make a file smaller, and when does making it smaller quietly throw away something you needed?</p>
    </div>

    <div class="lesson-section">
      <h2>Why We Compress Data</h2>
      <p><strong>Data compression</strong> reduces the number of bits used to store or transmit a piece of data. Smaller files take less storage space and travel faster across a network, which is why compression sits underneath streaming, messaging, backups, and nearly every download you make. A compression method looks for <strong>redundancy</strong> in the data, which is repeated or predictable patterns, and finds a shorter way to represent the same content.</p>
      <p>How much a file shrinks is not fixed. The amount of size reduction depends on <strong>both</strong> how much redundancy the original contains <strong>and</strong> which compression method is used. A page of text with long repeated stretches compresses a great deal; data that is already varied or close to random barely compresses at all, no matter how clever the algorithm.</p>
      <div class="callout-exam">
        <div class="callout-exam-label">🎯 A distinction the exam loves</div>
        <p>Fewer bits does <strong>not</strong> automatically mean less information. Removing redundancy shortens how the data is written down without changing what it says, so a smaller file can still carry all of the original information. Only certain methods actually discard information. Keep "fewer bits" and "less information" as two separate ideas.</p>
      </div>
      <p>That last point splits every compression method into two families. Some methods promise the original can be rebuilt exactly, and some trade that promise away for a much smaller file. Those two families are <strong>lossless</strong> and <strong>lossy</strong>, and knowing which one a scenario needs is the whole skill.</p>
    </div>

    <div class="lesson-section">
      <h2>Lossless Compression</h2>
      <p><strong>Lossless compression</strong> reduces the number of bits while <strong>guaranteeing that the original data can be reconstructed exactly</strong>. Nothing is lost. You compress, and later you decompress, and what comes back is bit-for-bit identical to what you started with. Common lossless formats include <strong>ZIP</strong> for general files, <strong>PNG</strong> for images, and <strong>run-length encoding</strong> as a simple teaching example. Lossless is the only acceptable choice whenever the exact original must survive, which is why it is used for text, source code, spreadsheets, and archives.</p>

      <h3>A worked example: run-length encoding</h3>
      <p>Run-length encoding (RLE) is the clearest way to see lossless compression happen. It scans the data left to right and replaces each <strong>run</strong> of identical symbols with a <strong>count</strong> followed by the <strong>symbol</strong>. Watch it compress an 8-character string:</p>
      <div class="mcq-code">Original (8 characters):   A A A A A B B B
                           |---- 5 A ----| |-3 B-|
Encoded (4 characters):    5A3B
Decoded back:              AAAAABBB   (exactly the original)</div>
      <p>The five A characters become <code>5A</code> and the three B characters become <code>3B</code>, so <code>AAAAABBB</code> shrinks to <code>5A3B</code>: from 8 characters down to 4, a saving of 4. Crucially, the counts and symbols carry everything needed to rebuild the string, so decoding returns <code>AAAAABBB</code> perfectly. That exact-recovery guarantee is what makes RLE lossless.</p>
      <div class="callout-trap">
        <div class="callout-trap-label">⚠ Redundancy is what RLE feeds on</div>
        <p>RLE only helps when there are long runs. Encode <code>ABABAB</code> and you get <code>1A1B1A1B1A1B</code>, which is <strong>longer</strong> than the original because there is no redundancy to remove. This is the general rule in miniature: compression pays off in proportion to how much repetition the data actually contains.</p>
      </div>

      <div class="mini-ex">
        <div class="mini-ex-label">✍ Mini Exercise 1 • Predict first</div>
        <div class="mini-ex-q">A file is compressed, stored, and later decompressed. The decompressed file is confirmed to be bit-for-bit identical to the original. Which statement must be true?</div>
        <div class="mini-opts" id="me1-opts">
          <button class="mini-opt" onclick="miniMCQ('me1','A','C','me1-fb')"><span class="mini-opt-letter">A</span> A lossy method was used, since only lossy can shrink files</button>
          <button class="mini-opt" onclick="miniMCQ('me1','B','C','me1-fb')"><span class="mini-opt-letter">B</span> The file contained no redundancy before it was compressed</button>
          <button class="mini-opt" onclick="miniMCQ('me1','C','C','me1-fb')"><span class="mini-opt-letter">C</span> A lossless method was used, since the exact original was recovered</button>
          <button class="mini-opt" onclick="miniMCQ('me1','D','C','me1-fb')"><span class="mini-opt-letter">D</span> The compressed file must have been larger than the original</button>
        </div>
        <div class="mini-fb" id="me1-fb"></div>
      </div>
    </div>

    <div class="lesson-section">
      <h2>Lossy Compression</h2>
      <p><strong>Lossy compression</strong> can reduce the number of bits far more than lossless, but it does so by <strong>permanently discarding some of the data</strong>. Once compressed, the exact original <strong>cannot</strong> be reconstructed; decompressing gives back an approximation, not a perfect copy. The classic lossy formats are <strong>JPEG</strong> for photos and <strong>MP3</strong> for audio. They work by throwing away detail a human is unlikely to notice, such as subtle color shifts or sounds masked by louder ones, so the file gets much smaller while still looking or sounding acceptable.</p>
      <p>Lossy is the right tool when transmission and storage efficiency matter more than a perfect reproduction, and when a person perceiving the media will tolerate the loss. That describes most photos, music, and video on the web. It is the wrong tool the instant an exact copy is required, because the discarded data is gone for good and no amount of decompressing brings it back.</p>
      <div class="callout-trap">
        <div class="callout-trap-label">⚠ The one-way door</div>
        <p>Lossy loss is <strong>permanent</strong>. Saving a JPEG at high compression and later "saving it again at full quality" does not restore the detail; that detail no longer exists in the file. Re-compressing a lossy file repeatedly only degrades it further. Treat lossy as a door that opens one way only.</p>
      </div>

      <div class="mini-ex">
        <div class="mini-ex-label">✍ Mini Exercise 2 • Spot the flawed reasoning</div>
        <div class="mini-ex-q">A student says: "Lossy compression is strictly better than lossless because it makes files smaller." Which choice best identifies the flaw in that reasoning?</div>
        <div class="mini-opts" id="me2-opts">
          <button class="mini-opt" onclick="miniMCQ('me2','A','B','me2-fb')"><span class="mini-opt-letter">A</span> The reasoning is sound, because a smaller file is always the better outcome</button>
          <button class="mini-opt" onclick="miniMCQ('me2','B','B','me2-fb')"><span class="mini-opt-letter">B</span> It ignores that lossy discards data permanently, so it fails when the exact original is required</button>
          <button class="mini-opt" onclick="miniMCQ('me2','C','B','me2-fb')"><span class="mini-opt-letter">C</span> It is wrong because lossy compression actually produces larger files than lossless</button>
          <button class="mini-opt" onclick="miniMCQ('me2','D','B','me2-fb')"><span class="mini-opt-letter">D</span> It is wrong because lossless compression can never reduce a file at all</button>
        </div>
        <div class="mini-fb" id="me2-fb"></div>
      </div>
    </div>

    <div class="lesson-section">
      <h2>The Size-versus-Quality Trade-off</h2>
      <p>Choosing a compression method is a trade-off between <strong>size</strong> and <strong>fidelity</strong> (how faithful the copy is to the original). Lossless keeps perfect fidelity but reduces size less. Lossy sacrifices some fidelity to reduce size much more. Neither is "better" in the abstract; the right choice depends entirely on what the data is for.</p>
      <p>A reliable way to decide is to ask one question: <strong>must the reconstructed data be exactly the original?</strong></p>
      <ul>
        <li>
<strong>If yes, use lossless.</strong> Text, source code, spreadsheets, executable programs, legal contracts, and medical scans all break or lose meaning if a single value changes. When the data must be reconstructed exactly, lossless is preferred.</li>
        <li>
<strong>If no, lossy is often the smart choice.</strong> For photos, music, and video that a human will simply view or hear, lossy delivers a much smaller file at a quality the person will accept, which is why it dominates streaming and the web.</li>
      </ul>
      <div class="callout-exam">
        <div class="callout-exam-label">🎯 How the exam frames it</div>
        <p>Scenario questions almost always hinge on one clue: does the situation demand a perfect copy or just a good-enough one? "Archive," "legal record," "source code," and "must be recovered exactly" point to lossless. "Stream," "download quickly," "small thumbnail," and "a listener or viewer" point to lossy. Read the stem for that clue before you look at the options.</p>
      </div>

      <div class="mini-ex">
        <div class="mini-ex-label">✍ Mini Exercise 3 • Encode it yourself</div>
        <div class="mini-ex-q">Using run-length encoding (count then symbol for each run), what is the encoding of the string <code>AAAAABBB</code>? Type it with no spaces.</div>
        <div class="mini-fib-row">
          <span style="font-size:14px;color:#374151;">encoding:</span>
          <input type="text" class="mini-fib-input" id="me3-inp" placeholder="?">
          <button class="mini-fib-btn" onclick="miniFIB('me3','me3-fb')">Check</button>
        </div>
        <div class="mini-fb" id="me3-fb"></div>
      </div>
    </div>

    <div class="lesson-section">
      <h2>Key Vocabulary</h2>
      <table class="vocab-table">
        <thead><tr>
<th>Term</th>
<th>Definition</th>
<th>Example</th>
</tr></thead>
        <tbody>
          <tr>
<td>Data compression</td>
<td>Reducing the number of bits used to store or transmit data</td>
<td>Zipping a folder before emailing it</td>
</tr>
          <tr>
<td>Redundancy</td>
<td>Repeated or predictable patterns in data that compression can remove</td>
<td>A long run of the same pixel color</td>
</tr>
          <tr>
<td>Lossless</td>
<td>Compression that guarantees the original can be reconstructed exactly</td>
<td>ZIP, PNG, RLE</td>
</tr>
          <tr>
<td>Lossy</td>
<td>Compression that permanently discards data for a much smaller file</td>
<td>JPEG, MP3</td>
</tr>
          <tr>
<td>Run-length encoding</td>
<td>A lossless method that replaces each run of repeats with count + symbol</td>
<td>
<code>AAAAABBB</code> becomes <code>5A3B</code>
</td>
</tr>
          <tr>
<td>Reconstruction</td>
<td>Rebuilding the data from its compressed form when decompressing</td>
<td>Unzipping restores every byte</td>
</tr>
          <tr>
<td>Trade-off</td>
<td>Balancing smaller file size against loss of quality or detail</td>
<td>Lower JPEG quality for a smaller photo</td>
</tr>
        </tbody>
      </table>

    <div class="cpt-connection">
      <div class="cpt-connection-label">📋 Create Performance Task • Where data choices earn points</div>
      <p>The Create Task is a program you build, and your written response has to explain how the program manages data. You will not compress files by hand, but the same reasoning you just practiced, choosing a representation that fits the purpose, is exactly what graders want to see described clearly. When your program stores or moves data, the format you pick is a decision you can justify.</p>
      <h3>What a clear data explanation sounds like</h3>
      <p>Suppose your Create Task saves a list of user scores and reads them back later:</p>
      <div class="cpt-code">scores <- [88, 92, 75, 100]
DISPLAY(scores)</div>
      <p>A response earns credit when it names the data, states how it is stored, and ties that choice to the program's purpose. The habit is the same one compression teaches: match the representation to what the data is for.</p>
      <ul class="cpt-stems">
        <li>"The list <code>scores</code> stores each user's results so the program can display and total them later."</li>
        <li>"Because every score must be kept exactly, the data is stored without any loss, the way lossless compression preserves the original values."</li>
        <li>"Choosing a list lets the program handle any number of scores, which is how it manages the complexity of varied input."</li>
      </ul>
      <h3>The idea that carries over</h3>
      <p>Compression is a concrete case of a bigger CSP theme: data must be represented in a way that fits its use. Exact-copy data (text, records, code) is kept losslessly; human-perceived media (images, sound) can accept lossy trade-offs. Being able to state <em>why</em> a representation fits the purpose is what turns a vague answer into a point-earning one. <a href="/pages/ap-csp-course-create-task">See the full Create Task module →</a></p>

      <div class="mcq-item" data-activity="quiz" data-item="q1">
        <div class="mcq-q-num">Question 1 of 6<span class="diff-tag">Spot the flaw</span>
</div>
        <div class="predict-note">Predict first: decide what is wrong with the claim before you read the choices.</div>
        <div class="mcq-q-text">A student argues: "Run-length encoding is lossy, because the encoded string <code>5A3B</code> has fewer characters than <code>AAAAABBB</code>, and fewer characters means information was lost." Which choice best identifies the error in this argument?</div>
        <div class="mcq-options" id="q1-options">
<button class="mcq-option" onclick="checkMCQ('q1','A','B','q1-fb-A')"><span class="mcq-option-letter">A</span> The argument is correct; any method that removes characters is lossy</button>
<button class="mcq-option" onclick="checkMCQ('q1','B','B','q1-fb-B')"><span class="mcq-option-letter">B</span> The error is equating fewer characters with lost information; the exact original is still fully recoverable</button>
<button class="mcq-option" onclick="checkMCQ('q1','C','B','q1-fb-C')"><span class="mcq-option-letter">C</span> The error is the claim that <code>5A3B</code> is shorter; it is actually longer than the original</button>
<button class="mcq-option" onclick="checkMCQ('q1','D','B','q1-fb-D')"><span class="mcq-option-letter">D</span> The error is that RLE cannot be applied to a string of letters at all</button>
</div>
<div id="q1-fb-A" class="mcq-feedback incorrect-fb">Incorrect. Removing characters is not what makes a method lossy; discarding recoverable information is. RLE removes redundancy while keeping everything needed to rebuild the original.</div>
<div id="q1-fb-B" class="mcq-feedback correct-fb">Correct. Fewer bits does not mean less information. RLE removes only redundancy, and <code>5A3B</code> decodes back to <code>AAAAABBB</code> exactly, so nothing was lost and the method is lossless.</div>
<div id="q1-fb-C" class="mcq-feedback incorrect-fb">Incorrect. <code>5A3B</code> is 4 characters and <code>AAAAABBB</code> is 8, so the encoded form really is shorter. The flaw is elsewhere in the reasoning.</div>
<div id="q1-fb-D" class="mcq-feedback incorrect-fb">Incorrect. RLE applies to any sequence of symbols, including letters. That is not the flaw in the argument.</div>
      </div>
      <div class="mcq-item" data-activity="quiz" data-item="q2">
        <div class="mcq-q-num">Question 2 of 6<span class="diff-tag">I, II, III</span>
</div>
        <div class="mcq-q-text">A team needs a compression method that guarantees the original data can be reconstructed exactly. Which of the following formats satisfy that requirement?</div>
        <ul class="mcq-roman">
          <li>
<strong>I.</strong> Saving a diagram as a PNG image</li>
          <li>
<strong>II.</strong> Compressing a folder of documents into a ZIP file</li>
          <li>
<strong>III.</strong> Saving a photograph as a JPEG image</li>
        </ul>
        <div class="mcq-options" id="q2-options">
<button class="mcq-option" onclick="checkMCQ('q2','A','D','q2-fb-A')"><span class="mcq-option-letter">A</span> I only</button>
<button class="mcq-option" onclick="checkMCQ('q2','B','D','q2-fb-B')"><span class="mcq-option-letter">B</span> II and III only</button>
<button class="mcq-option" onclick="checkMCQ('q2','C','D','q2-fb-C')"><span class="mcq-option-letter">C</span> I, II, and III</button>
<button class="mcq-option" onclick="checkMCQ('q2','D','D','q2-fb-D')"><span class="mcq-option-letter">D</span> I and II only</button>
</div>
<div id="q2-fb-A" class="mcq-feedback incorrect-fb">Incorrect. PNG (I) is lossless, but ZIP (II) is lossless too, so I alone is incomplete.</div>
<div id="q2-fb-B" class="mcq-feedback incorrect-fb">Incorrect. JPEG (III) is lossy, so it cannot guarantee exact reconstruction. II is lossless, but it must pair with I, not III.</div>
<div id="q2-fb-C" class="mcq-feedback incorrect-fb">Incorrect. JPEG (III) is lossy and cannot rebuild the original exactly. Only the lossless formats, I and II, satisfy the requirement.</div>
<div id="q2-fb-D" class="mcq-feedback correct-fb">Correct. PNG and ZIP are both lossless, so each guarantees exact reconstruction. JPEG (III) is lossy and permanently discards data, so it fails the requirement.</div>
      </div>
      <div class="mcq-item" data-activity="quiz" data-item="q3">
        <div class="mcq-q-num">Question 3 of 6<span class="diff-tag">NOT question</span>
</div>
        <div class="mcq-q-text">Which of the following is <strong>NOT</strong> a property of lossy compression?</div>
        <div class="mcq-options" id="q3-options">
<button class="mcq-option" onclick="checkMCQ('q3','A','D','q3-fb-A')"><span class="mcq-option-letter">A</span> It can reach smaller file sizes than lossless for the same media</button>
<button class="mcq-option" onclick="checkMCQ('q3','B','D','q3-fb-B')"><span class="mcq-option-letter">B</span> The data it removes cannot be recovered by decompressing</button>
<button class="mcq-option" onclick="checkMCQ('q3','C','D','q3-fb-C')"><span class="mcq-option-letter">C</span> It is well suited to streaming photos, music, and video</button>
<button class="mcq-option" onclick="checkMCQ('q3','D','D','q3-fb-D')"><span class="mcq-option-letter">D</span> The original data can always be reconstructed exactly</button>
</div>
<div id="q3-fb-A" class="mcq-feedback incorrect-fb">Incorrect. This IS a property of lossy compression, so it is not the answer. Lossy can achieve smaller sizes precisely because it discards data.</div>
<div id="q3-fb-B" class="mcq-feedback incorrect-fb">Incorrect. This IS true of lossy compression: what it discards is gone permanently. The question asks for the property that does not fit.</div>
<div id="q3-fb-C" class="mcq-feedback incorrect-fb">Incorrect. This IS a property of lossy compression, which dominates streaming media. Look for the statement that describes lossless instead.</div>
<div id="q3-fb-D" class="mcq-feedback correct-fb">Correct. Exact reconstruction is a property of lossless, not lossy. Lossy permanently discards data, so the original cannot be rebuilt exactly, which makes this the statement that does NOT belong.</div>
      </div>
      <div class="mcq-item" data-activity="quiz" data-item="q4">
        <div class="mcq-q-num">Question 4 of 6<span class="diff-tag">Best use case</span>
</div>
        <div class="predict-note">Predict first: does this scenario demand a perfect copy or just a good-enough one?</div>
        <div class="mcq-q-text">A hospital must store an MRI scan that radiologists will later zoom into to make a diagnosis. Which compression choice is best, and why?</div>
        <div class="mcq-options" id="q4-options">
<button class="mcq-option" onclick="checkMCQ('q4','A','A','q4-fb-A')"><span class="mcq-option-letter">A</span> Lossless, because no diagnostic detail can be discarded</button>
<button class="mcq-option" onclick="checkMCQ('q4','B','A','q4-fb-B')"><span class="mcq-option-letter">B</span> Lossy, because a smaller file is faster to transfer between systems</button>
<button class="mcq-option" onclick="checkMCQ('q4','C','A','q4-fb-C')"><span class="mcq-option-letter">C</span> Lossy, because the scan will be viewed only a single time</button>
<button class="mcq-option" onclick="checkMCQ('q4','D','A','q4-fb-D')"><span class="mcq-option-letter">D</span> Lossless, because lossless always produces the smallest possible file</button>
</div>
<div id="q4-fb-A" class="mcq-feedback correct-fb">Correct. Diagnosis depends on exact detail, so the data must be reconstructed exactly. That requires lossless compression, which preserves every value.</div>
<div id="q4-fb-B" class="mcq-feedback incorrect-fb">Incorrect. Faster transfer does not justify discarding detail here. A lossy artifact could hide or invent something clinically important, so the smaller size is not worth it.</div>
<div id="q4-fb-C" class="mcq-feedback incorrect-fb">Incorrect. How often the scan is viewed is irrelevant; what matters is that the detail must be exact each time it is examined, which requires lossless.</div>
<div id="q4-fb-D" class="mcq-feedback incorrect-fb">Incorrect. The choice of lossless is right, but the reason is wrong. Lossless does not produce the smallest file; lossy usually produces smaller files. Lossless is chosen to preserve exact detail.</div>
      </div>
      <div class="mcq-item" data-activity="quiz" data-item="q5">
        <div class="mcq-q-num">Question 5 of 6<span class="diff-tag">Best use case</span>
</div>
        <div class="mcq-q-text">A music app must stream a 3-minute song over a limited mobile data connection while keeping the sound acceptable to listeners. Which choice is best, and why?</div>
        <div class="mcq-options" id="q5-options">
<button class="mcq-option" onclick="checkMCQ('q5','A','B','q5-fb-A')"><span class="mcq-option-letter">A</span> Lossless, because audio must be reconstructed bit for bit to be usable</button>
<button class="mcq-option" onclick="checkMCQ('q5','B','B','q5-fb-B')"><span class="mcq-option-letter">B</span> Lossy, because discarding barely audible detail greatly shrinks the file at a quality listeners accept</button>
<button class="mcq-option" onclick="checkMCQ('q5','C','B','q5-fb-C')"><span class="mcq-option-letter">C</span> Lossy, because it reconstructs the original waveform perfectly while shrinking it</button>
<button class="mcq-option" onclick="checkMCQ('q5','D','B','q5-fb-D')"><span class="mcq-option-letter">D</span> Lossless, because it produces the smallest file for streaming over limited data</button>
</div>
<div id="q5-fb-A" class="mcq-feedback incorrect-fb">Incorrect. Music for listening does not need bit-for-bit reconstruction. Insisting on it would waste bandwidth the scenario says is limited.</div>
<div id="q5-fb-B" class="mcq-feedback correct-fb">Correct. Efficiency matters more than a perfect copy here, and a listener will not notice the discarded detail. Lossy shrinks the file a lot while keeping acceptable quality, which is why streaming uses it.</div>
<div id="q5-fb-C" class="mcq-feedback incorrect-fb">Incorrect. The choice of lossy is right, but the reason is false. Lossy does NOT reconstruct the original perfectly; it discards data permanently. That is exactly why the file is smaller.</div>
<div id="q5-fb-D" class="mcq-feedback incorrect-fb">Incorrect. Lossless does not give the smallest file; lossy does. For acceptable-quality streaming over limited data, lossy is the better fit.</div>
      </div>
      <div class="mcq-item" data-activity="quiz" data-item="q6">
        <div class="mcq-q-num">Question 6 of 6<span class="diff-tag">Compare algorithms</span>
</div>
        <div class="mcq-q-text">Two different <strong>lossless</strong> algorithms compress the same text file. Algorithm X produces a 40 KB file and Algorithm Y produces a 55 KB file. Which statement is best supported?</div>
        <div class="mcq-options" id="q6-options">
<button class="mcq-option" onclick="checkMCQ('q6','A','A','q6-fb-A')"><span class="mcq-option-letter">A</span> Both files decompress to the exact original text, and X achieved more size reduction here</button>
<button class="mcq-option" onclick="checkMCQ('q6','B','A','q6-fb-B')"><span class="mcq-option-letter">B</span> Algorithm Y discarded more of the original data than Algorithm X did</button>
<button class="mcq-option" onclick="checkMCQ('q6','C','A','q6-fb-C')"><span class="mcq-option-letter">C</span> Algorithm X must actually be lossy, since its file is smaller</button>
<button class="mcq-option" onclick="checkMCQ('q6','D','A','q6-fb-D')"><span class="mcq-option-letter">D</span> Only Algorithm Y can recover the original text, because a larger file keeps more detail</button>
</div>
<div id="q6-fb-A" class="mcq-feedback correct-fb">Correct. Lossless means both outputs rebuild the original text exactly, regardless of size. X simply removed more redundancy on this file, so it compressed better here.</div>
<div id="q6-fb-B" class="mcq-feedback incorrect-fb">Incorrect. Both algorithms are lossless, so neither discards original data. A smaller output reflects better compression of redundancy, not lost content.</div>
<div id="q6-fb-C" class="mcq-feedback incorrect-fb">Incorrect. A smaller file does not make a method lossy. The problem states both algorithms are lossless, so X is lossless and just compressed more effectively.</div>
<div id="q6-fb-D" class="mcq-feedback incorrect-fb">Incorrect. Both are lossless, so both recover the original exactly. File size does not determine whether the original can be rebuilt.</div>
      </div>
    </div>

(function(){
  var TOTAL = 8;
  var score = 0, streak = 0, round = 0, locked = false;

  // Use-case bank for "choose the method" rounds.
  var USE = [
    {t:'Archive a signed legal contract PDF for the records.', a:'lossless',
     why:'Legal records must stay bit-for-bit identical, so use lossless. Every character and signature detail has to survive.'},
    {t:'Stream a 4 minute pop song to a phone over cellular data.', a:'lossy',
     why:'Audio streaming uses lossy (like MP3/AAC). Discarding sounds the ear barely notices shrinks the file a lot with acceptable quality loss.'},
    {t:'Send a tiny meme thumbnail in a group chat.', a:'lossy',
     why:'A small thumbnail can use lossy (JPEG). Minor quality loss is fine and the smaller size sends faster.'},
    {t:'Store a diagnostic X-ray a doctor will zoom into.', a:'lossless',
     why:'Medical images use lossless so no diagnostic detail is discarded. A lossy artifact could hide or fake something clinically important.'},
    {t:'Zip a folder of source code before emailing it.', a:'lossless',
     why:'Source code must be lossless. Losing even one character breaks the program, so nothing can be discarded.'},
    {t:'Upload a high-resolution vacation photo to social media.', a:'lossy',
     why:'Photos for the web use lossy (JPEG) to cut size for fast loading. A small, hard-to-see quality drop is acceptable.'},
    {t:'Back up a spreadsheet of bank account balances.', a:'lossless',
     why:'Financial data must be lossless. An altered digit would corrupt the numbers, so every bit has to be recoverable.'},
    {t:'Compress a voice memo reminder for yourself.', a:'lossy',
     why:'A casual voice memo can use lossy. You only need to understand the words, so discarding fine audio detail is fine.'},
    {t:'Save the raw text of a novel manuscript.', a:'lossless',
     why:'Text should be lossless. Every word must be recovered exactly, and text compresses well without dropping anything.'},
    {t:'Deliver background video for a website hero banner.', a:'lossy',
     why:'Web video uses lossy codecs to keep files small enough to stream. Slight quality loss is worth the smaller size.'}
  ];

  // RLE strings by difficulty tier.
  var RLE_EASY = ['AAAABBB','WWWWWW','XXXYY','QQQQQZ'];
  var RLE_MED = ['AAAABBBCCDAAA','MMMNNNNPP','RRRRRRSSSTT','KKLLLLLLMM'];
  var RLE_HARD = ['AAAAABBBBBBCCDDDDA','ZZZZWWXXXXXXXYY','GGGGGGGHHIIIIJJJJ','TTTTTUUUVVVVVVWWX'];

  var el = function(id){ return document.getElementById(id); };

  function rleEncode(s){
    var out='', i=0;
    while(i<s.length){
      var c=s[i], n=1;
      while(i+n<s.length && s[i+n]===c) n++;
      out += n + c; i += n;
    }
    return out;
  }
  function rleUnits(s){ // number of runs
    var i=0,u=0;
    while(i<s.length){ var c=s[i],n=1; while(i+n<s.length && s[i+n]===c) n++; u++; i+=n; }
    return u;
  }

  function shuffle(arr){
    for(var i=arr.length-1;i>0;i--){ var j=Math.floor(Math.random()*(i+1)); var t=arr[i];arr[i]=arr[j];arr[j]=t; }
    return arr;
  }

  // Build the sequence of rounds: interleave choose and rle, escalating.
  var sequence = [];
  function buildSequence(){
    sequence = [];
    var uses = shuffle(USE.slice()).slice(0, 4);
    var easy = shuffle(RLE_EASY.slice());
    var med = shuffle(RLE_MED.slice());
    var hard = shuffle(RLE_HARD.slice());
    var rle = [easy[0], med[0], med[1], hard[0]];
    // Interleave: choose, rle, choose, rle ...
    for(var i=0;i<4;i++){
      sequence.push({kind:'choose', data:uses[i]});
      sequence.push({kind:'rle', data:rle[i]});
    }
  }

  function setBar(){
    el('cc-score').textContent = score;
    el('cc-streak').textContent = streak;
    el('cc-round').textContent = Math.min(round+1, TOTAL);
    el('cc-streakbox').className = 'cc-stat' + (streak>=2 ? ' hot' : '');
    el('cc-progbar').style.width = (round/TOTAL*100) + '%';
  }

  function clearUI(){
    el('cc-opts').innerHTML = '';
    el('cc-datawrap').innerHTML = '';
    var fb = el('cc-fb'); fb.className='cc-fb'; fb.innerHTML='';
    el('cc-next').className = 'cc-btn cc-hidden';
    var note = el('cc-note'); note.className='cc-note cc-hidden'; note.textContent='';
  }

  function renderChoose(item){
    el('cc-tagtype').className='cc-tag choose';
    el('cc-tagtype').textContent='Choose the method';
    el('cc-q').textContent = item.t;
    var wrap = el('cc-opts'); wrap.className='cc-opts two';
    var opts = [
      {k:'lossless', label:'LOSSLESS', sub:'fully reversible, no data lost'},
      {k:'lossy', label:'LOSSY', sub:'much smaller, some data discarded'}
    ];
    opts.forEach(function(o){
      var b=document.createElement('button');
      b.className='cc-opt'; b.type='button';
      b.innerHTML = o.label + '<small>' + o.sub + '</small>';
      b.onclick = function(){ answerChoose(o.k, item, wrap); };
      wrap.appendChild(b);
    });
  }

  function answerChoose(pick, item, wrap){
    if(locked) return; locked=true;
    var correct = item.a;
    Array.prototype.forEach.call(wrap.children, function(b){
      b.disabled=true;
      var isThis = b.textContent.indexOf(pick==='lossless'?'LOSSLESS':'LOSSY')===0;
      var isCorrect = b.textContent.indexOf(correct==='lossless'?'LOSSLESS':'LOSSY')===0;
      if(isCorrect) b.classList.add('good');
      else if(isThis) b.classList.add('bad');
      else b.classList.add('dim');
    });
    resolve(pick===correct, item.why);
  }

  function renderRle(str){
    el('cc-tagtype').className='cc-tag rle';
    el('cc-tagtype').textContent='Run-length encoding';
    var enc = rleEncode(str);
    var units = rleUnits(str);
    var orig = str.length;
    var comp = enc.length;
    var mode = Math.random()<0.5 ? 'encode' : 'saved';

    el('cc-datawrap').innerHTML = '<div class="cc-data">' + str + '</div>';
    var note = el('cc-note'); note.className='cc-note';
    note.textContent = 'RLE replaces each run of repeats with count + symbol. Original is ' + orig + ' characters.';

    var wrap = el('cc-opts'); wrap.className='cc-opts';
    var correctVal, options, why;

    if(mode==='encode'){
      el('cc-q').textContent = 'What is the run-length encoding of this string?';
      correctVal = enc;
      // distractors
      var d1 = enc.replace(/(\d+)/, function(m){ return String(Math.max(1,parseInt(m,10)-1)); }); // off by one on first count
      var d2 = wrongOrder(str); // symbol then count
      var d3 = dropRun(str); // merge/miss a run
      options = uniq([correctVal, d1, d2, d3]);
      why = 'The RLE is ' + enc + '. Read left to right, writing count then symbol for each run. RLE is lossless: the original is fully rebuilt with no data lost.';
    } else {
      el('cc-q').textContent = 'The encoded form is ' + comp + ' characters. How many characters are saved versus the original?';
      correctVal = String(orig - comp);
      var s = orig - comp;
      options = uniq([String(s), String(s+1), String(Math.max(0,s-2)), String(orig-units)]);
      why = 'Original ' + orig + ' minus encoded ' + comp + ' equals ' + (orig-comp) + ' characters saved. RLE shrinks files by removing redundancy, and it stays lossless.';
    }

    options = shuffle(options).slice(0,4);
    if(options.indexOf(correctVal)<0){ options[0]=correctVal; options=shuffle(options); }

    options.forEach(function(o){
      var b=document.createElement('button');
      b.className='cc-opt'; b.type='button';
      b.style.fontFamily='"DM Sans",monospace';
      b.textContent=o;
      b.onclick=function(){ answerRle(o, correctVal, why, wrap); };
      wrap.appendChild(b);
    });
  }

  function wrongOrder(s){
    var out='',i=0;
    while(i<s.length){ var c=s[i],n=1; while(i+n<s.length && s[i+n]===c) n++; out+=c+n; i+=n; }
    return out;
  }
  function dropRun(s){
    var enc = rleEncode(s);
    // remove the first run's digit-symbol pair to simulate a missed run
    return enc.replace(/^\d+[A-Z]/, '');
  }
  function uniq(a){ var seen={},out=[]; a.forEach(function(x){ if(x!=null && x!=='' && !seen[x]){ seen[x]=1; out.push(x);} }); return out; }

  function answerRle(pick, correctVal, why, wrap){
    if(locked) return; locked=true;
    Array.prototype.forEach.call(wrap.children, function(b){
      b.disabled=true;
      if(b.textContent===correctVal) b.classList.add('good');
      else if(b.textContent===pick) b.classList.add('bad');
      else b.classList.add('dim');
    });
    resolve(pick===correctVal, why);
  }

  function resolve(correct, why){
    var fb = el('cc-fb');
    var pts = 0;
    if(correct){
      streak++;
      pts = 10 + (round*2) + Math.min(streak-1,5)*3; // escalating + streak bonus
      score += pts;
      fb.className='cc-fb show ok';
      fb.innerHTML = '✔ Correct! +' + pts + ' points' + (streak>=2?(' (streak x'+streak+')'):'') + '<br>' + why;
    } else {
      streak = 0;
      fb.className='cc-fb show no';
      fb.innerHTML = '✘ Not quite. ' + why;
    }
    setBar();
    var nb = el('cc-next');
    nb.className='cc-btn';
    nb.innerHTML = (round+1>=TOTAL) ? 'See results ▶' : 'Next round ▶';
  }

  function showRound(){
    clearUI();
    locked=false;
    setBar();
    var r = sequence[round];
    if(r.kind==='choose') renderChoose(r.data);
    else renderRle(r.data);
  }

  function nextRound(){
    round++;
    if(round>=TOTAL){ endGame(); return; }
    showRound();
  }

  function endGame(){
    el('cc-play').classList.add('cc-hidden');
    el('cc-progbar').style.width='100%';
    var es = el('cc-endscreen'); es.classList.remove('cc-hidden');
    el('cc-endscore').textContent = score;
    var title, msg;
    if(score>=140){ title='Compression Master!'; }
    else if(score>=90){ title='Strong work!'; }
    else { title='Good run!'; }
    el('cc-endtitle').textContent = title;
    msg = 'Key idea: lossless (RLE, ZIP, PNG) is fully reversible and needed when every bit matters. ' +
          'Lossy (JPEG, MP3) discards data for much smaller files when a little quality loss is fine. ' +
          'RLE shows how lossless compression works: it removes redundancy without losing anything.';
    el('cc-endmsg').textContent = msg;
    // fire final score for the leaderboard
    document.dispatchEvent(new CustomEvent('apcsGameScore',{detail:{value:score}}));
  }

  function reset(){
    score=0; streak=0; round=0; locked=false;
    buildSequence();
    el('cc-endscreen').classList.add('cc-hidden');
    el('cc-play').classList.remove('cc-hidden');
    showRound();
  }

  el('cc-next').onclick = nextRound;
  el('cc-again').onclick = reset;

  buildSequence();
  showRound();
})();
</script>

    <div class="faq-section">
      <h2>Frequently Asked Questions</h2>
      <div class="faq-item">
        <button class="faq-q" onclick="toggleFAQ(this)">What is the difference between lossless and lossy compression?<i class="faq-icon">+</i></button>
        <div class="faq-a">Lossless compression reduces the number of bits while guaranteeing that the original data can be reconstructed exactly, bit for bit. Lossy compression can reduce size much more, but it permanently discards some data, so the exact original can never be recovered. <code>ZIP</code>, <code>PNG</code>, and run-length encoding are lossless; <code>JPEG</code> and <code>MP3</code> are lossy.</div>
      </div>
      <div class="faq-item">
        <button class="faq-q" onclick="toggleFAQ(this)">Does fewer bits always mean less information?<i class="faq-icon">+</i></button>
        <div class="faq-a">No. Lossless compression removes redundancy, not information, so a smaller file can still hold all of the original information and be rebuilt exactly. Only lossy compression actually throws information away. This is why fewer bits does not automatically mean less information.</div>
      </div>
      <div class="faq-item">
        <button class="faq-q" onclick="toggleFAQ(this)">How does run-length encoding work?<i class="faq-icon">+</i></button>
        <div class="faq-a">Run-length encoding is a lossless method that replaces each run of repeated symbols with a count followed by the symbol. For example, <code>AAAAABBB</code> has a run of five A characters and a run of three B characters, so it encodes to <code>5A3B</code>. Because the counts and symbols are kept, the original can be rebuilt exactly, which makes it lossless.</div>
      </div>
      <div class="faq-item">
        <button class="faq-q" onclick="toggleFAQ(this)">When should I choose lossy compression over lossless?<i class="faq-icon">+</i></button>
        <div class="faq-a">Choose lossy when smaller size and faster transmission matter more than a perfect copy, and when a human viewer or listener will not notice the discarded detail. Streaming music, web photos, and video use lossy for this reason. Choose lossless when the data must be reconstructed exactly, such as text, source code, spreadsheets, and legal or medical records.</div>
      </div>
      <div class="faq-item">
        <button class="faq-q" onclick="toggleFAQ(this)">What decides how much a file shrinks when compressed?<i class="faq-icon">+</i></button>
        <div class="faq-a">The amount of size reduction depends on both how much redundancy the original data contains and which compression method is used. Data with long runs or repeated patterns compresses a great deal, while data that is already varied or random compresses very little no matter the algorithm.</div>
      </div>

<script>
var MINI_MSGS={"me1": {"A": "\u2717 Lossy is not the only way to shrink a file; lossless shrinks files too. And lossy could never return a bit-for-bit identical copy, so this cannot be lossy.", "B": "\u2717 Redundancy is what compression removes, but its presence or absence is not what this tells you.   .lesson-breadcrumb-inner{max-width:880px;margin:0 auto;display:flex;align-items:center;gap:8px;font-size:13px;color:var(--slate);flex-wrap:wrap;}
  .lesson-breadcrumb a{color:var(--bi3)!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:var(--bi3)!important;text-decoration:none;font-weight:500;}
  .bc-sep{color:#cbd5e1;}

  .social-proof-bar{background:#fff;border-bottom:1px solid #e2e8f0;padding:10px 24px;}
  .social-proof-inner{max-width:880px;margin:0 auto;display:flex;flex-wrap:wrap;align-items:center;gap:6px 20px;font-size:13px;color:var(--slate);}
  .social-proof-item{display:flex;align-items:center;gap:5px;font-weight:500;}
  .social-proof-item strong{color:var(--navy)!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:var(--navy)!important;}

  .lesson-hero{background:var(--navy);background-image:radial-gradient(ellipse 60% 70% at 90% 20%,rgba(26,86,219,.28) 0%,transparent 60%);padding:48px 24px 40px;}
  .lesson-hero-inner{max-width:880px;margin:0 auto;}
  .lesson-hero-meta{display:flex;align-items:center;gap:10px;flex-wrap:wrap;margin-bottom:16px;}
  .lesson-num-badge{display:inline-flex;align-items:center;justify-content:center;width:44px;height:44px;border-radius:10px;background:var(--bi3);font-weight:700;font-size:14px;color:#fff!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:#fff!important;flex-shrink:0;}
  .lesson-eyebrow{font-size:12px;font-weight:700;letter-spacing:.08em;text-transform:uppercase;color:var(--bi3-lt)!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:var(--bi3-lt)!important;}
  .lesson-hero h1{font-family:"DM Serif Display",serif!important;font-size:clamp(26px,4vw,40px)!important;line-height:1.2!important;color:#fff!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:#fff!important;margin-bottom:14px!important;}
  .lesson-hero-pills{display:flex;flex-wrap:wrap;gap:8px;}
  .lesson-pill{display:inline-flex;align-items:center;gap:5px;background:rgba(255,255,255,.08);border:1px solid rgba(255,255,255,.15);padding:5px 12px;border-radius:100px;font-size:12px;color:#e2e8f0!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:#e2e8f0!important;}
  .ced-tag{display:inline-flex;align-items:center;background:rgba(26,86,219,.25);border:1px solid rgba(147,197,253,.3);padding:4px 10px;border-radius:100px;font-size:11px;font-weight:600;color:#bfdbfe!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:#bfdbfe!important;letter-spacing:.04em;}

  /* PROGRESS STRIP */
  .bi3-progress{background:#fff!important;border-bottom:1px solid #e2e8f0!important;padding:14px 20px!important;overflow-x:auto!important;-webkit-overflow-scrolling:touch!important;}
  .bi3-progress-inner{display:flex!important;flex-direction:row!important;flex-wrap:nowrap!important;align-items:center!important;gap:0!important;width:max-content!important;min-width:100%!important;}
  .prog-step{display:flex!important;flex-direction:column!important;align-items:center!important;min-width:46px!important;text-align:center!important;flex-shrink:0!important;}
  .prog-step-link{display:flex!important;flex-direction:column!important;align-items:center!important;min-width:46px!important;text-align:center!important;flex-shrink:0!important;text-decoration:none!important;cursor:pointer!important;}
  .prog-step-link:hover .prog-dot{background:#dbeafe!important;color:var(--bi3)!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:var(--bi3)!important;border-color:var(--bi3)!important;}
  .prog-dot{width:26px!important;height:26px!important;border-radius:50%!important;display:flex!important;align-items:center!important;justify-content:center!important;font-size:9px!important;font-weight:700!important;margin-bottom:4px!important;flex-shrink:0!important;}
  .prog-dot.active{background:var(--bi3)!important;color:#fff!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:#fff!important;}
  .prog-dot.upcoming{background:#f1f5f9!important;color:#94a3b8!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:#94a3b8!important;border:2px solid #e2e8f0!important;}
  .prog-dot.done{background:#dbeafe!important;color:var(--bi3)!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:var(--bi3)!important;border:2px solid var(--bi3)!important;}
  .prog-label{font-size:8px!important;font-weight:600!important;color:#64748b!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:#64748b!important;line-height:1.2!important;white-space:nowrap!important;}
  .prog-label.active-label{color:var(--bi3)!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:var(--bi3)!important;}
  .prog-arrow{flex:1 0 4px!important;height:2px!important;background:#e2e8f0!important;margin-bottom:18px!important;min-width:4px!important;max-width:16px!important;flex-shrink:0!important;}

  /* MAIN */
  .lesson-main{max-width:880px;margin:0 auto;padding:40px 24px 80px;}
  .lesson-objectives{background:var(--bi3-bg);border-left:4px solid var(--bi3);border-radius:0 10px 10px 0;padding:20px 24px;margin-bottom:28px;}
  .lesson-objectives h2{font-size:14px!important;font-weight:700!important;color:var(--bi3-dk)!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:var(--bi3-dk)!important;text-transform:uppercase!important;letter-spacing:.06em!important;margin-bottom:12px!important;}
  .lesson-objectives ul{list-style:none;padding:0;display:flex;flex-direction:column;gap:8px;}
  .lesson-objectives li{display:flex;align-items:flex-start;gap:10px;font-size:14px;color:#1e3a8a;line-height:1.5;}
  .lesson-objectives li::before{content:"\2713";color:var(--bi3);font-weight:700;flex-shrink:0;margin-top:1px;}
  .score-impact{background:#f0fdf4;border:1px solid #bbf7d0;border-radius:8px;padding:12px 18px;margin-bottom:28px;display:flex;align-items:center;gap:10px;font-size:14px;color:#14532d;}
  .score-impact strong{color:#14532d!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:#14532d!important;}

  /* HOOK */
  .hook-box{background:linear-gradient(135deg,#1e3a8a 0%,#1e40af 100%);border-radius:12px;padding:24px 28px;margin-bottom:32px;}
  .hook-label{font-size:11px;font-weight:700;letter-spacing:.1em;text-transform:uppercase;color:var(--bi3-lt)!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:var(--bi3-lt)!important;margin-bottom:8px;}
  .hook-box p{font-size:15px!important;color:#bfdbfe!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:#bfdbfe!important;line-height:1.7!important;margin-bottom:0!important;}

  /* LESSON SECTIONS */
  .lesson-section{margin-bottom:40px;}
  .lesson-section h2{font-family:"DM Serif Display",serif!important;font-size:24px!important;color:var(--navy)!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:var(--navy)!important;margin-bottom:14px!important;padding-bottom:10px!important;border-bottom:2px solid var(--bi3-bg)!important;}
  .lesson-section h3{font-size:17px!important;font-weight:700!important;color:var(--navy)!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:var(--navy)!important;margin-top:24px!important;margin-bottom:10px!important;}
  .lesson-section p{font-size:15px;color:#374151;line-height:1.8;margin-bottom:14px;}
  .lesson-section ul,.lesson-section ol{padding-left:20px;margin-bottom:14px;}
  .lesson-section li{font-size:15px;color:#374151;line-height:1.7;margin-bottom:6px;}
  .lesson-section code{background:#eef2ff;color:#1e3a8a!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:#1e3a8a!important;padding:1px 6px;border-radius:5px;font-size:13px;}

  /* DUAL CODE PANEL */
  .code-panel-wrap{margin:20px 0;border-radius:12px;overflow:hidden;border:1px solid #e2e8f0;}
  .code-panel-tabs{display:flex;background:#1e293b;}
  .code-tab{padding:8px 16px;font-size:12px;font-weight:700;cursor:pointer;border:none;background:transparent;letter-spacing:.04em;transition:background .15s;font-family:inherit;}
  .code-tab.py{color:#93c5fd!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:#93c5fd!important;}
  .code-tab.pseudo{color:#c4b5fd!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:#c4b5fd!important;}
  .code-tab.active{background:rgba(255,255,255,.15)!important;}
  .code-tab-label{font-size:10px;opacity:.6;margin-left:4px;font-weight:400;}
  .code-pane{background:#0f172a;padding:18px 20px;overflow-x:auto;height:0;overflow:hidden;padding:0;}
  .code-pane.active{height:auto;overflow-x:auto;padding:18px 20px;}
  .code-pane pre{font-family:monospace;font-size:13px;line-height:1.8;margin:0;white-space:pre-wrap;word-break:break-word;max-width:100%;color:#e2e8f0!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:#e2e8f0!important;}
  .py-kw{color:#93c5fd!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:#93c5fd!important;font-weight:700;}
  .py-fn{color:#6ee7b7!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:#6ee7b7!important;}
  .py-num{color:#fde68a!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:#fde68a!important;}
  .py-str{color:#f9a8d4!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:#f9a8d4!important;}
  .py-comment{color:#475569!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:#475569!important;font-style:italic;}
  .py-var{color:#e2e8f0!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:#e2e8f0!important;}
  .py-op{color:#94a3b8!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:#94a3b8!important;}
  .ps-kw{color:#c4b5fd!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:#c4b5fd!important;font-weight:700;}
  .ps-op{color:#f9a8d4!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:#f9a8d4!important;}
  .ps-num{color:#fde68a!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:#fde68a!important;}
  .ps-str{color:#86efac!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:#86efac!important;}
  .ps-comment{color:#475569!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:#475569!important;font-style:italic;}
  .ps-var{color:#e2e8f0!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:#e2e8f0!important;}

  /* CALLOUTS */
  .callout-exam{background:#fffbeb;border:1px solid #fcd34d;border-left:4px solid var(--amber);border-radius:0 8px 8px 0;padding:16px 20px;margin:20px 0;}
  .callout-exam-label{font-size:11px;font-weight:700;letter-spacing:.08em;text-transform:uppercase;color:var(--amber)!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:var(--amber)!important;margin-bottom:6px;}
  .callout-exam p{font-size:14px!important;color:#78350f!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:#78350f!important;margin-bottom:0!important;line-height:1.6!important;}
  .callout-trap{background:#fef2f2;border:1px solid #fca5a5;border-left:4px solid var(--red);border-radius:0 8px 8px 0;padding:16px 20px;margin:20px 0;}
  .callout-trap-label{font-size:11px;font-weight:700;letter-spacing:.08em;text-transform:uppercase;color:var(--red)!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:var(--red)!important;margin-bottom:6px;}
  .callout-trap p{font-size:14px!important;color:#7f1d1d!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:#7f1d1d!important;margin-bottom:0!important;line-height:1.6!important;}

  /* MINI EXERCISES */
  .mini-ex{background:#fff;border:1px solid #bfdbfe;border-radius:12px;padding:20px 24px;margin:24px 0;}
  .mini-ex-label{display:flex;align-items:center;gap:8px;font-size:11px;font-weight:700;letter-spacing:.08em;text-transform:uppercase;color:var(--bi3-dk)!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:var(--bi3-dk)!important;margin-bottom:12px;}
  .mini-ex-q{font-size:15px;font-weight:600;color:var(--navy)!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:var(--navy)!important;margin-bottom:14px;line-height:1.5;}
  .mini-ex-code{background:#0f172a;border-radius:8px;padding:14px 16px;font-family:monospace;font-size:13px;line-height:1.8;margin-bottom:14px;overflow-x:auto;white-space:pre;display:block;}
  .mini-opts{display:flex;flex-direction:column;gap:7px;margin-bottom:10px;}
  .mini-opt{display:flex;align-items:center;gap:10px;padding:10px 14px;border:2px solid #e2e8f0;border-radius:8px;cursor:pointer;font-size:14px;font-family:monospace;color:#374151!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:#374151!important;background:#f8fafc;text-align:left;width:100%;transition:border-color .15s;}
  .mini-opt:hover{border-color:var(--bi3-lt);background:var(--bi3-bg);}
  .mini-opt.correct{border-color:var(--green)!important;background:#f0fdf4!important;color:#14532d!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:#14532d!important;}
  .mini-opt.incorrect{border-color:var(--red)!important;background:#fef2f2!important;color:#7f1d1d!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:#7f1d1d!important;}
  .mini-opt.reveal{border-color:var(--green)!important;background:#f0fdf4!important;}
  .mini-opt-letter{font-weight:700;color:var(--bi3)!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:var(--bi3)!important;min-width:18px;font-family:inherit;}
  .mini-opt.correct .mini-opt-letter{color:#14532d!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:#14532d!important;}
  .mini-opt.incorrect .mini-opt-letter{color:#7f1d1d!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:#7f1d1d!important;}
  .mini-fib-row{display:flex;gap:8px;align-items:center;flex-wrap:wrap;margin-bottom:10px;}
  .mini-fib-input{padding:8px 12px;border:2px solid #e2e8f0;border-radius:8px;font-family:monospace;font-size:14px;width:130px;outline:none;color:var(--navy)!important;background:#f8fafc;}
  .mini-fib-input:focus{border-color:var(--bi3-lt);}
  .mini-fib-input.correct{border-color:var(--green);background:#f0fdf4;}
  .mini-fib-input.incorrect{border-color:var(--red);background:#fef2f2;}
  .mini-fib-btn{padding:8px 18px;background:var(--bi3);border:none;border-radius:8px;color:#fff!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:#fff!important;font-size:13px;font-weight:700;cursor:pointer;font-family:inherit;}
  .mini-fb{font-size:13px;font-weight:500;padding:8px 12px;border-radius:7px;margin-top:6px;display:none;line-height:1.5;}
  .mini-fb.c{background:#f0fdf4;color:var(--green)!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:var(--green)!important;display:block;}
  .mini-fb.w{background:#fef2f2;color:var(--red)!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:var(--red)!important;display:block;}

  /* VOCAB */
  .vocab-table{width:100%;border-collapse:collapse;margin-bottom:24px;font-size:14px;}
  .vocab-table thead tr{background:var(--bi3);}
  .vocab-table thead th{padding:10px 16px;text-align:left;font-weight:600;color:#fff!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:#fff!important;font-size:13px;}
  .vocab-table tbody tr:nth-child(even){background:var(--bi3-bg);}
  .vocab-table tbody tr:nth-child(odd){background:#fff;}
  .vocab-table tbody td{padding:10px 16px;border-bottom:1px solid #bfdbfe;color:#374151;vertical-align:top;line-height:1.5;}
  .vocab-table tbody td:first-child{font-weight:700;color:var(--bi3-dk)!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:var(--bi3-dk)!important;white-space:nowrap;}

  /* CPT CONNECTION */
  .cpt-connection{background:#fefce8;border:1px solid #fde68a;border-left:4px solid #f59e0b;border-radius:0 10px 10px 0;padding:20px 24px;margin:28px 0;}
  .cpt-connection-label{font-size:11px;font-weight:700;letter-spacing:.08em;text-transform:uppercase;color:#92400e!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:#92400e!important;margin-bottom:8px;}
  .cpt-connection h3{font-size:16px!important;font-weight:700!important;color:#78350f!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:#78350f!important;margin:16px 0 8px!important;}
  .cpt-connection p{font-size:14px!important;color:#78350f!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:#78350f!important;line-height:1.7!important;margin-bottom:12px!important;}
  .cpt-connection a{color:#b45309!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:#b45309!important;font-weight:600;text-decoration:underline;}
  .cpt-connection code{background:#fef3c7;color:#78350f!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:#78350f!important;padding:1px 6px;border-radius:5px;font-size:13px;}
  .cpt-stems{list-style:none;padding:0;margin:0 0 8px;display:flex;flex-direction:column;gap:8px;}
  .cpt-stems li{background:#fffef5;border:1px solid #fde68a;border-radius:8px;padding:10px 14px;font-size:13px!important;color:#78350f!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:#78350f!important;line-height:1.6;}
  .cpt-code{background:#0f172a;border-radius:8px;padding:14px 16px;font-family:monospace;font-size:13px;line-height:1.8;margin:6px 0 12px;overflow-x:auto;white-space:pre;display:block;color:#e2e8f0!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:#e2e8f0!important;}

  /* EMAIL */
  .email-capture{background:linear-gradient(135deg,#1e3a8a 0%,#1e40af 100%);border-radius:12px;padding:24px 28px;margin-bottom:36px;display:flex;align-items:center;gap:24px;flex-wrap:wrap;}
  .email-capture-text{flex:1;min-width:200px;}
  .email-capture-eyebrow{font-size:11px;font-weight:700;letter-spacing:.1em;text-transform:uppercase;color:var(--bi3-lt)!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:var(--bi3-lt)!important;margin-bottom:4px;}
  .email-capture h3{font-size:16px!important;font-weight:700!important;color:#fff!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:#fff!important;margin-bottom:4px!important;}
  .email-capture p{font-size:13px!important;color:#94a3b8!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:#94a3b8!important;margin-bottom:0!important;line-height:1.5!important;}
  .email-capture-form{display:flex;gap:8px;flex-wrap:wrap;flex-shrink:0;}
  .email-capture-input{padding:10px 14px;border-radius:8px;border:1px solid rgba(255,255,255,.2);background:rgba(255,255,255,.1);color:#fff!important;font-size:14px;font-family:inherit;min-width:180px;outline:none;}
  .email-capture-btn{padding:10px 20px!important;background:var(--bi3)!important;color:#fff!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:#fff!important;border:none!important;border-radius:8px!important;font-size:14px!important;font-weight:600!important;cursor:pointer!important;font-family:inherit!important;}
  .email-capture-success{display:none;font-size:14px;color:#93c5fd!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:#93c5fd!important;font-weight:600;padding:10px 0;}

  /* MCQ */
  .mcq-section{background:#fff;border:1px solid #e2e8f0;border-radius:14px;padding:28px;margin-bottom:40px;}
  .mcq-section-header{display:flex;align-items:center;gap:12px;margin-bottom:24px;padding-bottom:16px;border-bottom:2px solid var(--bi3-bg);}
  .mcq-section-icon{width:40px;height:40px;border-radius:10px;background:var(--bi3-bg);display:flex;align-items:center;justify-content:center;font-size:18px;flex-shrink:0;}
  .mcq-section-title{font-family:"DM Serif Display",serif;font-size:20px;color:var(--navy)!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:var(--navy)!important;}
  .mcq-section-sub{font-size:13px;color:var(--slate);}
  .mcq-item{margin-bottom:28px;padding-bottom:28px;border-bottom:1px solid #f1f5f9;}
  .mcq-item:last-child{border-bottom:none;margin-bottom:0;padding-bottom:0;}
  .mcq-q-num{font-size:11px;font-weight:700;letter-spacing:.08em;text-transform:uppercase;color:var(--slate);margin-bottom:8px;}
  .diff-tag{display:inline-block;font-size:10px;font-weight:700;letter-spacing:.06em;text-transform:uppercase;padding:2px 8px;border-radius:100px;margin-left:8px;background:#fef2f2;color:#b91c1c!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:#b91c1c!important;border:1px solid #fca5a5;}
  .mcq-q-text{font-size:15px!important;font-weight:600!important;color:#0f1f3d!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:#0f1f3d!important;line-height:1.6!important;margin-bottom:12px!important;}
  .predict-note{font-size:12px;font-style:italic;color:#64748b!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:#64748b!important;margin-bottom:12px;}
  .mcq-code{background:#0f172a;border-radius:8px;padding:12px 14px;margin:10px 0 14px;font-family:monospace;font-size:13px;line-height:1.75;color:#e2e8f0!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:#e2e8f0!important;white-space:pre;overflow-x:auto;display:block;}
  .mcq-code .k{color:#93c5fd!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:#93c5fd!important;}
  .mcq-code .s{color:#f9a8d4!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:#f9a8d4!important;}
  .mcq-code .n{color:#fde68a!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:#fde68a!important;}
  .mcq-code .c{color:#64748b!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:#64748b!important;font-style:italic;}
  .mcq-roman{list-style:none;padding:0;margin:10px 0 14px;display:flex;flex-direction:column;gap:6px;}
  .mcq-roman li{font-family:monospace;font-size:13px;color:#1e293b!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:#1e293b!important;background:#f1f5f9;border-radius:6px;padding:8px 12px;}
  .mcq-roman li strong{color:var(--bi3-dk)!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:var(--bi3-dk)!important;font-family:"DM Sans",sans-serif;margin-right:8px;}
  .mcq-options{display:flex;flex-direction:column;gap:8px;margin-bottom:12px;}
  .mcq-option{display:flex!important;align-items:flex-start!important;gap:12px!important;padding:11px 14px!important;border:2px solid #e2e8f0!important;border-radius:8px!important;cursor:pointer!important;background:#f8fafc!important;font-size:14px!important;color:#374151!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:#374151!important;line-height:1.5!important;text-align:left!important;width:100%!important;font-family:inherit!important;}
  .mcq-option:hover{border-color:var(--bi3-lt)!important;background:var(--bi3-bg)!important;}
  .mcq-option.correct{border-color:var(--green)!important;background:#f0fdf4!important;color:#14532d!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:#14532d!important;}
  .mcq-option.incorrect{border-color:var(--red)!important;background:#fef2f2!important;color:#7f1d1d!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:#7f1d1d!important;}
  .mcq-option.revealed-correct{border-color:var(--green)!important;background:#f0fdf4!important;}

    <div class="lesson-objectives">
      <h2>After this lesson, you will be able to:</h2>
      <ul>
        <li><span>Explain how filtering, sorting, and searching extract information from a data set</span></li>
        <li><span>Describe how finding patterns and trends turns raw data into insight and knowledge</span></li>
        <li><span>Explain why combining and cross-referencing multiple data sets can reveal insight a single set cannot</span></li>
        <li><span>Define metadata and give examples, and explain its uses and privacy concerns</span></li>
        <li><span>Explain why correlation does not imply causation when reading patterns in data</span></li>
      </ul>
    </div>
    <div class="score-impact">📈 <span>Big Idea 2 (Data) is 17 to 22 percent of the AP CSP exam, the largest single Big Idea on the multiple-choice section. Topic 2.3 questions ask you to read small data tables, apply filtering and sorting logic, and avoid the correlation-versus-causation trap. These are recurring, learnable points.</span>
</div>
    <div class="hook-box">
      <div class="hook-label">💡 Think about this first</div>
      <p>A city notices that on days when more ice cream is sold, more people also get sunburned, and the two rise and fall together almost perfectly all summer. A council member proposes banning ice cream to reduce sunburns. The data really does show the pattern, so what is wrong with the conclusion, and what would you have to check before deciding ice cream causes sunburns?</p>
    </div>
    <div class="lesson-section">
      <h2>From Data to Insight</h2>
      <p>Programs and data are used to gain <strong>insight and knowledge</strong>. Raw data by itself is just records; the value comes from <strong>extracting information</strong> that answers a question. The framework names the main operations you use to do this:</p>
      <ul>
        <li>
<strong>Filtering</strong> selects only the records that meet a condition, such as "all sales over $100" or "customers in Texas."</li>
        <li>
<strong>Sorting</strong> orders records by a value, such as newest first or highest score to lowest.</li>
        <li>
<strong>Searching</strong> locates a specific record or value within the data.</li>
        <li>
<strong>Finding patterns and trends</strong> looks across many records for a relationship, a repeated behavior, or a change over time.</li>
      </ul>
      <p>Not all collected data is relevant to a given question. Part of extracting information is deciding <strong>which</strong> data matters and setting the rest aside. A data set about weather, traffic, and store sales may hold the answer to a sales question in only two of its columns.</p>
      <div class="callout-exam">
        <div class="callout-exam-label">🎯 What the exam rewards</div>
        <p>When a question asks how to <strong>answer a specific question</strong> from a data set, match the question to the operation. "Which records meet a condition?" is <strong>filtering</strong>. "What is the order or ranking?" is <strong>sorting</strong>. Do not answer "sort" when the task is really to select a subset.</p>
      </div>
    </div>

    <div class="lesson-section">
      <h2>Filtering, Sorting, and Metadata</h2>
      <p>Here is a tiny sample data set of orders. Reading a small table like this is exactly what the exam asks you to do.</p>
      <table class="vocab-table">
        <tr>
<th>OrderID</th>
<th>State</th>
<th>Amount</th>
<th>Date</th>
</tr>
        <tr>
<td>101</td>
<td>TX</td>
<td>$40</td>
<td>Jun 2</td>
</tr>
        <tr>
<td>102</td>
<td>CA</td>
<td>$120</td>
<td>Jun 3</td>
</tr>
        <tr>
<td>103</td>
<td>TX</td>
<td>$95</td>
<td>Jun 5</td>
</tr>
        <tr>
<td>104</td>
<td>CA</td>
<td>$60</td>
<td>Jun 9</td>
</tr>
      </table>
      <p><strong>Filtering</strong> for <code>State = TX</code> returns rows 101 and 103. <strong>Sorting</strong> by <code>Amount</code> from high to low returns 102, 103, 104, 101. Notice that filtering changes <em>which</em> rows you see, while sorting changes only the <em>order</em>. The two operations answer different questions.</p>
      <p><strong>Metadata</strong> is data about data. It is not the content itself but information that describes it. Examples include a photo's file size, the date and time it was created, its author, its pixel dimensions, and the GPS location where it was taken. Metadata is powerful for <strong>organizing and finding patterns</strong> quickly, but because it can reveal things like where and when you were, it is also a <strong>privacy concern</strong>.</p>
      <table class="vocab-table">
        <tr>
<th>Term</th>
<th>What it is</th>
<th>Example</th>
</tr>
        <tr>
<td><strong>Filtering</strong></td>
<td>Selecting records that meet a condition</td>
<td>Only orders over $100</td>
</tr>
        <tr>
<td><strong>Sorting</strong></td>
<td>Ordering records by a value</td>
<td>Orders newest to oldest</td>
</tr>
        <tr>
<td><strong>Metadata</strong></td>
<td>Data that describes other data</td>
<td>A photo's date, size, and GPS location</td>
</tr>
      </table>

    <div class="lesson-section">
      <h2>Combining and Cross-Referencing Data</h2>
      <p>Insight often hides between data sets, not inside one. <strong>Combining</strong> or <strong>cross-referencing</strong> multiple data sets can reveal a relationship that no single set shows on its own. For example, one data set of store sales and a separate data set of daily weather, joined by date, can reveal that umbrella sales spike on rainy days, something neither table shows alone.</p>
      <p>Before data sets can be combined, they often need <strong>cleaning</strong> (fixing errors, removing duplicates, handling missing values) and <strong>transforming</strong> (putting values in a consistent format, such as the same date style). This preparation is part of extracting reliable information; combining messy or mismatched data produces misleading results.</p>
      <div class="callout-trap">
        <div class="callout-trap-label">⚠ Common trap</div>
        <p>A bigger pile of data is not automatically more useful. <strong>Not all collected data is relevant</strong> to the question being asked, and a larger data set can even bury the answer in noise unless it is filtered and organized. Scale helps reveal patterns only when the data is processed efficiently and the irrelevant parts are set aside.</p>
      </div>
    </div>

    <div class="lesson-section">
      <h2>Correlation Is Not Causation</h2>
      <p>This is the single most tested idea in Topic 2.3. A <strong>correlation</strong> is a pattern in which two variables tend to change together. Finding a correlation does <strong>not</strong> prove that one variable <strong>causes</strong> the other. Ice cream sales and sunburns rise together all summer, but neither causes the other; a third factor, hot sunny weather, drives both.</p>
      <p>When you see a pattern in data, the correct move is to treat it as a question to investigate, not an answer. A relationship might be real causation, it might run the opposite direction, or it might be explained by a hidden third variable. Larger data sets can make correlations easier to spot, which makes it even more important not to jump to a causal claim.</p>
      <p>Scale also matters for processing: bigger data sets can reveal patterns that small samples miss, but they demand <strong>efficient processing</strong>. Classifying and filtering records is what keeps a large data set manageable enough to search for those patterns.</p>
      <div class="mini-ex">
        <div class="mini-ex-label">Quick check</div>
        <div class="mini-ex-q">A data set shows that towns with more firefighters also tend to have more fires. Which conclusion is best supported?</div>
        <div class="mini-opts" id="mc-extract-2-opts">
          <button class="mini-opt" onclick="miniMCQ('mc-extract-2','A','C','mc-extract-2-fb')"><span class="mini-opt-letter">A</span> Firefighters cause fires, so towns should hire fewer</button>
          <button class="mini-opt" onclick="miniMCQ('mc-extract-2','B','C','mc-extract-2-fb')"><span class="mini-opt-letter">B</span> Fires prevent firefighters from being hired</button>
          <button class="mini-opt" onclick="miniMCQ('mc-extract-2','C','C','mc-extract-2-fb')"><span class="mini-opt-letter">C</span> The two are correlated, likely because larger towns have both more fires and more firefighters</button>
          <button class="mini-opt" onclick="miniMCQ('mc-extract-2','D','C','mc-extract-2-fb')"><span class="mini-opt-letter">D</span> There is no relationship between the two variables</button>
        </div>
        <div class="mini-fb" id="mc-extract-2-fb"></div>
      </div>
    </div>

    <div class="lesson-section">
      <h2>How Topic 2.3 Is Tested on the MCQ Exam</h2>
      <p>On the multiple-choice section, 2.3 shows up as short <strong>data-table questions</strong>. You will be given a small table of records and asked what a filter or a sort would return, or which operation answers a stated question. Read carefully: a question that says "which records" is filtering, while "in what order" or "rank" is sorting. Watch for tasks that need <strong>two steps</strong>, such as filter first, then sort the result.</p>
      <p>The other guaranteed 2.3 question type is the <strong>correlation-versus-causation trap</strong>. A scenario presents two variables that move together and an answer choice that jumps straight to "X causes Y." The credited answer recognizes the pattern as a correlation and points to a possible third variable or the need for more investigation. Expect at least one metadata question too, usually asking you to identify data-about-data (file size, timestamp, GPS) or to name its privacy risk. None of these require coding; they reward careful reading and knowing the vocabulary.</p>
    </div>
