<div id="q1-fb-B" class="mcq-feedback incorrect-fb">Incorrect. Searching for one value finds a single record, not the full list of Cardiology visits.</div>
<div id="q1-fb-C" class="mcq-feedback correct-fb">Correct. Filtering selects only the records that meet a condition, so filtering on department equal to Cardiology returns exactly the Cardiology visits.</div>
<div id="q1-fb-D" class="mcq-feedback incorrect-fb">Incorrect. Sorting by age reorders the rows but still contains every department, so it does not produce the required subset.</div>
      </div>
      <div class="mcq-item" data-activity="quiz" data-item="q2">
        <div class="mcq-q-num">Question 2 of 6<span class="diff-tag">Read the table</span>
</div>
        <div class="predict-note">Work out the two steps in order before you look.</div>
        <div class="mcq-q-text"><p>Consider this table of student projects. Filter to only Science projects, then sort those by Score from highest to lowest. Which two projects appear at the top, in order?</p></div>
        <div class="mcq-code">Name    Subject   Score
Ava     Science   88
Ben     History   75
Cara    Science   93
Dan     History   91
Eli     Science   79</div>
        <div class="mcq-options" id="q2-options">
<button class="mcq-option" onclick="checkMCQ('q2','A','C','q2-fb-A')"><span class="mcq-option-letter">A</span> Ava, then Cara</button>
<button class="mcq-option" onclick="checkMCQ('q2','B','C','q2-fb-B')"><span class="mcq-option-letter">B</span> Dan, then Cara</button>
<button class="mcq-option" onclick="checkMCQ('q2','C','C','q2-fb-C')"><span class="mcq-option-letter">C</span> Cara, then Ava</button>
<button class="mcq-option" onclick="checkMCQ('q2','D','C','q2-fb-D')"><span class="mcq-option-letter">D</span> Cara, then Eli</button>
</div>
<div id="q2-fb-A" class="mcq-feedback incorrect-fb">Incorrect. Ava scored 88 and Cara scored 93, so Cara must come before Ava when sorting highest first.</div>
<div id="q2-fb-B" class="mcq-feedback incorrect-fb">Incorrect. Dan is in History, so the Science filter removes him before any sorting happens.</div>
<div id="q2-fb-C" class="mcq-feedback correct-fb">Correct. Filtering to Science keeps Ava (88), Cara (93), and Eli (79); sorting those by Score highest first gives Cara, then Ava, then Eli, so the top two are Cara then Ava.</div>
<div id="q2-fb-D" class="mcq-feedback incorrect-fb">Incorrect. Eli scored 79, the lowest Science score, so Eli cannot be in the top two.</div>
      </div>
      <div class="mcq-item" data-activity="quiz" data-item="q3">
        <div class="mcq-q-num">Question 3 of 6<span class="diff-tag">Correlation vs causation</span>
</div>
        <div class="predict-note">Predict the flaw in the causal claim first.</div>
        <div class="mcq-q-text"><p>A researcher finds that months with higher sales of sunglasses also have higher numbers of drowning incidents, and the two track each other closely across the year. A newspaper concludes that buying sunglasses causes drownings. Which statement best evaluates this conclusion?</p></div>
        <div class="mcq-options" id="q3-options">
<button class="mcq-option" onclick="checkMCQ('q3','A','B','q3-fb-A')"><span class="mcq-option-letter">A</span> The conclusion is valid because the two variables are strongly correlated</button>
<button class="mcq-option" onclick="checkMCQ('q3','B','B','q3-fb-B')"><span class="mcq-option-letter">B</span> The conclusion is flawed because a correlation between two variables does not establish that one causes the other</button>
<button class="mcq-option" onclick="checkMCQ('q3','C','B','q3-fb-C')"><span class="mcq-option-letter">C</span> The conclusion is flawed because the two variables are not correlated at all</button>
<button class="mcq-option" onclick="checkMCQ('q3','D','B','q3-fb-D')"><span class="mcq-option-letter">D</span> The conclusion is valid because both variables increase at the same time</button>
</div>
<div id="q3-fb-A" class="mcq-feedback incorrect-fb">Incorrect. A strong correlation still does not prove causation; the reasoning error is treating the pattern as cause.</div>
<div id="q3-fb-B" class="mcq-feedback correct-fb">Correct. The variables are correlated, but correlation does not imply causation. A third factor such as warm summer weather plausibly drives both sunglasses sales and swimming, and thus drownings.</div>
<div id="q3-fb-C" class="mcq-feedback incorrect-fb">Incorrect. The data does show a correlation; the flaw is not the absence of a pattern but the leap to causation.</div>
<div id="q3-fb-D" class="mcq-feedback incorrect-fb">Incorrect. Increasing together is exactly what correlation means, and that alone does not establish cause.</div>
      </div>
      <div class="mcq-item" data-activity="quiz" data-item="q4">
        <div class="mcq-q-num">Question 4 of 6<span class="diff-tag">Metadata</span>
</div>
        <div class="predict-note">Name what metadata is before scanning the choices.</div>
        <div class="mcq-q-text"><p>A photo-sharing app stores, for every uploaded image, the file size, the date and time it was taken, and the GPS coordinates of where it was taken. Which statement about this stored information is most accurate?</p></div>
        <div class="mcq-options" id="q4-options">
<button class="mcq-option" onclick="checkMCQ('q4','A','B','q4-fb-A')"><span class="mcq-option-letter">A</span> It is the image content itself, so it carries no privacy risk</button>
<button class="mcq-option" onclick="checkMCQ('q4','B','B','q4-fb-B')"><span class="mcq-option-letter">B</span> It is metadata that can help organize and find images but can also reveal a user's location and habits</button>
<button class="mcq-option" onclick="checkMCQ('q4','C','B','q4-fb-C')"><span class="mcq-option-letter">C</span> It is metadata that has no use for finding patterns because it is not the actual picture</button>
<button class="mcq-option" onclick="checkMCQ('q4','D','B','q4-fb-D')"><span class="mcq-option-letter">D</span> It is raw pixel data that must be decompressed before it can be read</button>
</div>
<div id="q4-fb-A" class="mcq-feedback incorrect-fb">Incorrect. File size, timestamp, and GPS are data about the image, not the pixels, and location data is a real privacy risk.</div>
<div id="q4-fb-B" class="mcq-feedback correct-fb">Correct. This is metadata, data about data. It is useful for organizing and finding patterns, but details like GPS and timestamps can expose where a user was and when, a privacy concern.</div>
<div id="q4-fb-C" class="mcq-feedback incorrect-fb">Incorrect. Metadata is very useful for finding patterns and organizing, for example grouping photos by date or place.</div>
<div id="q4-fb-D" class="mcq-feedback incorrect-fb">Incorrect. The described fields are metadata describing the image, not the pixel data of the image.</div>
      </div>
      <div class="mcq-item" data-activity="quiz" data-item="q5">
        <div class="mcq-q-num">Question 5 of 6<span class="diff-tag">II only style</span>
</div>
        <div class="predict-note">Judge each statement true or false before matching to an option.</div>
        <div class="mcq-q-text"><p>An analyst has two separate data sets: one of daily bike-rental counts and one of daily rainfall, each keyed by date. Consider these statements:</p></div>
        <ul class="mcq-roman">
          <li>
<strong>I.</strong> Cross-referencing the two data sets by date could reveal how rainfall relates to rentals, an insight neither set shows alone.</li>
          <li>
<strong>II.</strong> Because the rainfall data set is larger, all of its columns are automatically relevant to the rentals question.</li>
          <li>
<strong>III.</strong> Finding that rentals drop on rainy days would prove that rain directly causes every rider's decision.</li>
        </ul>
        <div class="mcq-options" id="q5-options">
<button class="mcq-option" onclick="checkMCQ('q5','A','D','q5-fb-A')"><span class="mcq-option-letter">A</span> I and II only</button>
<button class="mcq-option" onclick="checkMCQ('q5','B','D','q5-fb-B')"><span class="mcq-option-letter">B</span> II and III only</button>
<button class="mcq-option" onclick="checkMCQ('q5','C','D','q5-fb-C')"><span class="mcq-option-letter">C</span> I, II, and III</button>
<button class="mcq-option" onclick="checkMCQ('q5','D','D','q5-fb-D')"><span class="mcq-option-letter">D</span> I only</button>
</div>
<div id="q5-fb-A" class="mcq-feedback incorrect-fb">Incorrect. Statement II is false; a larger data set does not make all of its data relevant to the question.</div>
<div id="q5-fb-B" class="mcq-feedback incorrect-fb">Incorrect. Both II and III are false, so this pairing cannot be correct.</div>
<div id="q5-fb-C" class="mcq-feedback incorrect-fb">Incorrect. Statements II and III are both false, so not all three can be correct.</div>
<div id="q5-fb-D" class="mcq-feedback correct-fb">Correct. Only statement I is sound: cross-referencing the sets by date can reveal a relationship neither shows alone. II is false because size does not make data relevant, and III overclaims causation from a pattern.</div>
      </div>
      <div class="mcq-item" data-activity="quiz" data-item="q6">
        <div class="mcq-q-num">Question 6 of 6<span class="diff-tag">Cross-reference</span>
</div>
        <div class="predict-note">Predict which combination of steps is required first.</div>
        <div class="mcq-q-text"><p>A store has a customers table (customer ID, home city) and a separate orders table (order ID, customer ID, amount). A manager wants the total amount ordered by customers who live in Denver. Which approach correctly extracts this information?</p></div>
        <div class="mcq-options" id="q6-options">
<button class="mcq-option" onclick="checkMCQ('q6','A','D','q6-fb-A')"><span class="mcq-option-letter">A</span> Sort the orders table by amount and report the largest value</button>
<button class="mcq-option" onclick="checkMCQ('q6','B','D','q6-fb-B')"><span class="mcq-option-letter">B</span> Filter the orders table on amount greater than zero and add every result</button>
<button class="mcq-option" onclick="checkMCQ('q6','C','D','q6-fb-C')"><span class="mcq-option-letter">C</span> Read the metadata of the orders file to find the Denver total</button>
<button class="mcq-option" onclick="checkMCQ('q6','D','D','q6-fb-D')"><span class="mcq-option-letter">D</span> Cross-reference the tables on customer ID, filter to customers whose city is Denver, then sum those customers' order amounts</button>
</div>
<div id="q6-fb-A" class="mcq-feedback incorrect-fb">Incorrect. Sorting by amount and taking the largest value ignores city entirely and returns one order, not a Denver total.</div>
<div id="q6-fb-B" class="mcq-feedback incorrect-fb">Incorrect. Filtering only on amount greater than zero keeps every order from every city, so the total is not limited to Denver.</div>
<div id="q6-fb-C" class="mcq-feedback incorrect-fb">Incorrect. Metadata describes the file, not the order amounts by city, so it cannot produce the Denver total.</div>
<div id="q6-fb-D" class="mcq-feedback correct-fb">Correct. City lives in the customers table and amount lives in the orders table, so you must cross-reference on customer ID, filter to Denver customers, and then sum their order amounts.</div>
      </div>
    </div>

<script>
(function(){
  var STUDENT_COLS = [
    {key:'name',  label:'Name',  type:'text', filter:false, sort:true},
    {key:'grade', label:'Grade', type:'num',  filter:true,  sort:true},
    {key:'score', label:'Score', type:'num',  filter:true,  sort:true},
    {key:'club',  label:'Club',  type:'cat',  filter:true,  sort:true}

    {key:'name',     label:'Product',  type:'text', filter:false, sort:true},
    {key:'price',    label:'Price ($)',type:'num',  filter:true,  sort:true},
    {key:'rating',   label:'Rating',   type:'num',  filter:true,  sort:true},
    {key:'category', label:'Category', type:'cat',  filter:true,  sort:true}
  ];

  var ROUNDS = [
    { cols:STUDENT_COLS,
      goal:'Select every student in Grade 11.',
      data:[
        {id:1,name:'Ava',grade:11,score:88,club:'Robotics'},
        {id:2,name:'Ben',grade:12,score:74,club:'Debate'},
        {id:3,name:'Cara',grade:11,score:91,club:'Robotics'},
        {id:4,name:'Dan',grade:10,score:66,club:'Chess'},
        {id:5,name:'Eli',grade:12,score:85,club:'Debate'},
        {id:6,name:'Fay',grade:11,score:79,club:'Chess'}
      ],
      spec:{filters:[{col:'grade',op:'=',val:11}]} },

    { cols:PRODUCT_COLS,
      goal:'Find every product priced under $20.',
      data:[
        {id:1,name:'Cable',price:8,rating:4.5,category:'Accessory'},
        {id:2,name:'Mouse',price:22,rating:4.1,category:'Peripheral'},
        {id:3,name:'Charger',price:15,rating:3.8,category:'Accessory'},
        {id:4,name:'Stand',price:35,rating:4.7,category:'Furniture'},
        {id:5,name:'Cover',price:12,rating:4.2,category:'Accessory'},

        {id:3,name:'Cara',grade:12,score:91,club:'Robotics'},
        {id:4,name:'Dan',grade:10,score:66,club:'Chess'},
        {id:5,name:'Eli',grade:12,score:85,club:'Robotics'},
        {id:6,name:'Fay',grade:11,score:79,club:'Robotics'},
        {id:7,name:'Gus',grade:12,score:95,club:'Chess'},
        {id:8,name:'Hana',grade:12,score:82,club:'Robotics'},
        {id:9,name:'Ivy',grade:11,score:90,club:'Robotics'}
      ],
      spec:{filters:[{col:'club',op:'=',val:'Robotics'},{col:'score',op:'>',val:80}],sort:{col:'score',dir:'desc'},limit:2} },

    { cols:PRODUCT_COLS,
      goal:'Select the 3 cheapest products that are rated 4 or higher.',
      data:[
        {id:1,name:'Cable',price:8,rating:4.5,category:'Accessory'},
        {id:2,name:'Mouse',price:22,rating:4.1,category:'Peripheral'},
        {id:3,name:'Charger',price:15,rating:3.8,category:'Accessory'},
        {id:4,name:'Stand',price:35,rating:4.7,category:'Furniture'},
        {id:5,name:'Cover',price:12,rating:4.2,category:'Accessory'},
        {id:6,name:'Pad',price:18,rating:3.5,category:'Accessory'},
        {id:7,name:'Hub',price:24,rating:4.0,category:'Peripheral'},
        {id:8,name:'Lamp',price:45,rating:4.8,category:'Furniture'},
        {id:9,name:'Clip',price:6,rating:4.3,category:'Accessory'}
      ],
      spec:{filters:[{col:'rating',op:'>=',val:4}],sort:{col:'price',dir:'asc'},limit:3} }
  ];

  var CONCEPTS = [
    'A filter keeps only the rows that meet a condition, then you read the survivors.',
    'Sorting reorders rows by a field so the extremes (top or bottom) land where you can grab them.',
    'To find a top N, filter to the right group first, then sort, then take from the front.',
    'Combining filters with AND narrows the data to exactly the rows that satisfy every condition.'
  ];

  var NUM_OPS = [['>','>'],['>=','>='],['=','='],['<=','<='],['<','<']];

  var roundIdx=0, totalScore=0, ended=false;
  var round, filters, sort, opsUsed, wrongSubmits, selected;

  var $=function(id){return document.getElementById(id);};

  function passes(row,f){
    var v=row[f.col];
    if(typeof v==='string') return String(v)===String(f.val);
    var rv=Number(v), fv=Number(f.val);
    if(f.op==='>') return rv>fv;
    if(f.op==='>=') return rv>=fv;
    if(f.op==='=') return rv===fv;
    if(f.op==='<=') return rv<=fv;
    if(f.op==='<') return rv<fv;
    return false;
  }
  function filtered(rows){
    return rows.filter(function(r){ return filters.every(function(f){ return passes(r,f); }); });
  }
  function sortRows(rows,s){
    var c=rows.slice();
    c.sort(function(a,b){
      var av=a[s.col], bv=b[s.col];
      if(typeof av==='string'){
        if(av===bv) return 0;
        return s.dir==='asc' ? (av<bv?-1:1) : (av>bv?-1:1);
      }
      return s.dir==='asc' ? av-bv : bv-av;
    });
    return c;
  }
  function view(){
    var v=filtered(round.data);
    if(sort) v=sortRows(v,sort);
    return v;
  }
  function target(){
    var pool=round.data.filter(function(r){ return round.spec.filters.every(function(f){ return passes(r,f); }); });
    if(round.spec.limit){ pool=sortRows(pool,round.spec.sort).slice(0,round.spec.limit); }
    return pool.map(function(r){ return r.id; });
  }
  function optimalOps(){ return round.spec.filters.length + (round.spec.limit?1:0); }

  function colByKey(k){ for(var i=0;i<round.cols.length;i++){ if(round.cols[i].key===k) return round.cols[i]; } return null; }
  function distinct(key){
    var seen={}, out=[];
    round.data.forEach(function(r){ if(!(r[key] in seen)){ seen[r[key]]=1; out.push(r[key]); } });
    return out;
  }

  function buildValControl(){
    var col=colByKey($('fsd-fcol').value);
    var opSel=$('fsd-fop'), wrap=$('fsd-fvalwrap');
    opSel.innerHTML=''; wrap.innerHTML='';
    if(!col) return;
    if(col.type==='cat'){
      var o=document.createElement('option'); o.value='='; o.innerHTML='='; opSel.appendChild(o);
      var sel=document.createElement('select'); sel.id='fsd-fval';
      distinct(col.key).forEach(function(v){ var op=document.createElement('option'); op.value=v; op.textContent=v; sel.appendChild(op); });
      wrap.appendChild(sel);
    } else {
      NUM_OPS.forEach(function(p){ var o=document.createElement('option'); o.value=p[0]; o.innerHTML=p[1]; opSel.appendChild(o); });
      opSel.value='>=';
      var inp=document.createElement('input'); inp.type='number'; inp.id='fsd-fval'; inp.step='any';
      var vals=round.data.map(function(r){return Number(r[col.key]);});
      inp.value=Math.round(vals.reduce(function(a,b){return a+b;},0)/vals.length);
      wrap.appendChild(inp);
    }
  }

  function buildControls(){
    var fcol=$('fsd-fcol'), scol=$('fsd-scol');
    fcol.innerHTML=''; scol.innerHTML='';
    round.cols.forEach(function(c){
      if(c.filter){ var o=document.createElement('option'); o.value=c.key; o.textContent=c.label; fcol.appendChild(o); }
      if(c.sort){ var s=document.createElement('option'); s.value=c.key; s.textContent=c.label; scol.appendChild(s); }
    });
    buildValControl();
  }

  function pruneSelection(){
    var vis={}; filtered(round.data).forEach(function(r){ vis[r.id]=1; });
    selected=selected.filter(function(id){ return vis[id]; });
  }

  function renderChips(){
    var c=$('fsd-chips'); c.innerHTML='';
    filters.forEach(function(f,i){
      var col=colByKey(f.col);
      var opTxt=({'>':'>','>=':'>=','=':'=','<=':'<=','<':'<'})[f.op]||f.op;
      var chip=document.createElement('span'); chip.className='fsd-chip';
      chip.innerHTML=col.label+' '+opTxt+' '+f.val+' <span class="x" data-i="'+i+'">×</span>';
      chip.querySelector('.x').onclick=function(){ filters.splice(i,1); pruneSelection(); renderAll(); };
      c.appendChild(chip);
    });
    if(sort){
      var col=colByKey(sort.col);
      var chip=document.createElement('span'); chip.className='fsd-chip sortchip';
      chip.innerHTML='Sorted by '+col.label+' ('+sort.dir+') <span class="x">×</span>';
      chip.querySelector('.x').onclick=function(){ sort=null; renderAll(); };
      c.appendChild(chip);
    }
  }

  function renderTable(){
    var thead=$('fsd-thead'), tbody=$('fsd-tbody');
    var head='<tr><th>Pick</th>';
    round.cols.forEach(function(c){ head+='<th>'+c.label+'</th>'; });
    thead.innerHTML=head+'</tr>';
    var rows=view();
    if(!rows.length){ tbody.innerHTML='<tr><td colspan="'+(round.cols.length+1)+'" class="fsd-empty">No rows match the current filters. Remove a filter to bring rows back.</td></tr>'; return; }
    tbody.innerHTML='';
    rows.forEach(function(r){
      var isSel=selected.indexOf(r.id)>=0;
      var tr=document.createElement('tr'); tr.className='pick'+(isSel?' sel':'');
      var cells='<td><span class="box">'+(isSel?'✓':'')+'</span></td>';
      round.cols.forEach(function(c){ cells+='<td>'+r[c.key]+'</td>'; });
      tr.innerHTML=cells;
      tr.onclick=function(){
        var p=selected.indexOf(r.id);
        if(p>=0) selected.splice(p,1); else selected.push(r.id);
        renderTable(); updateSelHint();
      };
      tbody.appendChild(tr);
    });
  }

  function updateSelHint(){ $('fsd-selhint').textContent='Selected '+selected.length+' row'+(selected.length===1?'':'s')+'. Click rows to toggle.'; }

  function renderStats(){
    $('fsd-round').textContent=(roundIdx+1)+' / '+ROUNDS.length;
    $('fsd-score').textContent=totalScore;
    $('fsd-ops').textContent=opsUsed;
  }
  function renderAll(){ renderChips(); renderTable(); renderStats(); updateSelHint(); }

  function loadRound(i){
    round=ROUNDS[i]; filters=[]; sort=null; opsUsed=0; wrongSubmits=0; selected=[];
    $('fsd-goaltxt').textContent=round.goal;
    $('fsd-fb').innerHTML='';
    buildControls(); renderAll();
  }

  function feedback(cls,msg){ $('fsd-fb').innerHTML='<div class="fsd-fb '+cls+'">'+msg+'</div>'; }

  function sameSet(a,b){
    if(a.length!==b.length) return false;
    var s={}; a.forEach(function(x){ s[x]=1; });
    return b.every(function(x){ return s[x]; });
  }

  function submit(){
    if(!selected.length){ feedback('no','Select at least one row before submitting. Filter and sort the table, then click the matching rows.'); return; }
    var tgt=target();
    if(sameSet(selected,tgt)){
      var extra=Math.max(0,opsUsed-optimalOps());
      var pts=Math.max(20, 100 - extra*12 - wrongSubmits*20);
      totalScore+=pts;
      var eff = extra===0 && wrongSubmits===0 ? 'Perfect efficiency! ' : '';
      feedback('ok',eff+'Correct. +'+pts+' points. You used '+opsUsed+' operation'+(opsUsed===1?'':'s')+' (best case '+optimalOps()+').');
      renderStats();
      var btn=$('fsd-submit'); btn.textContent = roundIdx+1<ROUNDS.length ? 'Next round →' : 'See results →';
      btn.innerHTML = roundIdx+1<ROUNDS.length ? 'Next round →' : 'See results →';
      btn.onclick=nextRound;
    } else {
      wrongSubmits++;
      var why;
      if(selected.length>tgt.length) why='Too many rows selected. Add a filter so only rows meeting the condition remain, then pick those.';
      else if(selected.length<tgt.length) why='Too few rows. You may have filtered out an answer or missed selecting a match.';
      else why='Right count, wrong rows. Recheck the exact condition and, for a top N, the sort direction.';
      feedback('no', why+' <br>'+CONCEPTS[Math.floor(Math.random()*CONCEPTS.length)]);
      renderStats();
    }
  }

  function nextRound(){
    var btn=$('fsd-submit'); btn.textContent='Submit answer'; btn.innerHTML='Submit answer'; btn.onclick=submit;
    if(roundIdx+1<ROUNDS.length){ roundIdx++; loadRound(roundIdx); }
    else endGame();
  }

  function endGame(){
    ended=true;
    $('fsd-play').style.display='none';
    $('fsd-endscreen').style.display='block';
    $('fsd-endscore').textContent=totalScore;
    var msg;
    if(totalScore>=520) msg='Elite detective work. You filtered to the right rows and sorted to the answer with almost no wasted operations, exactly how a program processes data.';
    else if(totalScore>=400) msg='Strong work. You extracted every answer by filtering and sorting. Trim a few extra operations to push the score higher.';
    else msg='Case solved. Remember: filter to keep rows meeting a condition, then sort to order a field. That two step move answers most data questions.';
    $('fsd-endmsg').textContent=msg;
    document.dispatchEvent(new CustomEvent('apcsGameScore',{detail:{value:totalScore}}));
  }

  function resetGame(){
    roundIdx=0; totalScore=0; ended=false;
    $('fsd-endscreen').style.display='none';
    $('fsd-play').style.display='block';
    var btn=$('fsd-submit'); btn.textContent='Submit answer'; btn.innerHTML='Submit answer'; btn.onclick=submit;
    loadRound(0);
  }

  $('fsd-fcol').onchange=buildValControl;
  $('fsd-fadd').onclick=function(){
    var col=colByKey($('fsd-fcol').value);
    var valEl=$('fsd-fval');
    var raw=valEl.value;
    var val = col.type==='cat' ? raw : Number(raw);
    if(col.type!=='cat' && (raw===''||isNaN(val))){ feedback('no','Enter a number for the filter value.'); return; }
    filters.push({col:col.key, op:$('fsd-fop').value, val:val});
    opsUsed++; pruneSelection(); $('fsd-fb').innerHTML=''; renderAll();
  };
  $('fsd-sapply').onclick=function(){
    sort={col:$('fsd-scol').value, dir:$('fsd-sdir').value};
    opsUsed++; $('fsd-fb').innerHTML=''; renderAll();
  };
  $('fsd-clear').onclick=function(){
    filters=[]; sort=null; pruneSelection(); $('fsd-fb').innerHTML='';
    feedback('no','Operations cleared, but the operation counter still reflects what you used. Plan the fewest moves for the best score.');
    renderAll();
  };
  $('fsd-submit').onclick=submit;
  $('fsd-again').onclick=resetGame;

  loadRound(0);
})();
</script>

    <div class="faq-section">
      <h2>Frequently Asked Questions</h2>
      <div class="faq-item">
        <button class="faq-q" onclick="toggleFAQ(this)">What is the difference between filtering and sorting?<i class="faq-icon">+</i></button>
        <div class="faq-a">Filtering selects a subset of records that meet a condition, changing which records you see. Sorting orders records by a value, changing only the arrangement, not which records are present. A question asking which records meet a condition needs a filter; a question asking for a ranking or order needs a sort.</div>
      </div>
      <div class="faq-item">
        <button class="faq-q" onclick="toggleFAQ(this)">What is metadata, in simple terms?<i class="faq-icon">+</i></button>
        <div class="faq-a">Metadata is data about data. It describes a piece of content rather than being the content itself. For a photo, the pixels are the data, while the file size, creation date and time, author, dimensions, and GPS location are metadata. Metadata helps organize and find patterns, but details like location can be a privacy concern.</div>
      </div>
      <div class="faq-item">
        <button class="faq-q" onclick="toggleFAQ(this)">Why does correlation not imply causation?<i class="faq-icon">+</i></button>
        <div class="faq-a">A correlation just means two variables change together. That pattern can be a coincidence, can run in the opposite direction from what you assume, or can be caused by a hidden third variable. Because the data alone cannot tell you which, a correlation is a reason to investigate further, not proof that one variable causes the other.</div>
      </div>
      <div class="faq-item">
        <button class="faq-q" onclick="toggleFAQ(this)">Why combine or cross-reference multiple data sets?<i class="faq-icon">+</i></button>
        <div class="faq-a">A single data set has limits. Joining two sets, for example sales and weather by date, can reveal a relationship that neither set shows on its own. Before combining, the data often needs cleaning and transforming so the sets line up, otherwise the combined result can be misleading.</div>
      </div>
      <div class="faq-item">
        <button class="faq-q" onclick="toggleFAQ(this)">Is more data always better?<i class="faq-icon">+</i></button>
        <div class="faq-a">No. Not all collected data is relevant to a given question, and a larger data set can bury the answer in noise. Larger data sets can reveal patterns that small samples miss, but only when they are processed efficiently and the irrelevant parts are filtered out. Classifying and filtering are what keep large data manageable.</div>
      </div>

    <div class="lesson-objectives">
      <h2>After this lesson, you will be able to:</h2>
      <ul>
        <li><span>Explain how programs process large data sets to gain insight and knowledge</span></li>
        <li><span>Describe why data must be cleaned and give examples of cleaning steps</span></li>
        <li><span>Distinguish transforming and standardizing data from removing bad records</span></li>
        <li><span>Choose a data visualization that fits the question being asked</span></li>
        <li><span>Judge whether a claim is actually supported by the data behind a visualization</span></li>
      </ul>
    </div>
    <div class="score-impact">📈 <span>Big Idea 2 (Data) is 17 to 22 percent of the AP CSP exam, the largest single Big Idea. Questions on cleaning data, choosing visualizations, and deciding whether a claim is supported are frequent and predictable points, and the skill of processing a list with a program is exactly what the Create Performance Task asks you to demonstrate.</span>
</div>
    <div class="hook-box">
      <div class="hook-label">💡 Think about this first</div>
      <p>A city posts a spreadsheet of 2 million bike-share trips. Half the rows have the date written three different ways, some riders appear twice, and a few trips claim to last 40 hours. You want to answer one question: which hour of the day is busiest? You cannot read 2 million rows by hand. What does a program have to do to that messy pile before any chart you make can be trusted?</p>
    </div>
    <div class="lesson-section">
      <h2>Why We Point Programs at Data</h2>
      <p>The core idea of this topic is simple and heavily tested: <strong>programs are used to process data in order to gain insight and knowledge</strong>. A person can eyeball a list of ten numbers, but real data sets have thousands or millions of records. A program can <strong>filter</strong> (keep only the rows that match a condition), <strong>aggregate</strong> (count, sum, or average groups of rows), <strong>transform</strong> (change each value into a new form), and <strong>combine</strong> data from more than one source, and it can do all of that in seconds.</p>
      <p>This ability to run operations over huge collections quickly is what makes programs valuable for data. The insight is not in the raw rows; it appears only after the program has organized, summarized, or filtered them. When a question asks what a program contributes to working with data, the answer is that it <strong>finds patterns and produces information a human could not extract by hand at that scale</strong>.</p>
      <div class="callout-exam">
        <div class="callout-exam-label">🎯 What the exam rewards</div>
        <p>Tie every data operation back to a <strong>question</strong>. Programs process data to answer something specific. "Count trips per hour to find the busiest hour" is a purpose; "run some code on the data" is not. Strong answers name the operation (filter, aggregate, transform, combine) and the insight it produces.</p>
      </div>
    </div>

    <div class="lesson-section">
      <h2>Clean First, Then Analyze</h2>
      <p>Raw data is almost never ready to use. Before a program can produce a trustworthy result, the data usually has to be <strong>cleaned</strong>. Cleaning covers two different jobs, and the exam expects you to tell them apart:</p>
      <ul>
        <li>
<strong>Removing bad records:</strong> deleting rows that are incomplete (missing values), duplicated (the same record twice), or invalid (a trip that lasts 40 hours, an age of 900).</li>
        <li>
<strong>Transforming and standardizing:</strong> putting values into one consistent format so they can be compared, such as writing every date as YYYY-MM-DD, converting all distances to the same unit, or making all text the same capitalization.</li>
      </ul>
      <p>Both jobs make the data <strong>usable and consistent</strong>. If you skip cleaning, the program will happily compute a wrong answer: duplicate riders inflate the count, mixed date formats break the sorting, and a stray 40-hour trip wrecks the average. Cleaning is not optional polish; it is what makes the later insight valid.</p>
      <table class="vocab-table">
        <tr>
<th>Messy data problem</th>
<th>Cleaning step that fixes it</th>
</tr>
        <tr>
<td>Dates stored as 03/04/25, March 4 2025, and 2025-03-04</td>
<td>Transform every date into one standard format so they sort and group correctly</td>
</tr>
        <tr>
<td>The same customer appears in three rows</td>
<td>Remove duplicate records so counts are not inflated</td>
</tr>
        <tr>
<td>Some rows have a blank price field</td>
<td>Remove or flag incomplete records so averages are not distorted</td>
</tr>
        <tr>
<td>City names as "boston", "Boston", and "BOSTON"</td>
<td>Standardize capitalization so the three are treated as one city</td>
</tr>
        <tr>
<td>A recorded age of 900 years</td>
<td>Remove or correct invalid records that fall outside a possible range</td>
</tr>
      </table>
      <div class="mini-ex">
        <div class="mini-ex-label">Quick check</div>
        <div class="mini-ex-q">A data set lists temperatures where some rows are in Celsius and others in Fahrenheit, with no label. Before a program can compute a meaningful average, the most important cleaning step is to:</div>
        <div class="mini-opts" id="mc-progdata-1-opts">
          <button class="mini-opt" onclick="miniMCQ('mc-progdata-1','A','C','mc-progdata-1-fb')"><span class="mini-opt-letter">A</span> Delete every row, since the data is unusable</button>
          <button class="mini-opt" onclick="miniMCQ('mc-progdata-1','B','C','mc-progdata-1-fb')"><span class="mini-opt-letter">B</span> Sort the rows from lowest to highest number</button>
          <button class="mini-opt" onclick="miniMCQ('mc-progdata-1','C','C','mc-progdata-1-fb')"><span class="mini-opt-letter">C</span> Transform all temperatures into a single consistent unit</button>
          <button class="mini-opt" onclick="miniMCQ('mc-progdata-1','D','C','mc-progdata-1-fb')"><span class="mini-opt-letter">D</span> Round every value to the nearest whole number</button>
        </div>
        <div class="mini-fb" id="mc-progdata-1-fb"></div>
      </div>
    </div>

    <div class="lesson-section">
      <h2>Classify, Filter, and Combine at Scale</h2>
      <p>Once data is clean, programs do the heavy lifting a person cannot. They <strong>classify</strong> records into groups, <strong>filter</strong> out the rows that do not matter, and <strong>combine</strong> data from separate sources to answer richer questions. The key property is <strong>scalability</strong>: the same program that handles 100 rows handles 100 million rows, so insights that would take a human lifetimes appear almost instantly.</p>
      <p>Scale is also why <strong>efficiency</strong> matters. A slow program that works on a small sample may be unusable on the full data set. The framework connects the size of the data to the need for programs that process it efficiently, because "it works on the test file" is not the same as "it finishes on the real one."</p>
      <div class="callout-trap">
        <div class="callout-trap-label">⚠ Common trap</div>
        <p>Do not assume more data always means a better answer. A larger data set only helps if it is <strong>cleaned and relevant to the question</strong>. Ten million rows full of duplicates and invalid values will mislead a program faster than a hundred clean rows. Size supports a claim only when the data actually measures what the claim is about.</p>
      </div>
    </div>

    <div class="lesson-section">
      <h2>Visualizations: The Right Chart for the Question</h2>
      <p>After a program processes data, a <strong>data visualization</strong> (a chart, table, graph, or map) communicates the pattern to people. Visualizations make trends and outliers visible and can <strong>support or challenge a hypothesis</strong>. But the right visualization depends entirely on the question you are asking, and the wrong one can hide the pattern or mislead the reader.</p>
      <table class="vocab-table">
        <tr>
<th>Question you are asking</th>
<th>Visualization that fits</th>
</tr>
        <tr>
<td>How has a value changed over time?</td>
<td>A line graph, with time on the horizontal axis</td>
</tr>
        <tr>
<td>How do a few categories compare in size?</td>
<td>A bar chart comparing the categories</td>
</tr>
        <tr>
<td>Where do events happen geographically?</td>
<td>A map with the locations plotted</td>
</tr>
        <tr>
<td>Is there a relationship between two numeric variables?</td>
<td>A scatter plot of one variable against the other</td>
</tr>
      </table>
      <p>A visualization can also <strong>mislead</strong>, sometimes by accident and sometimes on purpose: a bar chart whose vertical axis starts at 90 instead of 0 makes a tiny difference look huge, and a chart built from uncleaned data shows a pattern that is not real. Reading a visualization critically means asking what the axes show, what data it came from, and whether the picture actually supports the claim being made about it.</p>
      <div class="callout-exam">
        <div class="callout-exam-label">🎯 What the exam rewards</div>
        <p>Any conclusion drawn from data must be <strong>supported by that data</strong>. If a visualization shows sales rising and someone claims a specific ad campaign caused it, the exam wants you to notice that the chart shows a trend, not a cause. Match the strength of the claim to what the data can actually show.</p>
      </div>
      <div class="mini-ex">
        <div class="mini-ex-label">Quick check</div>
        <div class="mini-ex-q">You want to show how a store's monthly revenue changed across the twelve months of one year. Which visualization best fits that question?</div>
        <div class="mini-opts" id="mc-progdata-2-opts">
          <button class="mini-opt" onclick="miniMCQ('mc-progdata-2','A','B','mc-progdata-2-fb')"><span class="mini-opt-letter">A</span> A map of the store's location</button>
          <button class="mini-opt" onclick="miniMCQ('mc-progdata-2','B','B','mc-progdata-2-fb')"><span class="mini-opt-letter">B</span> A line graph with months on the horizontal axis</button>
          <button class="mini-opt" onclick="miniMCQ('mc-progdata-2','C','B','mc-progdata-2-fb')"><span class="mini-opt-letter">C</span> A single number showing the yearly total</button>
          <button class="mini-opt" onclick="miniMCQ('mc-progdata-2','D','B','mc-progdata-2-fb')"><span class="mini-opt-letter">D</span> A scatter plot of revenue against store size</button>
        </div>
        <div class="mini-fb" id="mc-progdata-2-fb"></div>
      </div>
    </div>

    <div class="lesson-section">
      <h2>How This Shows Up on the Create Performance Task</h2>
      <p>The Create Performance Task is completed <strong>individually</strong>, and a very common design is a program that <strong>processes a list of data</strong>. You are expected to include a list that stores several elements and a <strong>student-developed procedure</strong> that does meaningful work on that list, such as filtering it, counting matches, or computing a summary. That is exactly the data processing this lesson describes: your procedure loops over the collection and produces a result, which is the "gain insight from data" idea in miniature.</p>
      <p>The same concepts score on the multiple-choice section. Questions about which cleaning step fixes a described problem, which visualization fits a question, and whether a claim is supported by the data are frequent, so the vocabulary here (clean, transform, standardize, filter, aggregate, visualization, supported claim, scalability) pays off on both parts of the exam.</p>

      <div class="mcq-item" data-activity="quiz" data-item="q1">
        <div class="mcq-q-num">Question 1 of 6<span class="diff-tag">Concept</span>
</div>
        <div class="predict-note">Predict what a program adds to a large data set before reading the options.</div>
        <div class="mcq-q-text"><p>A researcher has a data set of 5 million weather readings and wants to know the average temperature for each month. Which statement best describes why a program is used for this task?</p></div>
        <div class="mcq-options" id="q1-options">
<button class="mcq-option" onclick="checkMCQ('q1','A','D','q1-fb-A')"><span class="mcq-option-letter">A</span> A program guarantees the readings were measured correctly by the sensors</button>
<button class="mcq-option" onclick="checkMCQ('q1','B','D','q1-fb-B')"><span class="mcq-option-letter">B</span> A program makes the data set smaller so it fits on the screen</button>
<button class="mcq-option" onclick="checkMCQ('q1','C','D','q1-fb-C')"><span class="mcq-option-letter">C</span> A program removes the need to decide what question is being asked</button>
<button class="mcq-option" onclick="checkMCQ('q1','D','D','q1-fb-D')"><span class="mcq-option-letter">D</span> A program can aggregate the readings into monthly averages far faster than a person could by hand</button>
</div>
<div id="q1-fb-A" class="mcq-feedback incorrect-fb">Incorrect. A program cannot verify how the physical measurements were taken; it processes the values it is given.</div>
<div id="q1-fb-B" class="mcq-feedback incorrect-fb">Incorrect. Producing an average is not about shrinking the data to fit a screen; it is about summarizing to answer a question.</div>
<div id="q1-fb-C" class="mcq-feedback incorrect-fb">Incorrect. A program still needs a question to answer. Choosing the question is the human's job, not something the program removes.</div>
<div id="q1-fb-D" class="mcq-feedback correct-fb">Correct. Programs process data to gain insight, here by aggregating millions of readings into monthly averages at a scale no person could match.</div>
      </div>
      <div class="mcq-item" data-activity="quiz" data-item="q2">
        <div class="mcq-q-num">Question 2 of 6<span class="diff-tag">Data cleaning scenario</span>
</div>
        <div class="predict-note">Name the cleaning problem before matching it to a fix.</div>
        <div class="mcq-q-text"><p>A store combines two customer files. Some customers appear in both files, several rows have a blank email field, and the join date is written as 1/2/25 in one file and 2025-01-02 in the other. To get a trustworthy count of unique customers per join date, which combination of cleaning steps is most appropriate?</p></div>
        <div class="mcq-options" id="q2-options">
<button class="mcq-option" onclick="checkMCQ('q2','A','A','q2-fb-A')"><span class="mcq-option-letter">A</span> Remove duplicate customers and standardize the date format so dates group correctly</button>
<button class="mcq-option" onclick="checkMCQ('q2','B','A','q2-fb-B')"><span class="mcq-option-letter">B</span> Sort the rows alphabetically and compute the count</button>
<button class="mcq-option" onclick="checkMCQ('q2','C','A','q2-fb-C')"><span class="mcq-option-letter">C</span> Delete the email column and leave everything else unchanged</button>
<button class="mcq-option" onclick="checkMCQ('q2','D','A','q2-fb-D')"><span class="mcq-option-letter">D</span> Round the dates to the nearest month and keep all rows</button>
</div>
<div id="q2-fb-A" class="mcq-feedback correct-fb">Correct. Removing duplicates prevents an inflated count, and standardizing the date format lets the same day group together instead of splitting across formats.</div>
<div id="q2-fb-B" class="mcq-feedback incorrect-fb">Incorrect. Sorting does not remove the duplicates or reconcile the two date formats, so the count would still be wrong.</div>
<div id="q2-fb-C" class="mcq-feedback incorrect-fb">Incorrect. Dropping the email column ignores the real problems: duplicate customers and inconsistent dates both still corrupt the count.</div>
<div id="q2-fb-D" class="mcq-feedback incorrect-fb">Incorrect. Rounding to the nearest month loses the join date detail and does nothing about the duplicate customers.</div>
      </div>
      <div class="mcq-item" data-activity="quiz" data-item="q3">
        <div class="mcq-q-num">Question 3 of 6<span class="diff-tag">II and III only style</span>
</div>
        <div class="predict-note">Decide which statements are true before matching to an option.</div>
        <div class="mcq-q-text"><p>Consider these claims about cleaning a data set before analysis:</p></div>
        <ul class="mcq-roman">
          <li>
<strong>I.</strong> Cleaning always means the data set becomes larger and more detailed.</li>
          <li>
<strong>II.</strong> Standardizing formats, such as writing all dates the same way, lets a program compare and group records correctly.</li>
          <li>
<strong>III.</strong> Removing incomplete, duplicate, or invalid records helps prevent misleading results.</li>
        </ul>
        <div class="mcq-options" id="q3-options">
<button class="mcq-option" onclick="checkMCQ('q3','A','A','q3-fb-A')"><span class="mcq-option-letter">A</span> II and III only</button>
<button class="mcq-option" onclick="checkMCQ('q3','B','A','q3-fb-B')"><span class="mcq-option-letter">B</span> I and II only</button>
<button class="mcq-option" onclick="checkMCQ('q3','C','A','q3-fb-C')"><span class="mcq-option-letter">C</span> I and III only</button>
<button class="mcq-option" onclick="checkMCQ('q3','D','A','q3-fb-D')"><span class="mcq-option-letter">D</span> I, II, and III</button>
</div>
<div id="q3-fb-A" class="mcq-feedback correct-fb">Correct. Standardizing formats (II) and removing bad records (III) are both cleaning steps. I is false because cleaning frequently shrinks the data set.</div>
<div id="q3-fb-B" class="mcq-feedback incorrect-fb">Incorrect. Statement I is false. Cleaning often removes records, so the data set does not always grow.</div>
<div id="q3-fb-C" class="mcq-feedback incorrect-fb">Incorrect. Statement I is false, and statement II is true, so this pairing cannot be right.</div>
<div id="q3-fb-D" class="mcq-feedback incorrect-fb">Incorrect. Statement I is false, so not all three can be correct.</div>
      </div>
      <div class="mcq-item" data-activity="quiz" data-item="q4">
        <div class="mcq-q-num">Question 4 of 6<span class="diff-tag">Does the visualization support the claim</span>
</div>
        <div class="predict-note">Decide what the chart can and cannot prove before you read the choices.</div>
        <div class="mcq-q-text"><p>A blog shows a line graph of a company's website visits rising steadily over six months. The caption claims, "Our new logo caused visits to grow." Which criticism of this claim is most valid?</p></div>
        <div class="mcq-options" id="q4-options">
<button class="mcq-option" onclick="checkMCQ('q4','A','C','q4-fb-A')"><span class="mcq-option-letter">A</span> A line graph can never be used to show change over time</button>
<button class="mcq-option" onclick="checkMCQ('q4','B','C','q4-fb-B')"><span class="mcq-option-letter">B</span> The claim is fine because the line goes up, which proves the logo worked</button>
<button class="mcq-option" onclick="checkMCQ('q4','C','C','q4-fb-C')"><span class="mcq-option-letter">C</span> The graph shows visits increased, but it does not show that the logo, rather than some other factor, caused the increase</button>
<button class="mcq-option" onclick="checkMCQ('q4','D','C','q4-fb-D')"><span class="mcq-option-letter">D</span> The claim would only be valid if the data set were smaller</button>
</div>
<div id="q4-fb-A" class="mcq-feedback incorrect-fb">Incorrect. A line graph is an appropriate choice for change over time; that is not the flaw.</div>
<div id="q4-fb-B" class="mcq-feedback incorrect-fb">Incorrect. An upward line shows a trend, not a cause. Concluding the logo caused it goes beyond what the data supports.</div>
<div id="q4-fb-C" class="mcq-feedback correct-fb">Correct. The visualization supports that visits rose, but a rising trend is not evidence of cause. Other factors could explain the growth, so the causal claim is unsupported.</div>
<div id="q4-fb-D" class="mcq-feedback incorrect-fb">Incorrect. Shrinking the data set would weaken evidence, not fix the problem. The issue is claiming cause from a trend.</div>
      </div>
      <div class="mcq-item" data-activity="quiz" data-item="q5">
        <div class="mcq-q-num">Question 5 of 6<span class="diff-tag">Choose the visualization</span>
</div>
        <div class="predict-note">Match the question to a chart type before looking.</div>
        <div class="mcq-q-text"><p>An analyst wants to know whether students who spend more hours studying tend to score higher on a test, using data for 500 students. Which visualization most directly reveals the relationship between the two numeric variables?</p></div>
        <div class="mcq-options" id="q5-options">
<button class="mcq-option" onclick="checkMCQ('q5','A','C','q5-fb-A')"><span class="mcq-option-letter">A</span> A map of where each student lives</button>
<button class="mcq-option" onclick="checkMCQ('q5','B','C','q5-fb-B')"><span class="mcq-option-letter">B</span> A single bar showing the average test score</button>
<button class="mcq-option" onclick="checkMCQ('q5','C','C','q5-fb-C')"><span class="mcq-option-letter">C</span> A scatter plot of study hours against test score</button>
<button class="mcq-option" onclick="checkMCQ('q5','D','C','q5-fb-D')"><span class="mcq-option-letter">D</span> A table listing all 500 students in the order they enrolled</button>
</div>
<div id="q5-fb-A" class="mcq-feedback incorrect-fb">Incorrect. A map answers a location question, not whether two numeric variables are related.</div>
<div id="q5-fb-B" class="mcq-feedback incorrect-fb">Incorrect. A single average hides the relationship between the two variables entirely.</div>
<div id="q5-fb-C" class="mcq-feedback correct-fb">Correct. A scatter plot of one numeric variable against another is built to reveal whether a relationship exists, such as higher study hours pairing with higher scores.</div>
<div id="q5-fb-D" class="mcq-feedback incorrect-fb">Incorrect. An unsorted table of 500 rows does not make the relationship visible; that is exactly the pattern a visualization should surface.</div>
      </div>
      <div class="mcq-item" data-activity="quiz" data-item="q6">
        <div class="mcq-q-num">Question 6 of 6<span class="diff-tag">Scalability application</span>
</div>
        <div class="predict-note">Predict why the sample worked but the full data set did not.</div>
        <div class="mcq-q-text"><p>A program that flags fraudulent transactions runs in a second on a test file of 1,000 records but takes several days on the real file of 2 billion records, making it useless in practice. Which conclusion is best supported?</p></div>
        <div class="mcq-options" id="q6-options">
<button class="mcq-option" onclick="checkMCQ('q6','A','B','q6-fb-A')"><span class="mcq-option-letter">A</span> The program produces incorrect results on small data sets</button>
<button class="mcq-option" onclick="checkMCQ('q6','B','B','q6-fb-B')"><span class="mcq-option-letter">B</span> The program is not efficient enough to scale to the size of the real data set</button>
<button class="mcq-option" onclick="checkMCQ('q6','C','B','q6-fb-C')"><span class="mcq-option-letter">C</span> The real data set must contain invalid records that cannot be cleaned</button>
<button class="mcq-option" onclick="checkMCQ('q6','D','B','q6-fb-D')"><span class="mcq-option-letter">D</span> Large data sets should always be reduced to 1,000 records before processing</button>
</div>
<div id="q6-fb-A" class="mcq-feedback incorrect-fb">Incorrect. It ran correctly on the small file in a second; the issue appears only at scale.</div>
<div id="q6-fb-B" class="mcq-feedback correct-fb">Correct. A program that is fast on a sample but too slow on the full data set is not scalable. Larger data sets demand more efficient programs.</div>
<div id="q6-fb-C" class="mcq-feedback incorrect-fb">Incorrect. Nothing here points to invalid records. The described problem is running time, not data quality.</div>
<div id="q6-fb-D" class="mcq-feedback incorrect-fb">Incorrect. Throwing away most of the data to make it fast would discard the very records the analysis needs; the fix is a more efficient program.</div>
      </div>

(function(){

  // ---- Chart drawing helpers (no libraries) ----
  function barChart(cap, data, hlIndex){
    var max = Math.max.apply(null, data.map(function(d){ return d.v; }));
    var html = '<div class="th-cap">' + cap + '</div><div class="th-bars">';
    data.forEach(function(d, i){
      var h = max > 0 ? Math.round((d.v / max) * 100) : 0;
      var hl = (hlIndex === i) ? ' hl' : '';
      html += '<div class="th-col' + hl + '">'
        + '<div class="th-colval">' + d.v + '</div>'
        + '<div class="th-colbar" style="height:' + h + '%"></div>'
        + '<div class="th-collab">' + d.l + '</div></div>';
    });
    return html + '</div>';
  }

  function lineChart(cap, data){
    var W = 500, H = 170, padL = 34, padR = 14, padT = 12, padB = 26;
    var vals = data.map(function(d){ return d.v; });
    var max = Math.max.apply(null, vals), min = Math.min.apply(null, vals);
    if(max === min){ max = max + 1; min = min - 1; }
    var iw = W - padL - padR, ih = H - padT - padB;
    var pts = data.map(function(d, i){
      var x = padL + (data.length === 1 ? iw / 2 : (i / (data.length - 1)) * iw);
      var y = padT + ih - ((d.v - min) / (max - min)) * ih;
      return { x: x, y: y, d: d };
    });
    var svg = '<div class="th-cap">' + cap + '</div>';
    svg += '<svg viewBox="0 0 ' + W + ' ' + H + '" role="img" aria-label="' + cap + '">';
    // gridlines
    for(var g = 0; g <= 3; g++){
      var gy = padT + (ih / 3) * g;
      svg += '<line x1="' + padL + '" y1="' + gy + '" x2="' + (W - padR) + '" y2="' + gy + '" stroke="#e2e8f0" stroke-width="1"/>';
    }
    // axis
    svg += '<line x1="' + padL + '" y1="' + padT + '" x2="' + padL + '" y2="' + (padT + ih) + '" stroke="#94a3b8" stroke-width="1"/>';
    svg += '<line x1="' + padL + '" y1="' + (padT + ih) + '" x2="' + (W - padR) + '" y2="' + (padT + ih) + '" stroke="#94a3b8" stroke-width="1"/>';
    // path
    var dstr = pts.map(function(p, i){ return (i === 0 ? 'M' : 'L') + p.x.toFixed(1) + ' ' + p.y.toFixed(1); }).join(' ');
    svg += '<path d="' + dstr + '" fill="none" stroke="#1a56db" stroke-width="2.5" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round"/>';
    // points + labels
    pts.forEach(function(p){
      svg += '<circle cx="' + p.x.toFixed(1) + '" cy="' + p.y.toFixed(1) + '" r="3.5" fill="#1a56db"/>';
      svg += '<text x="' + p.x.toFixed(1) + '" y="' + (padT + ih + 16) + '" font-size="10" fill="#64748b" text-anchor="middle" font-family="DM Sans, sans-serif">' + p.d.l + '</text>';
    });
    svg += '</svg>';
    return svg;

  var TOTAL = ROUNDS.length;
  var order = [], idx = 0, score = 0, streak = 0, correctCount = 0, answered = false;

  function shuffle(a){
    for(var i = a.length - 1; i > 0; i--){
      var j = Math.floor(Math.random() * (i + 1));
      var t = a[i]; a[i] = a[j]; a[j] = t;
    }
    return a;

  function start(){
    order = ROUNDS.slice();
    idx = 0; score = 0; streak = 0; correctCount = 0;

  function updateBar(){
    $('th-round').textContent = Math.min(idx + 1, TOTAL);

  function render(){
    answered = false;
    var r = order[idx];
    $('th-qtext').textContent = r.q;
    $('th-qctx').textContent = r.ctx;

    // animate bars from 0 for a lively feel
    if(r.type === 'bar'){
      var bars = $('th-chart').querySelectorAll('.th-colbar');
      var heights = [];
      Array.prototype.forEach.call(bars, function(b){ heights.push(b.style.height); b.style.height = '0%'; });
      setTimeout(function(){ Array.prototype.forEach.call(bars, function(b, i){ b.style.height = heights[i]; }); }, 30);
    }

    var opts = $('th-opts');
    opts.innerHTML = '';
    var shuffled = shuffle(r.opts.map(function(o, i){ return { o:o, i:i }; }));
    shuffled.forEach(function(entry){
      var btn = document.createElement('button');
      btn.className = 'th-opt';
      btn.type = 'button';
      btn.textContent = entry.o.t;
      btn.onclick = function(){ choose(btn, entry.o, r); };
      opts.appendChild(btn);
    });

    var fb = $('th-fb'); fb.className = 'th-fb'; fb.textContent = '';
    $('th-next').className = 'th-next';
    $('th-next').innerHTML = (idx === TOTAL - 1) ? 'See results ▶' : 'Next round ▶';
    updateBar();
  }

  function choose(btn, opt, r){
    if(answered) return;
    answered = true;
    var buttons = $('th-opts').querySelectorAll('.th-opt');
    Array.prototype.forEach.call(buttons, function(b){
      b.disabled = true;
      if(b.textContent === r.opts.filter(function(o){ return o.ok; })[0].t){ b.classList.add('correct'); }
    });
    var fb = $('th-fb');
    if(opt.ok){
      score += 10 + streak * 5;
      streak += 1;
      correctCount += 1;
      fb.className = 'th-fb show good';
      fb.innerHTML = '<b>✅ Correct.</b> ' + r.fb;
    } else {
      streak = 0;
      btn.classList.add('wrong');
      fb.className = 'th-fb show bad';
      fb.innerHTML = '<b>❌ Not quite.</b> ' + r.fb;
    }
    updateBar();
    var nx = $('th-next');
    nx.className = 'th-next show';
  }

  function nextRound(){
    idx += 1;
    if(idx >= TOTAL){ end(); return; }
    render();
  }

  function end(){
    $('th-play').style.display = 'none';
    $('th-end').style.display = 'block';
    $('th-progfill').style.width = '100%';
    $('th-round').textContent = TOTAL;
    $('th-finalscore').textContent = score;
    $('th-accuracy').textContent = correctCount + ' of ' + TOTAL + ' rounds correct';
    var msg, title;
    if(correctCount === TOTAL){
      title = 'Master data detective!';
      msg = 'Flawless. You read every trend and never mistook a <b>correlation for causation</b>. Real analysts always ask what lurking variable might be hiding.';
    } else if(correctCount >= TOTAL - 2){
      title = 'Sharp analyst!';
      msg = 'Strong work spotting trends and outliers. Remember: data reveals patterns, but a correlation alone is <b>never proof of causation</b>.';
    } else {
      title = 'Keep hunting!';
      msg = 'Good start. The big idea: data shows patterns and outliers, yet two things moving together does <b>not</b> mean one causes the other. More data or metadata can change the picture.';
    }
    $('th-endt').textContent = title;
    $('th-endmsg').innerHTML = msg;
    document.dispatchEvent(new CustomEvent('apcsGameScore', { detail: { value: score } }));
  }

  $('th-next').addEventListener('click', nextRound);
  $('th-again').addEventListener('click', start);

  start();
})();
</script>

      <div class="faq-item">
        <button class="faq-q" onclick="toggleFAQ(this)">Why does data need to be cleaned before a program analyzes it?<i class="faq-icon">+</i></button>
        <div class="faq-a">Raw data usually contains incomplete, duplicate, or invalid records and inconsistent formats. If you analyze it as is, the program computes a wrong answer: duplicates inflate counts, blanks distort averages, and mixed formats break sorting and grouping. Cleaning makes the data usable and consistent so the insight is valid.</div>
      </div>
      <div class="faq-item">
        <button class="faq-q" onclick="toggleFAQ(this)">What is the difference between removing records and transforming data?<i class="faq-icon">+</i></button>
        <div class="faq-a">Removing records deletes rows that should not be counted, such as duplicates, blanks, or impossible values. Transforming, or standardizing, changes the form of the values that stay, such as writing every date the same way or converting units, so they can be compared. Both are cleaning, but one drops data and the other reformats it.</div>
      </div>
      <div class="faq-item">
        <button class="faq-q" onclick="toggleFAQ(this)">How do I know which visualization to use?<i class="faq-icon">+</i></button>
        <div class="faq-a">Start from the question. Change over time fits a line graph, comparing a few categories fits a bar chart, geographic patterns fit a map, and a relationship between two numeric variables fits a scatter plot. The right choice is the one that makes the pattern the question asks about easy to see.</div>
      </div>

A vertical axis that does not start at zero can exaggerate a tiny difference, a cherry-picked time range can hide a trend, and a chart can imply a cause that the data only shows as a correlation. Always check the axes, the source data, and whether the claim matches what the chart actually shows.</div>
