  .related-ext{color:var(--slate)!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:var(--slate)!important;border-color:#e2e8f0;}
  .superpack-slim{background:#fff;border:1px solid #bfdbfe;border-radius:10px;padding:16px 20px;display:flex;align-items:center;justify-content:space-between;gap:16px;flex-wrap:wrap;margin-bottom:36px;}
  .superpack-slim-icon{width:36px;height:36px;border-radius:8px;background:var(--bi3-bg);display:flex;align-items:center;justify-content:center;font-size:16px;flex-shrink:0;}
  .superpack-slim-text{font-size:14px;color:var(--navy)!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:var(--navy)!important;font-weight:600;line-height:1.3;}
  .superpack-slim-sub{font-size:12px;color:var(--slate);font-weight:400;display:block;margin-top:2px;}
  .superpack-slim-btn{display:inline-flex!important;align-items:center!important;gap:6px!important;background:var(--bi3)!important;color:#fff!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:#fff!important;padding:9px 18px!important;border-radius:7px!important;font-size:13px!important;font-weight:600!important;text-decoration:none!important;white-space:nowrap!important;}
  .superpack-slim-btn:link,.superpack-slim-btn:visited{color:#fff!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:#fff!important;}

The benefit-versus-limitation trade-off is a favorite trap, and a simulation is a natural Create Task program.</span>
</div>
    <div class="hook-box">
      <div class="hook-label">💡 Think about this first</div>
      <p>How would you find the chance of rolling a 6? You could roll a real die thousands of times, or you could write ten lines of code that rolls a virtual die a million times in a second, counts the sixes, and reports the fraction. That is a simulation: a safe, fast, repeatable model of the real world. The catch is that a model is only a model, and this lesson is about trusting it exactly as far as its assumptions allow.</p>
    </div>
    <div class="lesson-section">
      <h2>What a Simulation Is</h2>
      <p>A <strong>simulation</strong> is a program that imitates a real-world process so you can study it on a computer instead of in the real world. It is a kind of <strong>abstraction</strong>: it keeps the details that matter for the question you are asking and leaves out everything else. A flight simulator does not recreate every molecule of air; it keeps just enough physics to practice flying. Because a simulation is built on <strong>assumptions</strong> and <strong>hypotheses</strong> about how the real thing behaves, it is a simplified stand-in, not a perfect copy.</p>
      <p>Many simulations include <strong>randomness</strong>, because the real process being modeled has chance in it: a coin flip, a dice roll, whether it rains, which customer arrives next. The simulation uses a random number generator to mimic that uncertainty, and it uses a <strong>loop</strong> to run the scenario many times so it can see the range of things that could happen.</p>

The <code>random.seed(1)</code> line fixes the random sequence so the run is reproducible: everyone who runs it gets the same tally.     <div class="lesson-section">
      <h2>Why We Simulate</h2>
      <p>If you can flip a real coin, why write a program to flip a fake one? Because for most interesting questions the real experiment is expensive, slow, dangerous, or impossible to repeat. A simulation removes those obstacles:</p>
      <ul>
        <li>
<strong>Cheaper and safer:</strong> crash-test a bridge design or a rocket engine on a computer before spending money or risking harm.</li>
        <li>
<strong>Faster:</strong> a program can play out a hundred years of climate or a million dice games in seconds.</li>
        <li>
<strong>Repeatable and adjustable:</strong> you can run the exact same scenario again, or change one parameter (the rain chance, the number of trials) and immediately see the effect.</li>
        <li>
<strong>Observable:</strong> you can model things that are hard to watch directly, like the spread of a disease or the motion of galaxies.</li>
      </ul>

<span class="py-kw">print</span><span class="py-var">(</span><span class="py-var">sixes</span><span class="py-var"> </span><span class="py-var">*</span><span class="py-var"> </span><span class="py-num">100</span><span class="py-var"> </span><span class="py-comment">// trials)</span></pre></div>

<span class="ps-var">trials</span><span class="ps-var"> </span><span class="ps-var"><</span><span class="ps-var">-</span><span class="ps-var"> </span><span class="ps-num">600</span>
<span class="ps-kw">REPEAT</span><span class="ps-var"> </span><span class="ps-var">trials</span><span class="ps-var"> </span><span class="ps-kw">TIMES</span>
<span class="ps-var">{</span>
<span class="ps-var"> </span><span class="ps-var"> </span><span class="ps-var"> </span><span class="ps-var"> </span><span class="ps-var">roll</span><span class="ps-var"> </span><span class="ps-var"><</span><span class="ps-var">-</span><span class="ps-var"> </span><span class="ps-var">RANDOM</span><span class="ps-var">(</span><span class="ps-num">1</span><span class="ps-var">,</span><span class="ps-var"> </span><span class="ps-num">6</span><span class="ps-var">)</span>

<span class="ps-var"> </span><span class="ps-var"> </span><span class="ps-var"> </span><span class="ps-var"> </span><span class="ps-var">{</span>
<span class="ps-var"> </span><span class="ps-var"> </span><span class="ps-var"> </span><span class="ps-var"> </span><span class="ps-var"> </span><span class="ps-var"> </span><span class="ps-var"> </span><span class="ps-var"> </span><span class="ps-var">sixes</span><span class="ps-var"> </span><span class="ps-var"><</span><span class="ps-var">-</span><span class="ps-var"> </span><span class="ps-var">sixes</span><span class="ps-var"> </span><span class="ps-var">+</span><span class="ps-var"> </span><span class="ps-num">1</span>
<span class="ps-var"> </span><span class="ps-var"> </span><span class="ps-var"> </span><span class="ps-var"> </span><span class="ps-var">}</span>
<span class="ps-var">}</span>
<span class="ps-kw">DISPLAY</span><span class="ps-var">(</span><span class="ps-var">sixes</span><span class="ps-var"> </span><span class="ps-var">*</span><span class="ps-var"> </span><span class="ps-num">100</span><span class="ps-var"> </span><span class="ps-var">/</span><span class="ps-var"> </span><span class="ps-var">trials</span><span class="ps-var">)</span></pre></div>
</div>
      <p>Here the loop runs 600 trials of rolling a die and counts how often a 6 appears, then reports that count as a percent of the trials. That percent is an <strong>estimate</strong> of the true probability of rolling a 6. This is the core pattern of a probability simulation: run many trials, tally an outcome, report the fraction.</p>
      <div class="callout-exam">
        <div class="callout-exam-label">🎯 More trials, more reliable</div>
        <p>The more independent trials you run, the closer the estimate tends to land to the true probability. Six hundred rolls gives a steadier estimate than six rolls. A favorite exam idea: increasing the number of trials improves the reliability of the estimate but never makes it exact.</p>
      </div>
    </div>

    <div class="lesson-section">
      <h2>Randomness, Seeds, and Reproducibility</h2>
      <p>Randomness is what makes a simulation feel like the real, unpredictable world, and it is also why two runs can give slightly different answers. To make a run reproducible for testing or grading, you set a <strong>seed</strong>. Seeding fixes the random sequence, so the same seed always produces the same outcomes. That is useful, but the seed has to be set in the right place.</p>
      <div class="code-panel-wrap">
  <div class="code-panel-tabs">
    <button class="code-tab py active" onclick="switchTab(this,'py','pan-3')">🐛 Python (buggy)</button>
    <button class="code-tab pseudo" onclick="switchTab(this,'pseudo','pan-3')">📋 Pseudocode (fixed)</button>
  </div>
  <div class="code-pane active" id="pan-3-py"><pre><span class="py-comment"># BUG: seed is inside the loop</span>
<span class="py-kw">for</span><span class="py-var"> </span><span class="py-var">i</span><span class="py-var"> </span><span class="py-kw">in</span><span class="py-var"> </span><span class="py-kw">range</span><span class="py-var">(</span><span class="py-num">4</span><span class="py-var">)</span><span class="py-var">:</span>
<span class="py-var"> </span><span class="py-var"> </span><span class="py-var"> </span><span class="py-var"> </span><span class="py-var">random</span><span class="py-var">.</span><span class="py-var">seed</span><span class="py-var">(</span><span class="py-num">1</span><span class="py-var">)</span>
<span class="py-var"> </span><span class="py-var"> </span><span class="py-var"> </span><span class="py-var"> </span><span class="py-kw">print</span><span class="py-var">(</span><span class="py-var">random</span><span class="py-var">.</span><span class="py-var">randint</span><span class="py-var">(</span><span class="py-num">1</span><span class="py-var">,</span><span class="py-var"> </span><span class="py-num">6</span><span class="py-var">)</span><span class="py-var">)</span></pre></div>
  <div class="code-pane" id="pan-3-pseudo"><pre><span class="ps-comment"># FIX: seed once, before the loop</span>
<span class="ps-var">random</span><span class="ps-var">.</span><span class="ps-var">seed</span><span class="ps-var">(</span><span class="ps-num">1</span><span class="ps-var">)</span>
<span class="ps-kw">REPEAT</span><span class="ps-var"> </span><span class="ps-num">4</span><span class="ps-var"> </span><span class="ps-kw">TIMES</span>
<span class="ps-var">{</span>
<span class="ps-var"> </span><span class="ps-var"> </span><span class="ps-var"> </span><span class="ps-var"> </span><span class="ps-kw">DISPLAY</span><span class="ps-var">(</span><span class="ps-var">RANDOM</span><span class="ps-var">(</span><span class="ps-num">1</span><span class="ps-var">,</span><span class="ps-var"> </span><span class="ps-num">6</span><span class="ps-var">)</span><span class="ps-var">)</span>
<span class="ps-var">}</span></pre></div>
</div>
      <p>On the left the seed is placed <em>inside</em> the loop, so every iteration resets the generator to the same starting point and every roll comes out identical. That is not a simulation of four different rolls, it is the same roll printed four times. The fix on the right seeds <strong>once</strong>, before the loop, so the four rolls vary as intended while the whole run stays reproducible.</p>
      <div class="callout-trap">
        <div class="callout-trap-label">⚠ Runs differ, and that is expected</div>
        <p>Because a simulation uses randomness, two runs with different seeds can produce different tallies and different estimates. That variation is not a bug. It is a property of the model. It also means a single run is weak evidence: you judge a simulation by many trials, not one lucky result.</p>
      </div>

    <div class="lesson-section">
      <h2>Limitations: A Model Is Only as Good as Its Assumptions</h2>
      <p>A simulation is powerful precisely because it simplifies, and that simplification is also its weakness. Every simulation leaves things out, and its results are only as trustworthy as the assumptions built into it. If the model assumes a fair coin but the real coin is weighted, the simulation will confidently produce wrong conclusions. The output is an <strong>approximation</strong> of reality that depends entirely on the quality of the model.</p>
      <p>The parameterized weather model below assumes a fixed 40 percent chance of rain every single day, independent of the day before. Real weather does not work that way, so this simulation is a rough abstraction. It is still useful for exploring "what if the chance were higher," but its numbers should never be mistaken for a real forecast.</p>

<span class="py-kw">for</span><span class="py-var"> </span><span class="py-var">day</span><span class="py-var"> </span><span class="py-kw">in</span><span class="py-var"> </span><span class="py-kw">range</span><span class="py-var">(</span><span class="py-num">30</span><span class="py-var">)</span><span class="py-var">:</span>
<span class="py-var"> </span><span class="py-var"> </span><span class="py-var"> </span><span class="py-var"> </span><span class="py-kw">if</span><span class="py-var"> </span><span class="py-var">random</span><span class="py-var">.</span><span class="py-var">randint</span><span class="py-var">(</span><span class="py-num">1</span><span class="py-var">,</span><span class="py-var"> </span><span class="py-num">100</span><span class="py-var">)</span><span class="py-var"> </span><span class="py-var"><</span><span class="py-var">=</span><span class="py-var"> </span><span class="py-var">chance</span><span class="py-var">:</span>
<span class="py-var"> </span><span class="py-var"> </span><span class="py-var"> </span><span class="py-var"> </span><span class="py-var"> </span><span class="py-var"> </span><span class="py-var"> </span><span class="py-var"> </span><span class="py-var">rainy</span><span class="py-var"> </span><span class="py-var">=</span><span class="py-var"> </span><span class="py-var">rainy</span><span class="py-var"> </span><span class="py-var">+</span><span class="py-var"> </span><span class="py-num">1</span>
<span class="py-kw">print</span><span class="py-var">(</span><span class="py-var">rainy</span><span class="py-var">)</span></pre></div>

<span class="ps-kw">REPEAT</span><span class="ps-var"> </span><span class="ps-num">30</span><span class="ps-var"> </span><span class="ps-kw">TIMES</span>

<span class="ps-var"> </span><span class="ps-var"> </span><span class="ps-var"> </span><span class="ps-var"> </span><span class="ps-var">}</span>

      <p>When you evaluate a simulation, ask two questions: are the assumptions reasonable for the question being asked, and were enough trials run to make the estimate stable? A well-built simulation with sound assumptions and many trials gives a useful approximation. A simulation with bad assumptions gives precise-looking numbers that are simply wrong.</p>

      <div class="cpt-connection-label">📋 Create Performance Task • A simulation as your program</div>
      <p>A simulation is a strong choice for the Create Performance Task because it naturally uses a list, a loop, randomness, and a procedure that returns a result, which is exactly the machinery the rubric rewards. The key is to describe it honestly as a model with assumptions, not as reality.</p>
      <h3>A point-earning example</h3>
      <p>Imagine a program that estimates the chance of rolling a 6 by simulating many dice rolls and reporting the percentage:</p>
      <div class="cpt-code">sixes <- 0
trials <- 1000
REPEAT trials TIMES
{
    roll <- RANDOM(1, 6)
    IF (roll = 6)
    {
        sixes <- sixes + 1
    }
}
DISPLAY(sixes * 100 / trials)</div>
      <p>In your written response, name the phenomenon, the randomness, and the role of iteration:</p>
      <ul class="cpt-stems">
        <li>"My program simulates rolling a fair die, using <code>RANDOM(1, 6)</code> to model one roll."</li>
        <li>"The loop runs 1000 independent trials and tallies how many are a 6, so the output estimates the probability rather than computing it exactly."</li>
        <li>"Because the estimate depends on randomness, running more trials makes it more reliable, but it remains an approximation based on the assumption that the die is fair."</li>
      </ul>
      <h3>The trap to avoid</h3>
      <p>Do not claim your simulation produces the true, exact answer. A simulation reports an approximation that depends on its assumptions and the number of trials. Saying "this proves the probability is exactly 16 percent" loses the abstraction point. <a href="/pages/ap-csp-course-create-task">See the full Create Task module →</a></p>

<span class="k">n</span> = <span class="n">45</span>
<span class="k">t</span> = <span class="n">60</span>
<span class="k">print</span>(n * <span class="n">100</span> // t)</div>

<button class="mcq-option" onclick="checkMCQ('q1','A','D','q1-fb-A')"><span class="mcq-option-letter">A</span> 45</button>
<button class="mcq-option" onclick="checkMCQ('q1','B','D','q1-fb-B')"><span class="mcq-option-letter">B</span> 60</button>
<button class="mcq-option" onclick="checkMCQ('q1','C','D','q1-fb-C')"><span class="mcq-option-letter">C</span> 133</button>
<button class="mcq-option" onclick="checkMCQ('q1','D','D','q1-fb-D')"><span class="mcq-option-letter">D</span> 75</button>
</div>
<div id="q1-fb-A" class="mcq-feedback incorrect-fb">Incorrect. 45 is the raw success count n, not the percent. You still divide by the trials after multiplying by 100.</div>
<div id="q1-fb-B" class="mcq-feedback incorrect-fb">Incorrect. 60 is the number of trials t, not the percent of successes.</div>
<div id="q1-fb-C" class="mcq-feedback incorrect-fb">Incorrect. 133 is t * 100 // n, the ratio computed upside down. The successes go on top.</div>
<div id="q1-fb-D" class="mcq-feedback correct-fb">Correct. 45 * 100 is 4500, and 4500 // 60 is 75, so it reports 75 percent.</div>

      <div class="mcq-item" data-activity="quiz" data-item="q2">
        <div class="mcq-q-num">Question 2 of 6<span class="diff-tag">Spot the bug</span>
</div>
        <div class="mcq-q-text">This is meant to run a reproducible simulation of four <strong>different</strong> dice rolls. What is the bug?</div>
        <div class="mcq-code">
<span class="k">import</span> random
<span class="k">for</span> i <span class="k">in</span> <span class="k">range</span>(<span class="n">4</span>):
    random.seed(<span class="n">1</span>)
    <span class="k">print</span>(random.randint(<span class="n">1</span>, <span class="n">6</span>))</div>
        <div class="mcq-options" id="q2-options">
<button class="mcq-option" onclick="checkMCQ('q2','A','A','q2-fb-A')"><span class="mcq-option-letter">A</span> The seed is set inside the loop, so every roll restarts from the same point and all four rolls are identical</button>
<button class="mcq-option" onclick="checkMCQ('q2','B','A','q2-fb-B')"><span class="mcq-option-letter">B</span> The range should start at 1, so range(4) skips the first roll of the simulation</button>
<button class="mcq-option" onclick="checkMCQ('q2','C','A','q2-fb-C')"><span class="mcq-option-letter">C</span> randint(1, 6) can only return 1 or 6, so the other faces never appear</button>
<button class="mcq-option" onclick="checkMCQ('q2','D','A','q2-fb-D')"><span class="mcq-option-letter">D</span> A simulation is not allowed to call random more than once per program</button>
</div>
<div id="q2-fb-A" class="mcq-feedback correct-fb">Correct. Reseeding to 1 every iteration resets the generator, so randint returns the same value each time and the four rolls are the same, not four different rolls.</div>
<div id="q2-fb-B" class="mcq-feedback incorrect-fb">Incorrect. range(4) correctly produces four iterations. The problem is the seed placement, not the range.</div>
<div id="q2-fb-C" class="mcq-feedback incorrect-fb">Incorrect. randint(1, 6) returns any integer from 1 to 6 inclusive, not only the endpoints.</div>
<div id="q2-fb-D" class="mcq-feedback incorrect-fb">Incorrect. There is no such rule. Calling random repeatedly is exactly how a simulation runs many trials.</div>

<button class="mcq-option" onclick="checkMCQ('q3','A','B','q3-fb-A')"><span class="mcq-option-letter">A</span> The comparison should be = instead of ==, so the if never runs</button>
<button class="mcq-option" onclick="checkMCQ('q3','B','B','q3-fb-B')"><span class="mcq-option-letter">B</span> The counter c is reset to 0 inside the loop, so only the last entry is ever counted</button>
<button class="mcq-option" onclick="checkMCQ('q3','C','B','q3-fb-C')"><span class="mcq-option-letter">C</span> range(len(data)) skips the last index, so one entry is missed</button>
<button class="mcq-option" onclick="checkMCQ('q3','D','B','q3-fb-D')"><span class="mcq-option-letter">D</span> print(c) is outside the loop, so nothing is ever displayed</button>

<div id="q3-fb-B" class="mcq-feedback correct-fb">Correct. c = 0 sits inside the loop, so every iteration wipes the running total. The final value reflects only the last element, not the whole tally.</div>
<div id="q3-fb-C" class="mcq-feedback incorrect-fb">Incorrect. range(len(data)) visits every valid index from 0 to len(data) - 1, so no entry is skipped.</div>

        <div class="mcq-q-text">Which of the following statements about simulations are <strong>true</strong>?</div>
        <ul class="mcq-roman">
          <li>
<strong>I.</strong> A simulation uses simplifying assumptions, so its results are approximations of the real world.</li>
          <li>
<strong>II.</strong> Running more independent trials generally makes the estimate more reliable.</li>
          <li>
<strong>III.</strong> A simulation that uses randomness produces the exact same output on every run, no matter the seed.</li>
        </ul>
        <div class="mcq-options" id="q4-options">
<button class="mcq-option" onclick="checkMCQ('q4','A','C','q4-fb-A')"><span class="mcq-option-letter">A</span> I only</button>
<button class="mcq-option" onclick="checkMCQ('q4','B','C','q4-fb-B')"><span class="mcq-option-letter">B</span> II and III only</button>
<button class="mcq-option" onclick="checkMCQ('q4','C','C','q4-fb-C')"><span class="mcq-option-letter">C</span> I and II only</button>
<button class="mcq-option" onclick="checkMCQ('q4','D','C','q4-fb-D')"><span class="mcq-option-letter">D</span> I, II, and III</button>
</div>
<div id="q4-fb-A" class="mcq-feedback incorrect-fb">Incorrect. I is true, but II is also true: more independent trials generally give a more reliable estimate.</div>
<div id="q4-fb-B" class="mcq-feedback incorrect-fb">Incorrect. III is false. Runs with different seeds differ, so III cannot be part of the answer.</div>
<div id="q4-fb-C" class="mcq-feedback correct-fb">Correct. I and II are both true. III is false because different seeds produce different runs. Only a fixed seed makes a run repeat exactly.</div>
<div id="q4-fb-D" class="mcq-feedback incorrect-fb">Incorrect. III is false, so not all three are true. Different seeds give different outputs.</div>
      </div>

        <div class="mcq-options" id="q5-options">
<button class="mcq-option" onclick="checkMCQ('q5','A','D','q5-fb-A')"><span class="mcq-option-letter">A</span> It is often cheaper and safer than performing the real experiment</button>
<button class="mcq-option" onclick="checkMCQ('q5','B','D','q5-fb-B')"><span class="mcq-option-letter">B</span> It lets you repeat a scenario and vary parameters quickly</button>
<button class="mcq-option" onclick="checkMCQ('q5','C','D','q5-fb-C')"><span class="mcq-option-letter">C</span> It can model situations that are hard, slow, or dangerous to observe directly</button>
<button class="mcq-option" onclick="checkMCQ('q5','D','D','q5-fb-D')"><span class="mcq-option-letter">D</span> It guarantees results that are exactly correct for the real world</button>
</div>
<div id="q5-fb-A" class="mcq-feedback incorrect-fb">Incorrect. Being cheaper and safer IS a valid reason to simulate, so it is not the exception the question asks for.</div>
<div id="q5-fb-B" class="mcq-feedback incorrect-fb">Incorrect. Repeating and adjusting a scenario IS a real benefit of simulation, so it is not the exception.</div>
<div id="q5-fb-C" class="mcq-feedback incorrect-fb">Incorrect. Modeling hard-to-observe situations IS a genuine benefit, so it is not the exception.</div>
<div id="q5-fb-D" class="mcq-feedback correct-fb">Correct. A simulation gives an approximation based on its assumptions. It does not guarantee exactly correct real-world results, so this is not a valid reason.</div>
      </div>
      <div class="mcq-item" data-activity="quiz" data-item="q6">
        <div class="mcq-q-num">Question 6 of 6<span class="diff-tag">Benefit vs limitation</span>
</div>
        <div class="mcq-q-text">A team increases the number of trials in a probability simulation from 100 to 100,000. Which statement <strong>best</strong> describes the likely effect?</div>
        <div class="mcq-options" id="q6-options">
<button class="mcq-option" onclick="checkMCQ('q6','A','B','q6-fb-A')"><span class="mcq-option-letter">A</span> The estimate will now exactly equal the true probability</button>
<button class="mcq-option" onclick="checkMCQ('q6','B','B','q6-fb-B')"><span class="mcq-option-letter">B</span> The estimate is likely closer to the true probability, but it is still an approximation</button>
<button class="mcq-option" onclick="checkMCQ('q6','C','B','q6-fb-C')"><span class="mcq-option-letter">C</span> The simulation no longer relies on any assumptions about the model</button>
<button class="mcq-option" onclick="checkMCQ('q6','D','B','q6-fb-D')"><span class="mcq-option-letter">D</span> Randomness no longer affects the result of any individual trial</button>
</div>
<div id="q6-fb-A" class="mcq-feedback incorrect-fb">Incorrect. More trials improve reliability but do not make an estimate exact. A simulation still only approximates.</div>
<div id="q6-fb-B" class="mcq-feedback correct-fb">Correct. More independent trials generally push the estimate closer to the true probability, yet it remains an approximation, never a guarantee.</div>
<div id="q6-fb-C" class="mcq-feedback incorrect-fb">Incorrect. The number of trials does not change the model's assumptions. Those are built into how each trial works.</div>
<div id="q6-fb-D" class="mcq-feedback incorrect-fb">Incorrect. Each individual trial is still random. More trials change the reliability of the summary, not the randomness of a single trial.</div>
      </div>

      <div class="faq-item">
        <button class="faq-q" onclick="toggleFAQ(this)">What is a simulation in AP CSP?<i class="faq-icon">+</i></button>
        <div class="faq-a">A simulation is a program that models a real-world phenomenon so you can study it on a computer. It is an abstraction built on assumptions, it often uses randomness to mimic real uncertainty, and it uses iteration to run many trials. Because it simplifies reality, its results are approximations, not exact truths.</div>
      </div>
      <div class="faq-item">
        <button class="faq-q" onclick="toggleFAQ(this)">Why use a simulation instead of a real experiment?<i class="faq-icon">+</i></button>
        <div class="faq-a">Simulations are usually cheaper, safer, and faster than the real thing, and they are easy to repeat and adjust. You can crash-test a design, play out thousands of games, or model something dangerous or slow to observe, all without real-world cost or risk.</div>
      </div>
      <div class="faq-item">
        <button class="faq-q" onclick="toggleFAQ(this)">Why do two runs of the same simulation give different results?<i class="faq-icon">+</i></button>
        <div class="faq-a">Because the simulation uses <code>randomness</code>. Each run draws different random values, so the tallies differ. To make a run reproducible, set a <code>seed</code>; the same seed always produces the same sequence. Different seeds, or no seed, give runs that vary.</div>
      </div>
      <div class="faq-item">
        <button class="faq-q" onclick="toggleFAQ(this)">Does running more trials make a simulation exact?<i class="faq-icon">+</i></button>
        <div class="faq-a">No. More independent trials generally make the estimate more reliable and closer to the true value, but the result is always an approximation. A simulation reports an estimate, never a guaranteed exact answer.</div>
      </div>
      <div class="faq-item">
        <button class="faq-q" onclick="toggleFAQ(this)">What are the limitations of a simulation?<i class="faq-icon">+</i></button>
        <div class="faq-a">A simulation is only as good as its assumptions. It leaves out details, so if the model is wrong (for example, assuming a fair coin that is actually weighted), the results will be confidently wrong. Its output depends on the model and the number of trials, and it approximates rather than proves.</div>
      </div>

  document.head.appendChild(s);});}

function cleanErr(msg){if(!msg)return 'error';var lines=String(msg).trim().split('\n');return lines.slice(-3).join('\n');}
function execUser(py,code){var output='',err=null;
  try{py.runPython('import sys, io\n__old_out = sys.stdout\nsys.stdout = io.StringIO()\nsys.stderr = sys.stdout');
    try{var ns=py.globals.get('dict')();py.runPython(code,{globals:ns});ns.destroy();}
    catch(e){err=cleanErr(e.message);}
    output=py.runPython('sys.stdout.getvalue()');}
  catch(e2){err=cleanErr((e2&&e2.message)||String(e2));}
  finally{try{py.runPython('sys.stdout = __old_out\nsys.stderr = __old_out');}catch(e3){}}
  return {output:output,err:err};}

    <div class="lesson-objectives">
      <h2>After this lesson, you will be able to:</h2>
      <ul>
        <li><span>Explain that a string is an ordered sequence of characters, including spaces</span></li>
        <li><span>Concatenate strings and variables with + to build output</span></li>
        <li><span>Find the length of a string with len(), counting every character</span></li>
        <li><span>Convert a number to a string with str() before joining it to text</span></li>
        <li><span>Distinguish numeric addition from string concatenation when using +</span></li>
        <li><span>Assemble clear, labeled output for your Create Performance Task</span></li>
      </ul>
    </div>
    <div class="score-impact">📈 <span><strong>Exam weight:</strong> Strings appear throughout Big Idea 3 tracing and spot-the-bug items, and building output is part of almost every Create Task. Concatenation versus addition, missing str(), and length that ignores spaces are favorite trap topics.</span>
</div>
    <div class="hook-box">
      <div class="hook-label">💡 Think about this first</div>
      <p>Every message a program shows you is a string that someone built. When a game says Player Ada scored 95, that line was assembled from fixed text, a name, and a number glued together in order. Get one space wrong and it reads PlayerAdascored95. Forget one conversion and the program crashes. This lesson is about joining pieces of text cleanly and measuring how long they are.</p>
    </div>
    <div class="lesson-section">
      <h2>What a String Is</h2>
      <p>A <strong>string</strong> is an ordered sequence of characters: letters, digits, spaces, and punctuation, kept in order and treated as text. In Python you write a string inside quotation marks, like <code>"Hello"</code> or <code>"grade: A"</code>. The order matters, so <code>"ab"</code> and <code>"ba"</code> are different strings. Because a string is text, the characters inside it are not treated as numbers even when they look like digits: <code>"7"</code> is the character seven, not the value 7.</p>
      <p>The two string operations you must know for AP CSP are <strong>concatenation</strong> (joining strings together) and finding a string's <strong>length</strong> (how many characters it contains). Everything in this lesson is built from those two ideas plus one conversion rule for mixing numbers into text.</p>
      <div class="callout-exam">
        <div class="callout-exam-label">🎯 What the exam expects</div>
        <p>The CED (AAP-2.D) expects you to build output by joining strings and variables and to find a string's length. AP pseudocode keeps string handling limited, mainly concatenation and length, so the exam stays at the level of assembling text, not slicing it apart.</p>
      </div>
    </div>

    <div class="lesson-section">
      <h2>Concatenation: Joining Strings with +</h2>
      <p>Concatenation uses the <code>+</code> operator to glue two strings into one longer string, in order, left to right. The result contains every character of the first string followed by every character of the second. Nothing is added between them, so if you want a space, you must include it yourself.</p>
      <div class="code-panel-wrap">
  <div class="code-panel-tabs">
    <button class="code-tab py active" onclick="switchTab(this,'py','pan-1')">🐛 Python</button>
    <button class="code-tab pseudo" onclick="switchTab(this,'pseudo','pan-1')">📋 AP Pseudocode</button>
  </div>
  <div class="code-pane active" id="pan-1-py"><pre><span class="py-var">name</span><span class="py-var"> </span><span class="py-var">=</span><span class="py-var"> </span><span class="py-str">"Ada"</span>
<span class="py-var">greeting</span><span class="py-var"> </span><span class="py-var">=</span><span class="py-var"> </span><span class="py-str">"Hello, "</span><span class="py-var"> </span><span class="py-var">+</span><span class="py-var"> </span><span class="py-var">name</span>
<span class="py-kw">print</span><span class="py-var">(</span><span class="py-var">greeting</span><span class="py-var">)</span></pre></div>
  <div class="code-pane" id="pan-1-pseudo"><pre><span class="ps-var">name</span><span class="ps-var"> </span><span class="ps-var"><</span><span class="ps-var">-</span><span class="ps-var"> </span><span class="ps-str">"Ada"</span>
<span class="ps-var">greeting</span><span class="ps-var"> </span><span class="ps-var"><</span><span class="ps-var">-</span><span class="ps-var"> </span><span class="ps-str">"Hello, "</span><span class="ps-var"> </span><span class="ps-var">+</span><span class="ps-var"> </span><span class="ps-var">name</span>
<span class="ps-kw">DISPLAY</span><span class="ps-var">(</span><span class="ps-var">greeting</span><span class="ps-var">)</span></pre></div>
</div>
      <p>Here <code>"Hello, " + name</code> produces <code>"Hello, Ada"</code>. The space and comma are part of the first string, so they appear in the result. This is how programs build a message out of fixed text and a variable that changes.</p>
      <div class="callout-trap">
        <div class="callout-trap-label">⚠ The same + means two different things</div>
        <p>With numbers, <code>+</code> adds: <code>2 + 3</code> is <code>5</code>. With strings, <code>+</code> concatenates: <code>"2" + "3"</code> is <code>"23"</code>, not 5. Python decides which behavior to use based on the <strong>types</strong> of the values, not on how they look. Two characters that look like digits are still text, so they are joined, not summed.</p>
      </div>

      <div class="mini-ex">
        <div class="mini-ex-label">✍ Mini Exercise 1 • Predict the output</div>
        <div class="mini-ex-q">Both values are strings. What is printed?</div>
        <div class="mini-ex-code"><pre style="margin:0;white-space:pre;font-family:monospace;font-size:13px;color:#e2e8f0;"><span class="py-var">x</span><span class="py-var"> </span><span class="py-var">=</span><span class="py-var"> </span><span class="py-str">"2"</span><span class="py-var"> </span><span class="py-var">+</span><span class="py-var"> </span><span class="py-str">"3"</span>
<span class="py-kw">print</span><span class="py-var">(</span><span class="py-var">x</span><span class="py-var">)</span></pre></div>

      </div>
    </div>

    <div class="lesson-section">
      <h2>Mixing Numbers and Text: str()</h2>
      <p>You often need to put a number inside a message, like a score or a count. But Python will not concatenate a string and a number directly. Writing <code>"score: " + 7</code> raises a <code>TypeError</code>, because one side is text and the other is a number and Python refuses to guess what you meant. The fix is to convert the number to a string first with <code>str()</code>.</p>
      <div class="code-panel-wrap">
  <div class="code-panel-tabs">
    <button class="code-tab py active" onclick="switchTab(this,'py','pan-2')">🐛 Python (needs str)</button>
    <button class="code-tab pseudo" onclick="switchTab(this,'pseudo','pan-2')">📋 Pseudocode</button>
  </div>
  <div class="code-pane active" id="pan-2-py"><pre><span class="py-var">score</span><span class="py-var"> </span><span class="py-var">=</span><span class="py-var"> </span><span class="py-num">95</span>
<span class="py-var">label</span><span class="py-var"> </span><span class="py-var">=</span><span class="py-var"> </span><span class="py-str">"Score: "</span><span class="py-var"> </span><span class="py-var">+</span><span class="py-var"> </span><span class="py-var">str</span><span class="py-var">(</span><span class="py-var">score</span><span class="py-var">)</span>
<span class="py-kw">print</span><span class="py-var">(</span><span class="py-var">label</span><span class="py-var">)</span></pre></div>
  <div class="code-pane" id="pan-2-pseudo"><pre><span class="ps-var">score</span><span class="ps-var"> </span><span class="ps-var"><</span><span class="ps-var">-</span><span class="ps-var"> </span><span class="ps-num">95</span>
<span class="ps-var">label</span><span class="ps-var"> </span><span class="ps-var"><</span><span class="ps-var">-</span><span class="ps-var"> </span><span class="ps-str">"Score: "</span><span class="ps-var"> </span><span class="ps-var">+</span><span class="ps-var"> </span><span class="ps-var">score</span>
<span class="ps-kw">DISPLAY</span><span class="ps-var">(</span><span class="ps-var">label</span><span class="ps-var">)</span></pre></div>
</div>
      <p>The call <code>str(score)</code> turns the number 95 into the text <code>"95"</code>, which can then be concatenated. On the pseudocode side, AP pseudocode is looser about combining text and numbers, but in real Python the conversion is required. Whenever you build a message that includes a number, wrap the number in <code>str()</code>.</p>
      <div class="callout-trap">
        <div class="callout-trap-label">⚠ Forgetting str() is a classic error</div>
        <p>Any time you join text with a number using <code>+</code>, you must convert the number: <code>"total: " + str(count)</code>. Leaving out <code>str()</code> is one of the most common runtime errors on string output. The moment you see <code>+</code> between a quoted string and a number, reach for <code>str()</code>.</p>
      </div>

      <div class="mini-ex">
        <div class="mini-ex-label">✍ Mini Exercise 2 • Spot the flaw</div>
        <div class="mini-ex-q">Why does this segment raise an error instead of printing?</div>
        <div class="mini-ex-code"><pre style="margin:0;white-space:pre;font-family:monospace;font-size:13px;color:#e2e8f0;"><span class="py-var">n</span><span class="py-var"> </span><span class="py-var">=</span><span class="py-var"> </span><span class="py-num">7</span>
<span class="py-kw">print</span><span class="py-var">(</span><span class="py-str">"score: "</span><span class="py-var"> </span><span class="py-var">+</span><span class="py-var"> </span><span class="py-var">n</span><span class="py-var">)</span></pre></div>

          <button class="mini-opt" onclick="miniMCQ('me2','C','C','me2-fb')"><span class="mini-opt-letter">C</span> a string and a number cannot be joined without str()</button>
          <button class="mini-opt" onclick="miniMCQ('me2','D','C','me2-fb')"><span class="mini-opt-letter">D</span> n must be written in quotation marks when assigned</button>
        </div>
        <div class="mini-fb" id="me2-fb"></div>
      </div>
    </div>

    <div class="lesson-section">
      <h2>Length: Counting Every Character</h2>
      <p>The length of a string is how many characters it contains. In Python you find it with <code>len()</code>; AP describes this as finding the length of the string. The count includes <strong>every</strong> character: letters, digits, punctuation, and spaces all count. Only the quotation marks are left out, because they mark where the string begins and ends and are not part of the text.</p>
      <div class="code-panel-wrap">
  <div class="code-panel-tabs">
    <button class="code-tab py active" onclick="switchTab(this,'py','pan-3')">🐛 Python</button>
    <button class="code-tab pseudo" onclick="switchTab(this,'pseudo','pan-3')">📋 AP Pseudocode</button>
  </div>
  <div class="code-pane active" id="pan-3-py"><pre><span class="py-var">word</span><span class="py-var"> </span><span class="py-var">=</span><span class="py-var"> </span><span class="py-str">"banana"</span>
<span class="py-kw">print</span><span class="py-var">(</span><span class="py-kw">len</span><span class="py-var">(</span><span class="py-var">word</span><span class="py-var">)</span><span class="py-var">)</span></pre></div>
  <div class="code-pane" id="pan-3-pseudo"><pre><span class="ps-var">word</span><span class="ps-var"> </span><span class="ps-var"><</span><span class="ps-var">-</span><span class="ps-var"> </span><span class="ps-str">"banana"</span>
<span class="ps-kw">DISPLAY</span><span class="ps-var">(</span><span class="ps-kw">LENGTH</span><span class="ps-var">(</span><span class="ps-var">word</span><span class="ps-var">)</span><span class="ps-var">)</span></pre></div>
</div>
      <p>The string <code>"banana"</code> has 6 characters, so <code>len(word)</code> is 6. Watch spaces carefully: <code>"go team"</code> has 7 characters because the space between the words counts. A blank space is a real character, exactly like a letter.</p>
      <div class="callout-exam">
        <div class="callout-exam-label">🎯 Spaces are characters too</div>
        <p>When a length question includes spaces, count them. <code>"a b c"</code> has 5 characters: three letters and two spaces. Forgetting to count spaces is the number one mistake on length questions, so slow down and tick off each character, blanks included.</p>
      </div>

      <div class="mini-ex">
        <div class="mini-ex-label">✍ Mini Exercise 3 • Fill in the blank</div>

    <div class="lesson-section">
      <h2>Building Output from Pieces</h2>
      <p>Real programs assemble their output from several parts: fixed text, variables, and numbers converted with <code>str()</code>. You build the whole message by concatenating those pieces in the right order, remembering to add spaces and punctuation yourself.</p>
      <div class="code-panel-wrap">
  <div class="code-panel-tabs">
    <button class="code-tab py active" onclick="switchTab(this,'py','pan-4')">🐛 Python</button>
    <button class="code-tab pseudo" onclick="switchTab(this,'pseudo','pan-4')">📋 AP Pseudocode</button>
  </div>
  <div class="code-pane active" id="pan-4-py"><pre><span class="py-var">a</span><span class="py-var"> </span><span class="py-var">=</span><span class="py-var"> </span><span class="py-str">"AP"</span>
<span class="py-var">b</span><span class="py-var"> </span><span class="py-var">=</span><span class="py-var"> </span><span class="py-str">"CSP"</span>
<span class="py-kw">print</span><span class="py-var">(</span><span class="py-var">a</span><span class="py-var"> </span><span class="py-var">+</span><span class="py-var"> </span><span class="py-var">b</span><span class="py-var">)</span>
<span class="py-kw">print</span><span class="py-var">(</span><span class="py-var">a</span><span class="py-var"> </span><span class="py-var">+</span><span class="py-var"> </span><span class="py-str">" "</span><span class="py-var"> </span><span class="py-var">+</span><span class="py-var"> </span><span class="py-var">b</span><span class="py-var">)</span></pre></div>
  <div class="code-pane" id="pan-4-pseudo"><pre><span class="ps-var">a</span><span class="ps-var"> </span><span class="ps-var"><</span><span class="ps-var">-</span><span class="ps-var"> </span><span class="ps-str">"AP"</span>
<span class="ps-var">b</span><span class="ps-var"> </span><span class="ps-var"><</span><span class="ps-var">-</span><span class="ps-var"> </span><span class="ps-str">"CSP"</span>
<span class="ps-kw">DISPLAY</span><span class="ps-var">(</span><span class="ps-var">a</span><span class="ps-var"> </span><span class="ps-var">+</span><span class="ps-var"> </span><span class="ps-var">b</span><span class="ps-var">)</span>
<span class="ps-kw">DISPLAY</span><span class="ps-var">(</span><span class="ps-var">a</span><span class="ps-var"> </span><span class="ps-var">+</span><span class="ps-var"> </span><span class="ps-str">" "</span><span class="ps-var"> </span><span class="ps-var">+</span><span class="ps-var"> </span><span class="ps-var">b</span><span class="ps-var">)</span></pre></div>
</div>
      <p>The first print joins <code>"AP"</code> and <code>"CSP"</code> with nothing between them, so it shows <code>APCSP</code>. The second inserts <code>" "</code> between them, so it shows <code>AP CSP</code>. The only difference is one space that you chose to include. Building a clean output string is just deciding, piece by piece, exactly which characters belong and in what order.</p>

      <div class="cpt-connection-label">📋 Create Performance Task • Building readable output with strings</div>
      <p>Almost every Create Task program produces output a person will read, and that output is a string you build. Concatenation and str() are how you turn raw variables into a clear, labeled message instead of a bare number. Clean output makes your program easier to explain in your written response.</p>
      <h3>A point-earning example</h3>
      <p>Imagine a program that reports a player's result by joining fixed text with two variables:</p>
      <div class="cpt-code">name <- "Ada"
score <- 95
message <- "Player " + name + " scored " + score
DISPLAY(message)</div>
      <p>In real Python that score would be wrapped in <code>str()</code>. In your written response, describe how the output is assembled:</p>
      <ul class="cpt-stems">
        <li>"The program builds the output by concatenating the fixed text with the variables <code>name</code> and <code>score</code>."</li>
        <li>"Because <code>score</code> is a number, it is converted with <code>str()</code> before being joined to the text, so the message displays correctly."</li>
        <li>"Spaces are included inside the quoted pieces so the words in the final message are separated."</li>
      </ul>
      <h3>The trap to avoid</h3>
      <p>Do not concatenate a number to text without <code>str()</code>, and do not forget the spaces between pieces. A missing <code>str()</code> crashes the program, and a missing space produces run-together output like <code>PlayerAdascored95</code>. Both cost you clarity. <a href="/pages/ap-csp-course-create-task">See the full Create Task module →</a></p>

    <div class="faq-section">
      <h2>Frequently Asked Questions</h2>
      <div class="faq-item">
        <button class="faq-q" onclick="toggleFAQ(this)">What is a string?<i class="faq-icon">+</i></button>
        <div class="faq-a">A string is an ordered sequence of characters treated as text, written inside quotation marks, like <code>"Hello"</code>. The order matters, and characters that look like digits, such as <code>"7"</code>, are still text, not numbers.</div>
      </div>
      <div class="faq-item">
        <button class="faq-q" onclick="toggleFAQ(this)">What does concatenation mean?<i class="faq-icon">+</i></button>
        <div class="faq-a">Concatenation is joining two strings into one longer string with the <code>+</code> operator. The characters of the first string are followed by the characters of the second, with nothing added between them, so you must include any spaces yourself.</div>
      </div>
      <div class="faq-item">
        <button class="faq-q" onclick="toggleFAQ(this)">Why does "score: " + 7 cause an error?<i class="faq-icon">+</i></button>
        <div class="faq-a">Because one value is a string and the other is a number, and Python will not concatenate different types. It raises a <code>TypeError</code>. Convert the number first with <code>str()</code>, as in <code>"score: " + str(7)</code>.</div>
      </div>
      <div class="faq-item">
        <button class="faq-q" onclick="toggleFAQ(this)">Do spaces count toward a string's length?<i class="faq-icon">+</i></button>
        <div class="faq-a">Yes. <code>len()</code> counts every character, including spaces and punctuation. The string <code>"go team"</code> has a length of 7 because the space between the words counts. Only the surrounding quotation marks are not counted.</div>
      </div>
      <div class="faq-item">
        <button class="faq-q" onclick="toggleFAQ(this)">How do strings help my Create Task?<i class="faq-icon">+</i></button>
        <div class="faq-a">Your program's output is a string you build by concatenating fixed text with your variables. Using <code>str()</code> to include numbers and adding spaces between pieces gives clear, labeled output that is easy to describe in your written response.</div>

function loadScriptOnce(src){return new Promise(function(res,rej){
  if(document.querySelector('script[data-pyodide]')){res();return;}
  var s=document.createElement('script');s.src=src;s.setAttribute('data-pyodide','1');
  s.onload=function(){res();};s.onerror=function(){rej(new Error('script load failed'));};
  document.head.appendChild(s);});}
function ensurePy(){if(window.__pyPromise)return window.__pyPromise;
  window.__pyPromise=(async function(){await loadScriptOnce(PY_URL+'pyodide.js');
    var py=await loadPyodide({indexURL:PY_URL});window.__pyodide=py;return py;})();
  return window.__pyPromise;}
function cleanErr(msg){if(!msg)return 'error';var lines=String(msg).trim().split('\n');return lines.slice(-3).join('\n');}
function execUser(py,code){var output='',err=null;
  try{py.runPython('import sys, io\n__old_out = sys.stdout\nsys.stdout = io.StringIO()\nsys.stderr = sys.stdout');
    try{var ns=py.globals.get('dict')();py.runPython(code,{globals:ns});ns.destroy();}
    catch(e){err=cleanErr(e.message);}
    output=py.runPython('sys.stdout.getvalue()');}
  catch(e2){err=cleanErr((e2&&e2.message)||String(e2));}
  finally{try{py.runPython('sys.stdout = __old_out\nsys.stderr = __old_out');}catch(e3){}}
  return {output:output,err:err};}

  if(btn)btn.disabled=false;}

<style>
  @import url('https://fonts.googleapis.com/css2?family=DM+Serif+Display:ital@0;1&family=DM+Sans:ital,opsz,wght@0,9..40,300;0,9..40,400;0,9..40,500;0,9..40,600;0,9..40,700;1,9..40,400&display=swap');

      <p>Computers feel all-powerful, but there are yes-or-no questions no program can ever answer correctly for every case. Not slow to answer. Not answerable with a bigger computer.     <div class="lesson-section">
      <h2>Decision Problems: Yes-or-No Questions</h2>
      <p>A <strong>decision problem</strong> is any problem that can be phrased as a yes-or-no question about its input. "Is <code>n</code> even?" is a decision problem. "Does the value <code>x</code> appear in this list?" is a decision problem. "Is this number prime?" is a decision problem. The answer is always exactly one of two things: yes or no, which in code is <code>True</code> or <code>False</code>. A program that answers a decision problem is often called a <strong>decider</strong>.</p>

    <div class="lesson-section">
      <h2>Decidable Problems</h2>
      <p>A decision problem is <strong>decidable</strong> if an algorithm can be written that produces a correct yes-or-no answer for <strong>every</strong> possible input, and always finishes running. The words "every" and "always" carry the whole definition. It is not enough for the algorithm to work on the inputs you tried; it must be guaranteed correct on all of them, including inputs no one has tested yet.</p>

      <p>"Does <code>x</code> appear in list <code>t</code>?" is decidable. The decider walks the list, and because the list is finite it must reach the end, so the loop always stops and the answer is always right. "Is <code>n</code> prime?" is decidable too: test every candidate divisor up to <code>n</code>; there are finitely many, so the check always terminates with a correct verdict. Almost every algorithm you have written this year solves a decidable problem.</p>
      <div class="callout-exam">
        <div class="callout-exam-label">📈 The mental test</div>
        <p>To argue a problem is decidable, describe a specific algorithm and explain why it (1) is correct for every input and (2) always halts. If you can do both, the problem is decidable.</p>
      </div>

    <div class="lesson-section">
      <h2>Undecidable Problems and the Halting Problem</h2>
      <p>A decision problem is <strong>undecidable</strong> if <strong>no</strong> algorithm can be built that always gives a correct yes-or-no answer for every possible input. This is not a statement about today's computers or about clever people who have not tried hard enough. It is a proven mathematical fact: for an undecidable problem, a correct general algorithm cannot exist, ever, on any computer.</p>
      <p>The classic example is the <strong>halting problem</strong>: given an arbitrary program and an input to it, decide whether that program will eventually <strong>stop</strong> or will run <strong>forever</strong>. It sounds answerable, and for many specific programs you can tell at a glance. But there is no single algorithm that answers it correctly for <em>every</em> program and input. Alan Turing proved this in 1936.</p>
<div class="mini-ex-code"><pre style="margin:0;white-space:pre;font-family:monospace;font-size:13px;color:#e2e8f0;"><span class="py-comment"># IMAGINED function that CANNOT exist</span>
<span class="py-kw">def</span><span class="py-var"> </span><span class="py-var">halts</span><span class="py-var">(</span><span class="py-var">program</span><span class="py-var">,</span><span class="py-var"> </span><span class="py-var">data</span><span class="py-var">)</span><span class="py-var">:</span>
<span class="py-var"> </span><span class="py-var"> </span><span class="py-var"> </span><span class="py-var"> </span><span class="py-comment"># would return True if program stops on data,</span>
<span class="py-var"> </span><span class="py-var"> </span><span class="py-var"> </span><span class="py-var"> </span><span class="py-comment"># False if program runs forever</span>
<span class="py-var"> </span><span class="py-var"> </span><span class="py-var"> </span><span class="py-var"> </span><span class="py-var">.</span><span class="py-var">.</span><span class="py-var">.</span>

<span class="py-comment"># The proof of impossibility feeds this idea a copy</span>
<span class="py-comment"># of itself, forcing a contradiction either way.</span></pre></div>
      <p>The proof imagines a perfect halting-checker and then builds a program that asks the checker about itself and does the opposite of whatever the checker predicts. If the checker says "halts," the program loops forever; if it says "runs forever," the program stops. Either answer is wrong, so the perfect checker cannot exist. You are not expected to reproduce the proof, only to know that the halting problem is undecidable and is the standard example.</p>

    <div class="lesson-section">
      <h2>Undecidable Is NOT the Same as Slow</h2>
      <p>This is the single most tested trap in the topic, so read it twice. A problem being <strong>slow</strong>, even absurdly slow, is completely different from a problem being <strong>undecidable</strong>.</p>
      <ul class="rules">
        <li>
<strong>Slow / unreasonable time:</strong> a correct algorithm <em>exists</em>, but it may take an impractical amount of time (for example, checking every possible password, which grows exponentially). The answer is reachable in principle; you just might wait longer than a lifetime.</li>
        <li>
<strong>Undecidable:</strong> a correct general algorithm <em>does not exist at all</em>. No amount of waiting, faster hardware, or cleverness produces one, because it is impossible.</li>
      </ul>
      <p>An exponential-time problem is still decidable. Given unlimited time, its algorithm always finishes with the right answer. The halting problem is in a different league: there is nothing to run to completion because the deciding algorithm cannot be written in the first place.</p>
      <div class="callout-trap">
        <div class="callout-trap-label">⚠ The classic distractor</div>
        <p>If an answer choice says a problem is undecidable "because it would take too long" or "because there are too many cases to check," it is describing efficiency, not decidability, and it is wrong. Undecidable means no correct algorithm can exist, period. Also beware the reverse: a problem that can be solved for <em>some</em> inputs but is not guaranteed correct for <strong>every</strong> input is still undecidable.</p>
      </div>

      <h2>Writing Deciders You Can Actually Run</h2>
      <p>You cannot write a program that solves an undecidable problem, but you can and should master the deciders for <strong>decidable</strong> problems, because those are exactly what the code section drills. A good decider returns or prints <code>True</code> or <code>False</code>, is correct for every input in its domain, and always terminates. Watch out for the most common decider bug: returning an answer too early inside a loop before all the data has been examined.</p>

</tr></thead>

    <div class="cpt-connection">
      <div class="cpt-connection-label">📋 Create Performance Task • Your algorithm is a decidable computation</div>
      <p>Every procedure you write for the Create Task solves a decidable problem: it produces a correct result and it always finishes. Understanding decidability lets you reason clearly about your own program instead of just hoping it works.</p>
      <h3>A point-earning example</h3>
      <p>Suppose your program includes a decider that reports whether a target value is present in a list:</p>
      <div class="cpt-code">PROCEDURE inList(data, target)
{
    FOR EACH v IN data
    {
        IF (v = target)
        {
            RETURN (true)
        }
    }
    RETURN (false)
}</div>
      <p>In your written response you can describe this procedure precisely:</p>
      <ul class="cpt-stems">
        <li>"This procedure answers a yes-or-no decision problem: it returns <code>true</code> when <code>target</code> is in <code>data</code> and <code>false</code> otherwise."</li>
        <li>"Because <code>data</code> is a finite list, the loop always reaches the end, so the procedure always terminates with a correct result. The problem it solves is decidable."</li>
        <li>"The procedure uses a return value that the rest of my program depends on, which is why it is one of my two selected code segments."</li>
      </ul>
      <h3>The trap to avoid</h3>
      <p>Do not claim your program "solves" something no algorithm can, and do not confuse a slow procedure with an impossible one. If your algorithm always halts with the right answer, it is decidable, even if it is not the fastest possible. <a href="/pages/ap-csp-course-create-task">See the full Create Task module →</a></p>

<div id="q6-fb-C" class="mcq-feedback correct-fb">Correct. Decidable means the algorithm is correct for every possible input and always halts. Both the coverage (every input) and termination are required.</div>

    <div class="faq-section">
      <h2>Frequently Asked Questions</h2>
      <div class="faq-item">
        <button class="faq-q" onclick="toggleFAQ(this)">What is a decision problem?<i class="faq-icon">+</i></button>
        <div class="faq-a">A decision problem is any problem that can be phrased as a yes-or-no question about its input, such as "is this number prime?" A program that answers it returns or prints True or False and is called a decider.</div>
      </div>
      <div class="faq-item">
        <button class="faq-q" onclick="toggleFAQ(this)">What does decidable mean?<i class="faq-icon">+</i></button>
        <div class="faq-a">A decision problem is decidable if an algorithm can be written that gives a correct yes-or-no answer for every possible input and always terminates. The words every and always are essential to the definition.</div>
      </div>
      <div class="faq-item">
        <button class="faq-q" onclick="toggleFAQ(this)">What does undecidable mean, and what is the standard example?<i class="faq-icon">+</i></button>
        <div class="faq-a">Undecidable means no algorithm can be built that always gives a correct answer for every possible input. The classic example is the halting problem: deciding whether an arbitrary program will eventually stop or run forever. Alan Turing proved it is undecidable.</div>
      </div>
      <div class="faq-item">
        <button class="faq-q" onclick="toggleFAQ(this)">Is an undecidable problem just one that is very slow?<i class="faq-icon">+</i></button>
        <div class="faq-a">No, and this is the most common trap. A slow problem still has a correct algorithm and is decidable; you might just wait a very long time. An undecidable problem has no correct general algorithm at all, no matter how much time or how fast the computer.</div>
      </div>
      <div class="faq-item">
        <button class="faq-q" onclick="toggleFAQ(this)">Can undecidable problems be solved for some inputs?<i class="faq-icon">+</i></button>
        <div class="faq-a">Yes, you can often answer specific cases. But if no single algorithm is guaranteed correct for every possible input, the problem is still undecidable. Being solvable for some inputs is not the same as being decidable.</div>
      </div>

    catch(e){err=cleanErr(e.message);}

  catch(e2){err=cleanErr((e2&&e2.message)||String(e2));}
  finally{try{py.runPython('sys.stdout = __old_out\nsys.stderr = __old_out');}catch(e3){}}

  .py-num{color:#fde68a!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:#fde68a!important;}
  .py-str{color:#f9a8d4!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:#f9a8d4!important;}
  .py-comment{color:#475569!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:#475569!important;font-style:italic;}
  .py-var{color:#e2e8f0!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:#e2e8f0!important;}
  .py-op{color:#94a3b8!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:#94a3b8!important;}

  .ps-op{color:#f9a8d4!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:#f9a8d4!important;}
  .ps-num{color:#fde68a!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:#fde68a!important;}
  .ps-str{color:#86efac!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:#86efac!important;}
  .ps-comment{color:#475569!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:#475569!important;font-style:italic;}
  .ps-var{color:#e2e8f0!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:#e2e8f0!important;}

  /* CALLOUTS */
  .callout-exam{background:#fffbeb;border:1px solid #fcd34d;border-left:4px solid var(--amber);border-radius:0 8px 8px 0;padding:16px 20px;margin:20px 0;}
  .callout-exam-label{font-size:11px;font-weight:700;letter-spacing:.08em;text-transform:uppercase;color:var(--amber)!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:var(--amber)!important;margin-bottom:6px;}
  .callout-exam p{font-size:14px!important;color:#78350f!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:#78350f!important;margin-bottom:0!important;line-height:1.6!important;}
  .callout-trap{background:#fef2f2;border:1px solid #fca5a5;border-left:4px solid var(--red);border-radius:0 8px 8px 0;padding:16px 20px;margin:20px 0;}
  .callout-trap-label{font-size:11px;font-weight:700;letter-spacing:.08em;text-transform:uppercase;color:var(--red)!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:var(--red)!important;margin-bottom:6px;}
  .callout-trap p{font-size:14px!important;color:#7f1d1d!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:#7f1d1d!important;margin-bottom:0!important;line-height:1.6!important;}

  /* MINI EXERCISES */
  .mini-ex{background:#fff;border:1px solid #bfdbfe;border-radius:12px;padding:20px 24px;margin:24px 0;}
  .mini-ex-label{display:flex;align-items:center;gap:8px;font-size:11px;font-weight:700;letter-spacing:.08em;text-transform:uppercase;color:var(--bi3-dk)!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:var(--bi3-dk)!important;margin-bottom:12px;}
  .mini-ex-q{font-size:15px;font-weight:600;color:var(--navy)!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:var(--navy)!important;margin-bottom:14px;line-height:1.5;}
  .mini-ex-code{background:#0f172a;border-radius:8px;padding:14px 16px;font-family:monospace;font-size:13px;line-height:1.8;margin-bottom:14px;overflow-x:auto;white-space:pre;display:block;}
  .mini-opts{display:flex;flex-direction:column;gap:7px;margin-bottom:10px;}
  .mini-opt{display:flex;align-items:center;gap:10px;padding:10px 14px;border:2px solid #e2e8f0;border-radius:8px;cursor:pointer;font-size:14px;font-family:monospace;color:#374151!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:#374151!important;background:#f8fafc;text-align:left;width:100%;transition:border-color .15s;}
  .mini-opt:hover{border-color:var(--bi3-lt);background:var(--bi3-bg);}
  .mini-opt.correct{border-color:var(--green)!important;background:#f0fdf4!important;color:#14532d!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:#14532d!important;}
  .mini-opt.incorrect{border-color:var(--red)!important;background:#fef2f2!important;color:#7f1d1d!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:#7f1d1d!important;}
  .mini-opt.reveal{border-color:var(--green)!important;background:#f0fdf4!important;}
  .mini-opt-letter{font-weight:700;color:var(--bi3)!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:var(--bi3)!important;min-width:18px;font-family:inherit;}
  .mini-opt.correct .mini-opt-letter{color:#14532d!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:#14532d!important;}
  .mini-opt.incorrect .mini-opt-letter{color:#7f1d1d!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:#7f1d1d!important;}
  .mini-fib-row{display:flex;gap:8px;align-items:center;flex-wrap:wrap;margin-bottom:10px;}
  .mini-fib-input{padding:8px 12px;border:2px solid #e2e8f0;border-radius:8px;font-family:monospace;font-size:14px;width:130px;outline:none;color:var(--navy)!important;background:#f8fafc;}
  .mini-fib-input:focus{border-color:var(--bi3-lt);}
  .mini-fib-input.correct{border-color:var(--green);background:#f0fdf4;}
  .mini-fib-input.incorrect{border-color:var(--red);background:#fef2f2;}
  .mini-fib-btn{padding:8px 18px;background:var(--bi3);border:none;border-radius:8px;color:#fff!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:#fff!important;font-size:13px;font-weight:700;cursor:pointer;font-family:inherit;}
  .mini-fb{font-size:13px;font-weight:500;padding:8px 12px;border-radius:7px;margin-top:6px;display:none;line-height:1.5;}
  .mini-fb.c{background:#f0fdf4;color:var(--green)!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:var(--green)!important;display:block;}
  .mini-fb.w{background:#fef2f2;color:var(--red)!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:var(--red)!important;display:block;}

  /* VOCAB */
  .vocab-table{width:100%;border-collapse:collapse;margin-bottom:24px;font-size:14px;}
  .vocab-table thead tr{background:var(--bi3);}
  .vocab-table thead th{padding:10px 16px;text-align:left;font-weight:600;color:#fff!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:#fff!important;font-size:13px;}
  .vocab-table tbody tr:nth-child(even){background:var(--bi3-bg);}
  .vocab-table tbody tr:nth-child(odd){background:#fff;}
  .vocab-table tbody td{padding:10px 16px;border-bottom:1px solid #bfdbfe;color:#374151;vertical-align:top;line-height:1.5;}
  .vocab-table tbody td:first-child{font-weight:700;color:var(--bi3-dk)!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:var(--bi3-dk)!important;white-space:nowrap;}

  /* CPT CONNECTION */
  .cpt-connection{background:#fefce8;border:1px solid #fde68a;border-left:4px solid #f59e0b;border-radius:0 10px 10px 0;padding:20px 24px;margin:28px 0;}
  .cpt-connection-label{font-size:11px;font-weight:700;letter-spacing:.08em;text-transform:uppercase;color:#92400e!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:#92400e!important;margin-bottom:8px;}
  .cpt-connection h3{font-size:16px!important;font-weight:700!important;color:#78350f!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:#78350f!important;margin:16px 0 8px!important;}
  .cpt-connection p{font-size:14px!important;color:#78350f!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:#78350f!important;line-height:1.7!important;margin-bottom:12px!important;}
  .cpt-connection a{color:#b45309!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:#b45309!important;font-weight:600;text-decoration:underline;}
  .cpt-connection code{background:#fef3c7;color:#78350f!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:#78350f!important;padding:1px 6px;border-radius:5px;font-size:13px;}
  .cpt-stems{list-style:none;padding:0;margin:0 0 8px;display:flex;flex-direction:column;gap:8px;}
  .cpt-stems li{background:#fffef5;border:1px solid #fde68a;border-radius:8px;padding:10px 14px;font-size:13px!important;color:#78350f!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:#78350f!important;line-height:1.6;}
  .cpt-code{background:#0f172a;border-radius:8px;padding:14px 16px;font-family:monospace;font-size:13px;line-height:1.8;margin:6px 0 12px;overflow-x:auto;white-space:pre;display:block;color:#e2e8f0!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:#e2e8f0!important;}

  /* EMAIL */
  .email-capture{background:linear-gradient(135deg,#1e3a8a 0%,#1e40af 100%);border-radius:12px;padding:24px 28px;margin-bottom:36px;display:flex;align-items:center;gap:24px;flex-wrap:wrap;}
  .email-capture-text{flex:1;min-width:200px;}
  .email-capture-eyebrow{font-size:11px;font-weight:700;letter-spacing:.1em;text-transform:uppercase;color:var(--bi3-lt)!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:var(--bi3-lt)!important;margin-bottom:4px;}
  .email-capture h3{font-size:16px!important;font-weight:700!important;color:#fff!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:#fff!important;margin-bottom:4px!important;}
  .email-capture p{font-size:13px!important;color:#94a3b8!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:#94a3b8!important;margin-bottom:0!important;line-height:1.5!important;}
  .email-capture-form{display:flex;gap:8px;flex-wrap:wrap;flex-shrink:0;}
  .email-capture-input{padding:10px 14px;border-radius:8px;border:1px solid rgba(255,255,255,.2);background:rgba(255,255,255,.1);color:#fff!important;font-size:14px;font-family:inherit;min-width:180px;outline:none;}
  .email-capture-btn{padding:10px 20px!important;background:var(--bi3)!important;color:#fff!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:#fff!important;border:none!important;border-radius:8px!important;font-size:14px!important;font-weight:600!important;cursor:pointer!important;font-family:inherit!important;}
  .email-capture-success{display:none;font-size:14px;color:#93c5fd!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:#93c5fd!important;font-weight:600;padding:10px 0;}

  /* MCQ */
  .mcq-section{background:#fff;border:1px solid #e2e8f0;border-radius:14px;padding:28px;margin-bottom:40px;}
  .mcq-section-header{display:flex;align-items:center;gap:12px;margin-bottom:24px;padding-bottom:16px;border-bottom:2px solid var(--bi3-bg);}
  .mcq-section-icon{width:40px;height:40px;border-radius:10px;background:var(--bi3-bg);display:flex;align-items:center;justify-content:center;font-size:18px;flex-shrink:0;}
  .mcq-section-title{font-family:"DM Serif Display",serif;font-size:20px;color:var(--navy)!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:var(--navy)!important;}
  .mcq-section-sub{font-size:13px;color:var(--slate);}
  .mcq-item{margin-bottom:28px;padding-bottom:28px;border-bottom:1px solid #f1f5f9;}
  .mcq-item:last-child{border-bottom:none;margin-bottom:0;padding-bottom:0;}
  .mcq-q-num{font-size:11px;font-weight:700;letter-spacing:.08em;text-transform:uppercase;color:var(--slate);margin-bottom:8px;}
  .diff-tag{display:inline-block;font-size:10px;font-weight:700;letter-spacing:.06em;text-transform:uppercase;padding:2px 8px;border-radius:100px;margin-left:8px;background:#fef2f2;color:#b91c1c!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:#b91c1c!important;border:1px solid #fca5a5;}
  .mcq-q-text{font-size:15px!important;font-weight:600!important;color:#0f1f3d!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:#0f1f3d!important;line-height:1.6!important;margin-bottom:12px!important;}
  .predict-note{font-size:12px;font-style:italic;color:#64748b!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:#64748b!important;margin-bottom:12px;}
  .mcq-code{background:#0f172a;border-radius:8px;padding:12px 14px;margin:10px 0 14px;font-family:monospace;font-size:13px;line-height:1.75;color:#e2e8f0!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:#e2e8f0!important;white-space:pre;overflow-x:auto;display:block;}
  .mcq-code .k{color:#93c5fd!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:#93c5fd!important;}
  .mcq-code .s{color:#f9a8d4!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:#f9a8d4!important;}
  .mcq-code .n{color:#fde68a!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:#fde68a!important;}
  .mcq-code .c{color:#64748b!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:#64748b!important;font-style:italic;}
  .mcq-roman{list-style:none;padding:0;margin:10px 0 14px;display:flex;flex-direction:column;gap:6px;}
  .mcq-roman li{font-family:monospace;font-size:13px;color:#1e293b!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:#1e293b!important;background:#f1f5f9;border-radius:6px;padding:8px 12px;}
  .mcq-roman li strong{color:var(--bi3-dk)!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:var(--bi3-dk)!important;font-family:"DM Sans",sans-serif;margin-right:8px;}
  .mcq-options{display:flex;flex-direction:column;gap:8px;margin-bottom:12px;}
  .mcq-option{display:flex!important;align-items:flex-start!important;gap:12px!important;padding:11px 14px!important;border:2px solid #e2e8f0!important;border-radius:8px!important;cursor:pointer!important;background:#f8fafc!important;font-size:14px!important;color:#374151!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:#374151!important;line-height:1.5!important;text-align:left!important;width:100%!important;font-family:inherit!important;}
  .mcq-option:hover{border-color:var(--bi3-lt)!important;background:var(--bi3-bg)!important;}
  .mcq-option.correct{border-color:var(--green)!important;background:#f0fdf4!important;color:#14532d!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:#14532d!important;}
  .mcq-option.incorrect{border-color:var(--red)!important;background:#fef2f2!important;color:#7f1d1d!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:#7f1d1d!important;}
  .mcq-option.revealed-correct{border-color:var(--green)!important;background:#f0fdf4!important;}
  .mcq-option-letter{font-weight:700!important;color:var(--bi3)!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:var(--bi3)!important;flex-shrink:0!important;min-width:18px!important;}
  .mcq-option.correct .mcq-option-letter{color:#14532d!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:#14532d!important;}
  .mcq-option.incorrect .mcq-option-letter{color:#7f1d1d!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:#7f1d1d!important;}
  .mcq-feedback{display:none!important;padding:12px 16px!important;border-radius:8px!important;font-size:14px!important;line-height:1.6!important;margin-top:8px!important;}
  .mcq-feedback.show{display:block!important;}
  .mcq-feedback.correct-fb{background:#f0fdf4!important;color:#14532d!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:#14532d!important;border:1px solid #bbf7d0!important;}
  .mcq-feedback.incorrect-fb{background:#fef2f2!important;color:#7f1d1d!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:#7f1d1d!important;border:1px solid #fecaca!important;}

  /* GAME */
  .game-section{background:linear-gradient(135deg,#1e3a8a 0%,#1e40af 100%);border-radius:14px;padding:28px;margin-bottom:40px;}
  .game-badge{display:inline-block;background:rgba(147,197,253,.15);border:1px solid rgba(147,197,253,.35);color:var(--bi3-lt)!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:var(--bi3-lt)!important;font-size:11px;font-weight:700;letter-spacing:.1em;text-transform:uppercase;padding:5px 14px;border-radius:100px;margin-bottom:10px;}
  .game-title{font-family:"DM Serif Display",serif!important;font-size:24px!important;color:#fff!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:#fff!important;margin-bottom:4px!important;}
  .game-sub{font-size:13px!important;color:#94a3b8!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:#94a3b8!important;margin-bottom:20px!important;}
  .vt-score-bar{display:flex;justify-content:space-between;background:rgba(255,255,255,.06);border-radius:10px;padding:12px 20px;margin-bottom:20px;flex-wrap:wrap;gap:8px;}
  .vt-stat{text-align:center;}
  .vt-stat-val{font-size:20px;font-weight:800;color:#fff!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:#fff!important;line-height:1;}
  .vt-stat-lbl{font-size:10px;color:#94a3b8!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:#94a3b8!important;margin-top:2px;}
  .vt-code-card{background:rgba(255,255,255,.06);border:1px solid rgba(255,255,255,.1);border-radius:12px;padding:18px 20px;margin-bottom:16px;}
  .vt-code-label{font-size:11px;font-weight:700;letter-spacing:.06em;text-transform:uppercase;color:var(--bi3-lt)!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:var(--bi3-lt)!important;margin-bottom:10px;}
  .vt-code-lines{font-family:monospace;font-size:14px;line-height:2;color:#e2e8f0!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:#e2e8f0!important;}
  .vt-line{display:block;padding:2px 8px;border-radius:4px;white-space:pre;}
  .vt-line.hl{background:rgba(147,197,253,.2);color:#93c5fd!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:#93c5fd!important;}
  .vt-question{font-size:15px;font-weight:600;color:#e2e8f0!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:#e2e8f0!important;margin-bottom:14px;}
  .vt-options{display:grid;grid-template-columns:1fr 1fr;gap:8px;margin-bottom:14px;}
  .vt-btn{padding:12px;border-radius:9px;border:2px solid rgba(255,255,255,.15);background:rgba(255,255,255,.06);cursor:pointer;font-size:15px;font-weight:700;color:#e2e8f0!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:#e2e8f0!important;font-family:monospace;transition:all .15s;}
  .vt-btn:hover{border-color:var(--bi3-lt);background:rgba(26,86,219,.2);}
  .vt-btn.c{border-color:#4ade80;background:rgba(74,222,128,.15);color:#4ade80!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:#4ade80!important;}
  .vt-btn.w{border-color:#f87171;background:rgba(248,113,113,.15);color:#f87171!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:#f87171!important;}
  .vt-btn.rv{border-color:#4ade80;background:rgba(74,222,128,.08);}
  .vt-fb{padding:10px 14px;border-radius:8px;font-size:13px;font-weight:500;margin-bottom:12px;display:none;line-height:1.5;}
  .vt-fb.c{background:rgba(74,222,128,.1);color:#4ade80!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:#4ade80!important;display:block;}
  .vt-fb.w{background:rgba(248,113,113,.1);color:#f87171!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:#f87171!important;display:block;}
  .vt-next{display:none;width:100%;padding:12px;background:rgba(255,255,255,.1);border:2px solid rgba(255,255,255,.2);border-radius:8px;color:#fff!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:#fff!important;font-size:14px;font-weight:600;cursor:pointer;font-family:inherit;}

  .vt-results{display:none;text-align:center;padding:20px;}
  .vt-results.show{display:block;}
  .vt-res-score{font-family:"DM Serif Display",serif;font-size:52px;color:#fff!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:#fff!important;line-height:1;}
  .vt-res-lbl{font-size:14px;color:#94a3b8!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:#94a3b8!important;margin-bottom:12px;}
  .vt-res-msg{font-size:14px;color:#bfdbfe!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:#bfdbfe!important;margin-bottom:20px;line-height:1.6;}
  .vt-restart{background:rgba(255,255,255,.1);color:#fff!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:#fff!important;border:2px solid rgba(255,255,255,.2);border-radius:8px;padding:11px 24px;font-size:14px;font-weight:600;cursor:pointer;font-family:inherit;}

  /* CODE EDITOR (Pyodide live) */

  .code-editor-badge{display:inline-block;background:rgba(147,197,253,.15);border:1px solid rgba(147,197,253,.35);color:var(--bi3-lt)!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:var(--bi3-lt)!important;font-size:11px;font-weight:700;letter-spacing:.1em;text-transform:uppercase;padding:5px 14px;border-radius:100px;margin-bottom:10px;}
  .code-editor-title{font-family:"DM Serif Display",serif!important;font-size:22px!important;color:#fff!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:#fff!important;margin-bottom:4px!important;}
  .code-editor-sub{font-size:13px!important;color:#94a3b8!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:#94a3b8!important;margin-bottom:20px!important;line-height:1.6;}
