  .scaffold-badge{display:inline-block;font-size:10px;font-weight:700;letter-spacing:.06em;text-transform:uppercase;padding:3px 10px;border-radius:100px;background:rgba(147,197,253,.15);color:var(--bi3-lt)!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:var(--bi3-lt)!important;border:1px solid rgba(147,197,253,.35);margin-bottom:8px;}
  .code-problem-num{font-size:11px;font-weight:700;letter-spacing:.06em;text-transform:uppercase;color:var(--bi3-lt)!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:var(--bi3-lt)!important;margin-bottom:8px;}
  .code-problem-prompt{font-size:14px!important;color:#e2e8f0!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:#e2e8f0!important;line-height:1.6!important;margin-bottom:12px!important;}

  .code-btn-row{display:flex;gap:8px;margin-top:10px;flex-wrap:wrap;align-items:center;}
  .code-run-btn{padding:9px 20px!important;background:var(--bi3)!important;color:#fff!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:#fff!important;border:none!important;border-radius:7px!important;font-size:13px!important;font-weight:700!important;cursor:pointer!important;font-family:inherit!important;}

    <div class="lesson-objectives">
      <h2>After this lesson, you will be able to:</h2>
      <ul>
        <li><span>Explain that a variable is a named abstraction that holds a value</span></li>
        <li><span>Assign values in Python with = and in AP pseudocode with the left arrow</span></li>
        <li><span>Predict that a new assignment replaces the previous value of a variable</span></li>
        <li><span>Update a variable using its own current value, knowing the right side is evaluated first</span></li>
        <li><span>Trace a sequence of assignments with a variable table to find the final output</span></li>
        <li><span>Swap two variables correctly using a temporary variable</span></li>
      </ul>
    </div>
    <div class="score-impact">📈 <span><strong>Exam weight:</strong> Variables and assignment are the foundation of every tracing and code-reasoning question in Big Idea 3. Expect items that hinge on assignment replacing a value, on self-updates like <code>x = x + 1</code>, and on the difference between the value stored and the name printed.</span>
</div>
    <div class="hook-box">
      <div class="hook-label">💡 Think about this first</div>
      <p>Every program needs to remember things: a score, a total, a name. It does that with variables. A variable is just a labeled box that holds one value at a time, and assignment is how you put a value in the box. The catch is that putting a new value in replaces the old one, and updates like adding to a running total depend on reading the old value first. Master that and the rest of Big Idea 3 falls into place.</p>
    </div>
    <div class="lesson-section">
      <h2>What a Variable Is</h2>
      <p>A <strong>variable</strong> is a named location that holds a value. The name is an <strong>abstraction</strong>: instead of repeating a raw value everywhere, you refer to it by a memorable name and let the program remember the actual value for you. When the CED says a variable is "an abstraction inside a program that can hold a value," this is exactly what it means (AAP-1.A).</p>
      <p>You put a value into a variable with an <strong>assignment statement</strong>. In Python you use the single equals sign <code>=</code>. In AP pseudocode you use the left arrow <code><-</code>. Both mean the same thing: take the value on the right, and store it in the variable named on the left (AAP-1.B).</p>
      <div class="code-panel-wrap">
  <div class="code-panel-tabs">
    <button class="code-tab py active" onclick="switchTab(this,'py','pan-1')">🐛 Python</button>
    <button class="code-tab pseudo" onclick="switchTab(this,'pseudo','pan-1')">📋 AP Pseudocode</button>
  </div>
  <div class="code-pane active" id="pan-1-py"><pre><span class="py-var">color</span><span class="py-var"> </span><span class="py-var">=</span><span class="py-var"> </span><span class="py-str">"blue"</span>
<span class="py-var">count</span><span class="py-var"> </span><span class="py-var">=</span><span class="py-var"> </span><span class="py-num">3</span>
<span class="py-kw">print</span><span class="py-var">(</span><span class="py-var">count</span><span class="py-var">)</span></pre></div>
  <div class="code-pane" id="pan-1-pseudo"><pre><span class="ps-var">color</span><span class="ps-var"> </span><span class="ps-var"><</span><span class="ps-var">-</span><span class="ps-var"> </span><span class="ps-str">"blue"</span>
<span class="ps-var">count</span><span class="ps-var"> </span><span class="ps-var"><</span><span class="ps-var">-</span><span class="ps-var"> </span><span class="ps-num">3</span>
<span class="ps-kw">DISPLAY</span><span class="ps-var">(</span><span class="ps-var">count</span><span class="ps-var">)</span></pre></div>
</div>
      <p>After these two assignments, <code>color</code> holds the text "blue" and <code>count</code> holds the number 3. The statement <code>print(count)</code> shows the <strong>value</strong> stored in <code>count</code>, which is 3. It does not show the letters "count"; the variable name is just a label for the value inside.</p>
      <div class="callout-exam">
        <div class="callout-exam-label">🎯 What the exam expects</div>
        <p>Read the assignment direction right to left: the value on the right goes into the name on the left. Python writes <code>x = 5</code>; the AP reference sheet writes <code>x <- 5</code>. Both create or update the variable <code>x</code> so it holds 5. The <code>=</code> here is assignment, not a claim that two things are equal.</p>
      </div>
    </div>

    <div class="lesson-section">
      <h2>Assignment Replaces the Old Value</h2>
      <p>A variable holds exactly one value at a time. When you assign a new value, the previous value is <strong>replaced</strong> and is gone. There is no memory of what used to be there; only the most recent assignment survives.</p>
      <div class="code-panel-wrap">
  <div class="code-panel-tabs">
    <button class="code-tab py active" onclick="switchTab(this,'py','pan-2')">🐛 Python</button>
    <button class="code-tab pseudo" onclick="switchTab(this,'pseudo','pan-2')">📋 AP Pseudocode</button>
  </div>
  <div class="code-pane active" id="pan-2-py"><pre><span class="py-var">x</span><span class="py-var"> </span><span class="py-var">=</span><span class="py-var"> </span><span class="py-num">10</span>
<span class="py-var">x</span><span class="py-var"> </span><span class="py-var">=</span><span class="py-var"> </span><span class="py-num">25</span>
<span class="py-kw">print</span><span class="py-var">(</span><span class="py-var">x</span><span class="py-var">)</span></pre></div>
  <div class="code-pane" id="pan-2-pseudo"><pre><span class="ps-var">x</span><span class="ps-var"> </span><span class="ps-var"><</span><span class="ps-var">-</span><span class="ps-var"> </span><span class="ps-num">10</span>
<span class="ps-var">x</span><span class="ps-var"> </span><span class="ps-var"><</span><span class="ps-var">-</span><span class="ps-var"> </span><span class="ps-num">25</span>
<span class="ps-kw">DISPLAY</span><span class="ps-var">(</span><span class="ps-var">x</span><span class="ps-var">)</span></pre></div>
</div>
      <p>The first line stores 10 in <code>x</code>. The second line stores 25 in <code>x</code>, overwriting the 10. By the time <code>print(x)</code> runs, the only value <code>x</code> holds is 25, so 25 is displayed. The 10 was thrown away the instant the second assignment happened.</p>

    <div class="lesson-section">
      <h2>Updating a Variable Using Itself</h2>
      <p>One of the most useful patterns is updating a variable based on its own current value, like <code>count = count + 1</code>. At first this looks impossible, as if the variable is being defined in terms of itself. The trick is the order of operations: the <strong>right side is fully evaluated first</strong>, using the current (old) value, and only then is the result stored back into the variable.</p>
      <div class="code-panel-wrap">
  <div class="code-panel-tabs">
    <button class="code-tab py active" onclick="switchTab(this,'py','pan-3')">🐛 Python</button>
    <button class="code-tab pseudo" onclick="switchTab(this,'pseudo','pan-3')">📋 AP Pseudocode</button>
  </div>
  <div class="code-pane active" id="pan-3-py"><pre><span class="py-var">count</span><span class="py-var"> </span><span class="py-var">=</span><span class="py-var"> </span><span class="py-num">5</span>
<span class="py-var">count</span><span class="py-var"> </span><span class="py-var">=</span><span class="py-var"> </span><span class="py-var">count</span><span class="py-var"> </span><span class="py-var">+</span><span class="py-var"> </span><span class="py-num">1</span>
<span class="py-kw">print</span><span class="py-var">(</span><span class="py-var">count</span><span class="py-var">)</span></pre></div>
  <div class="code-pane" id="pan-3-pseudo"><pre><span class="ps-var">count</span><span class="ps-var"> </span><span class="ps-var"><</span><span class="ps-var">-</span><span class="ps-var"> </span><span class="ps-num">5</span>
<span class="ps-var">count</span><span class="ps-var"> </span><span class="ps-var"><</span><span class="ps-var">-</span><span class="ps-var"> </span><span class="ps-var">count</span><span class="ps-var"> </span><span class="ps-var">+</span><span class="ps-var"> </span><span class="ps-num">1</span>
<span class="ps-kw">DISPLAY</span><span class="ps-var">(</span><span class="ps-var">count</span><span class="ps-var">)</span></pre></div>
</div>
      <p>Here <code>count</code> starts at 5. On the update line, Python first computes the right side <code>count + 1</code>, which uses the current value 5 to get 6. Then it stores that 6 back into <code>count</code>, replacing the 5. So the final value is 6. The variable on the left is not touched until the right side is finished.</p>
      <div class="callout-trap">
        <div class="callout-trap-label">⚠ The self-update trap</div>
        <p>Students sometimes think <code>x = x + 1</code> is a contradiction because "x cannot equal x plus one." Remember that <code>=</code> is not an equality claim. It is an instruction: compute <code>x + 1</code> with the old value, then make that the new value of <code>x</code>. This is exactly how running totals and counters work.</p>
      </div>

      <p>When several assignments run one after another, trace them with a <strong>variable table</strong>: one column per variable, one row per line, and you rewrite a cell only when that line changes it. Always evaluate the right side using the values in the current row before you write the new value.</p>

  <div class="code-panel-tabs">

<span class="py-var">total</span><span class="py-var"> </span><span class="py-var">=</span><span class="py-var"> </span><span class="py-var">total</span><span class="py-var"> </span><span class="py-var">+</span><span class="py-var"> </span><span class="py-num">10</span>

    <div class="lesson-section">
      <h2>Swapping Two Variables</h2>
      <p>Suppose <code>a</code> holds 1 and <code>b</code> holds 9, and you want them to trade values. The natural first attempt, <code>a = b</code> then <code>b = a</code>, does not work. The moment you run <code>a = b</code>, the old value of <code>a</code> is overwritten and lost, so the second line just copies the value back. Both variables end up the same.</p>
      <p>The fix is a <strong>temporary variable</strong>. Save the first value in <code>temp</code> before you overwrite it, then restore it into the second variable:</p>
      <div class="code-panel-wrap">
  <div class="code-panel-tabs">
    <button class="code-tab py active" onclick="switchTab(this,'py','pan-5')">🐛 Python</button>
    <button class="code-tab pseudo" onclick="switchTab(this,'pseudo','pan-5')">📋 AP Pseudocode</button>
  </div>
  <div class="code-pane active" id="pan-5-py"><pre><span class="py-var">a</span><span class="py-var"> </span><span class="py-var">=</span><span class="py-var"> </span><span class="py-num">1</span>
<span class="py-var">b</span><span class="py-var"> </span><span class="py-var">=</span><span class="py-var"> </span><span class="py-num">9</span>
<span class="py-var">temp</span><span class="py-var"> </span><span class="py-var">=</span><span class="py-var"> </span><span class="py-var">a</span>
<span class="py-var">a</span><span class="py-var"> </span><span class="py-var">=</span><span class="py-var"> </span><span class="py-var">b</span>
<span class="py-var">b</span><span class="py-var"> </span><span class="py-var">=</span><span class="py-var"> </span><span class="py-var">temp</span>
<span class="py-kw">print</span><span class="py-var">(</span><span class="py-var">a</span><span class="py-var">,</span><span class="py-var"> </span><span class="py-var">b</span><span class="py-var">)</span></pre></div>
  <div class="code-pane" id="pan-5-pseudo"><pre><span class="ps-var">a</span><span class="ps-var"> </span><span class="ps-var"><</span><span class="ps-var">-</span><span class="ps-var"> </span><span class="ps-num">1</span>
<span class="ps-var">b</span><span class="ps-var"> </span><span class="ps-var"><</span><span class="ps-var">-</span><span class="ps-var"> </span><span class="ps-num">9</span>
<span class="ps-var">temp</span><span class="ps-var"> </span><span class="ps-var"><</span><span class="ps-var">-</span><span class="ps-var"> </span><span class="ps-var">a</span>
<span class="ps-var">a</span><span class="ps-var"> </span><span class="ps-var"><</span><span class="ps-var">-</span><span class="ps-var"> </span><span class="ps-var">b</span>
<span class="ps-var">b</span><span class="ps-var"> </span><span class="ps-var"><</span><span class="ps-var">-</span><span class="ps-var"> </span><span class="ps-var">temp</span>
<span class="ps-kw">DISPLAY</span><span class="ps-var">(</span><span class="ps-var">a</span><span class="ps-var">)</span>
<span class="ps-kw">DISPLAY</span><span class="ps-var">(</span><span class="ps-var">b</span><span class="ps-var">)</span></pre></div>
</div>
      <p>Now <code>temp</code> remembers the original 1 while <code>a</code> is overwritten with 9. Then <code>b</code> is set to <code>temp</code>, which is 1. The result is a real swap: <code>a</code> is 9 and <code>b</code> is 1. Compare that with the broken version that skips the temp holder:</p>
      <div class="code-panel-wrap">
  <div class="code-panel-tabs">
    <button class="code-tab py active" onclick="switchTab(this,'py','pan-6')">🐛 Python (buggy)</button>
    <button class="code-tab pseudo" onclick="switchTab(this,'pseudo','pan-6')">📋 Pseudocode (fixed)</button>
  </div>
  <div class="code-pane active" id="pan-6-py"><pre><span class="py-comment"># WRONG: no temp, one value is lost</span>
<span class="py-var">a</span><span class="py-var"> </span><span class="py-var">=</span><span class="py-var"> </span><span class="py-num">1</span>
<span class="py-var">b</span><span class="py-var"> </span><span class="py-var">=</span><span class="py-var"> </span><span class="py-num">9</span>
<span class="py-var">a</span><span class="py-var"> </span><span class="py-var">=</span><span class="py-var"> </span><span class="py-var">b</span>
<span class="py-var">b</span><span class="py-var"> </span><span class="py-var">=</span><span class="py-var"> </span><span class="py-var">a</span>
<span class="py-kw">print</span><span class="py-var">(</span><span class="py-var">a</span><span class="py-var">,</span><span class="py-var"> </span><span class="py-var">b</span><span class="py-var">)</span></pre></div>
  <div class="code-pane" id="pan-6-pseudo"><pre><span class="ps-comment"># RIGHT: hold the first value in temp</span>
<span class="ps-var">temp</span><span class="ps-var"> </span><span class="ps-var"><</span><span class="ps-var">-</span><span class="ps-var"> </span><span class="ps-var">a</span>
<span class="ps-var">a</span><span class="ps-var"> </span><span class="ps-var"><</span><span class="ps-var">-</span><span class="ps-var"> </span><span class="ps-var">b</span>
<span class="ps-var">b</span><span class="ps-var"> </span><span class="ps-var"><</span><span class="ps-var">-</span><span class="ps-var"> </span><span class="ps-var">temp</span></pre></div>
</div>
      <div class="callout-trap">
        <div class="callout-trap-label">⚠ Lost value</div>
        <p>Any time you assign into a variable, whatever it held is gone. If you still need that old value later, copy it somewhere first. Swapping is the classic case: without a temp variable, the first assignment destroys the value the second assignment needed.</p>
      </div>
    </div>

    <div class="cpt-connection">
      <div class="cpt-connection-label">📋 Create Performance Task • Variables that manage complexity</div>
      <p>Variables are the first tool your Create Task program uses to store and manage data. A well chosen variable, updated across several steps, is often what lets your program "produce a result" that depends on the input rather than a fixed constant. A running total is the classic example.</p>
      <h3>A point-earning example</h3>
      <p>Imagine a program that adds up points a user earns during a session:</p>
      <div class="cpt-code">score <- 0
score <- score + 10
score <- score + 5
DISPLAY(score)</div>
      <p>In your written response, name the variable, say what it represents, and describe how assignment changes it:</p>
      <ul class="cpt-stems">
        <li>"The variable <code>score</code> stores the running total of points the user has earned so far."</li>
        <li>"Each assignment updates <code>score</code> using its own current value, so the total grows as the program runs."</li>
        <li>"Because <code>score</code> holds a value that changes with the input, the program produces a result that is not fixed in advance."</li>
      </ul>
      <h3>The trap to avoid</h3>
      <p>Do not overwrite a value you still need. If you assign into a variable before saving its old contents, that data is gone, which is the exact bug behind a failed swap. When you update a total, use <code>score = score + n</code> so the old value is read before the new one replaces it. <a href="/pages/ap-csp-course-create-task">See the full Create Task module →</a></p>

</div>
<div id="q2-fb-A" class="mcq-feedback correct-fb">Correct. p = q makes p 8 and destroys the original 3. Then q = p copies 8 back, so both are 8. A temp variable is needed.</div>
<div id="q2-fb-B" class="mcq-feedback incorrect-fb">Incorrect. That would be a successful swap, but the original 3 is lost on the line p = q before it can be moved to q.</div>
<div id="q2-fb-C" class="mcq-feedback incorrect-fb">Incorrect. 3 8 is the unchanged starting state, but p is overwritten to 8 on the third line.</div>

<button class="mcq-option" onclick="checkMCQ('q3','C','B','q3-fb-C')"><span class="mcq-option-letter">C</span> <code>10 = k</code></button>
<button class="mcq-option" onclick="checkMCQ('q3','D','B','q3-fb-D')"><span class="mcq-option-letter">D</span> <code>k =: 10</code></button>
</div>
<div id="q3-fb-A" class="mcq-feedback incorrect-fb">Incorrect. Double equals <code>==</code> tests equality; it does not store a value. It would not assign 10 to k.</div>
<div id="q3-fb-B" class="mcq-feedback correct-fb">Correct. A single <code>=</code> is the assignment operator: it takes the value 10 on the right and stores it in k on the left.</div>
<div id="q3-fb-C" class="mcq-feedback incorrect-fb">Incorrect. The variable being assigned must be on the left. <code>10 = k</code> tries to assign into a number, which is not valid.</div>
<div id="q3-fb-D" class="mcq-feedback incorrect-fb">Incorrect. <code>=:</code> is not a Python operator. Python uses a single <code>=</code> for assignment.</div>

    <div class="faq-section">
      <h2>Frequently Asked Questions</h2>
      <div class="faq-item">
        <button class="faq-q" onclick="toggleFAQ(this)">What is a variable in AP CSP?<i class="faq-icon">+</i></button>
        <div class="faq-a">A variable is a named abstraction inside a program that holds a value. The name lets you refer to the value and change it later. Creating a variable and giving it a value is done with an assignment statement.</div>
      </div>
      <div class="faq-item">
        <button class="faq-q" onclick="toggleFAQ(this)">What does the equals sign mean in an assignment?<i class="faq-icon">+</i></button>
        <div class="faq-a">In Python <code>=</code> is the assignment operator. It takes the value on the right and stores it in the variable on the left. It is not a claim that two things are equal, which is why <code>x = x + 1</code> is valid. AP pseudocode writes the same idea as <code>x <- x + 1</code>.</div>
      </div>
      <div class="faq-item">
        <button class="faq-q" onclick="toggleFAQ(this)">Why is x = x + 1 not a contradiction?<i class="faq-icon">+</i></button>
        <div class="faq-a">Because the right side is evaluated first using the current value of <code>x</code>, and only then is the result stored back into <code>x</code>. If <code>x</code> was 5, the program computes 5 + 1 = 6 and makes 6 the new value. The variable is not updated until the right side is finished.</div>
      </div>
      <div class="faq-item">
        <button class="faq-q" onclick="toggleFAQ(this)">Why do I need a temp variable to swap two values?<i class="faq-icon">+</i></button>
        <div class="faq-a">When you assign into a variable, its old value is immediately replaced and lost. If you write <code>a = b</code> first, the original value of <code>a</code> is gone before you can move it to <code>b</code>. A temporary variable saves that value so the swap can finish correctly.</div>
      </div>
      <div class="faq-item">
        <button class="faq-q" onclick="toggleFAQ(this)">Does print show the variable name or its value?<i class="faq-icon">+</i></button>
        <div class="faq-a">It shows the value currently stored in the variable, not the letters of the name. If <code>x</code> holds 25, then <code>print(x)</code> displays 25, not the letter x.</div>
      </div>

function switchTab(btn, lang, panelId){

}
/* Gradebook hook: fire one standard event per graded interaction. The theme reporter
   listens for 'apcsActivity' and reads course/unit/lesson off the .lesson-page wrapper. */
function _activity(d){

    if(w){ d.course=w.getAttribute('data-course'); d.unit=w.getAttribute('data-unit'); d.lesson=w.getAttribute('data-lesson'); }

}

  var letters=['A','B','C','D'];
  opts[letters.indexOf(chosen)].classList.add(chosen===correct?'correct':'incorrect');
  if(chosen!==correct)opts[letters.indexOf(correct)].classList.add('reveal');

  if(MINI_MSGS[id]){fb.textContent=MINI_MSGS[id][chosen]||'';fb.className='mini-fb '+(chosen===correct?'c':'w');}

  var val=inp.value.trim().toLowerCase();var d=MINI_FIB[id];

function loadScriptOnce(src){return new Promise(function(res,rej){
  if(document.querySelector('script[data-pyodide]')){res();return;}
  var s=document.createElement('script');s.src=src;s.setAttribute('data-pyodide','1');
  s.onload=function(){res();};s.onerror=function(){rej(new Error('script load failed'));};
  document.head.appendChild(s);});}
function ensurePy(){if(window.__pyPromise)return window.__pyPromise;
  window.__pyPromise=(async function(){await loadScriptOnce(PY_URL+'pyodide.js');
    var py=await loadPyodide({indexURL:PY_URL});window.__pyodide=py;return py;})();
  return window.__pyPromise;}
function cleanErr(msg){if(!msg)return 'error';var lines=String(msg).trim().split('\n');return lines.slice(-3).join('\n');}
function execUser(py,code){var output='',err=null;
  try{py.runPython('import sys, io\n__old_out = sys.stdout\nsys.stdout = io.StringIO()\nsys.stderr = sys.stdout');
    try{var ns=py.globals.get('dict')();py.runPython(code,{globals:ns});ns.destroy();}
    catch(e){err=cleanErr(e.message);}
    output=py.runPython('sys.stdout.getvalue()');}
  catch(e2){err=cleanErr((e2&&e2.message)||String(e2));}
  finally{try{py.runPython('sys.stdout = __old_out\nsys.stderr = __old_out');}catch(e3){}}
  return {output:output,err:err};}
async function runPy(n){

    out.textContent='Could not load the Python engine. Check your connection and try Run again.';if(btn)btn.disabled=false;return;}
  var code=document.getElementById('ce-'+n).value;var res=execUser(py,code);
  var solBtn=document.getElementById('sol-btn-'+n);

    else{out.className='code-output show';out.textContent='Output:\n'+shown;}

  LESSON_USAGE.solutions[n]=1;LESSON_USAGE.totalSolutions=_sumv(LESSON_USAGE.solutions);updateUsage();}

function vtRender(){if(vtQ>=VT_QS.length){vtShowResults();return;}vtAnswered=false;var q=VT_QS[vtQ];

  .lesson-hero{background:var(--navy);background-image:radial-gradient(ellipse 60% 70% at 90% 20%,rgba(26,86,219,.28) 0%,transparent 60%);padding:48px 24px 40px;}

  .lesson-hero-meta{display:flex;align-items:center;gap:10px;flex-wrap:wrap;margin-bottom:16px;}
  .lesson-num-badge{display:inline-flex;align-items:center;justify-content:center;width:44px;height:44px;border-radius:10px;background:var(--bi3);font-weight:700;font-size:14px;color:#fff!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:#fff!important;flex-shrink:0;}
  .lesson-eyebrow{font-size:12px;font-weight:700;letter-spacing:.08em;text-transform:uppercase;color:var(--bi3-lt)!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:var(--bi3-lt)!important;}
  .lesson-hero h1{font-family:"DM Serif Display",serif!important;font-size:clamp(26px,4vw,40px)!important;line-height:1.2!important;color:#fff!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:#fff!important;margin-bottom:14px!important;}
  .lesson-hero-pills{display:flex;flex-wrap:wrap;gap:8px;}
  .lesson-pill{display:inline-flex;align-items:center;gap:5px;background:rgba(255,255,255,.08);border:1px solid rgba(255,255,255,.15);padding:5px 12px;border-radius:100px;font-size:12px;color:#e2e8f0!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:#e2e8f0!important;}
  .ced-tag{display:inline-flex;align-items:center;background:rgba(26,86,219,.25);border:1px solid rgba(147,197,253,.3);padding:4px 10px;border-radius:100px;font-size:11px;font-weight:600;color:#bfdbfe!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:#bfdbfe!important;letter-spacing:.04em;}

  /* PROGRESS STRIP */
  .bi3-progress{background:#fff!important;border-bottom:1px solid #e2e8f0!important;padding:14px 20px!important;overflow-x:auto!important;-webkit-overflow-scrolling:touch!important;}
  .bi3-progress-inner{display:flex!important;flex-direction:row!important;flex-wrap:nowrap!important;align-items:center!important;gap:0!important;width:max-content!important;min-width:100%!important;}
  .prog-step{display:flex!important;flex-direction:column!important;align-items:center!important;min-width:46px!important;text-align:center!important;flex-shrink:0!important;}
  .prog-step-link{display:flex!important;flex-direction:column!important;align-items:center!important;min-width:46px!important;text-align:center!important;flex-shrink:0!important;text-decoration:none!important;cursor:pointer!important;}
  .prog-step-link:hover .prog-dot{background:#dbeafe!important;color:var(--bi3)!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:var(--bi3)!important;border-color:var(--bi3)!important;}
  .prog-dot{width:26px!important;height:26px!important;border-radius:50%!important;display:flex!important;align-items:center!important;justify-content:center!important;font-size:9px!important;font-weight:700!important;margin-bottom:4px!important;flex-shrink:0!important;}
  .prog-dot.active{background:var(--bi3)!important;color:#fff!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:#fff!important;}
  .prog-dot.upcoming{background:#f1f5f9!important;color:#94a3b8!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:#94a3b8!important;border:2px solid #e2e8f0!important;}
  .prog-dot.done{background:#dbeafe!important;color:var(--bi3)!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:var(--bi3)!important;border:2px solid var(--bi3)!important;}
  .prog-label{font-size:8px!important;font-weight:600!important;color:#64748b!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:#64748b!important;line-height:1.2!important;white-space:nowrap!important;}
  .prog-label.active-label{color:var(--bi3)!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:var(--bi3)!important;}
  .prog-arrow{flex:1 0 4px!important;height:2px!important;background:#e2e8f0!important;margin-bottom:18px!important;min-width:4px!important;max-width:16px!important;flex-shrink:0!important;}

  /* MAIN */
  .lesson-main{max-width:880px;margin:0 auto;padding:40px 24px 80px;}
  .lesson-objectives{background:var(--bi3-bg);border-left:4px solid var(--bi3);border-radius:0 10px 10px 0;padding:20px 24px;margin-bottom:28px;}
  .lesson-objectives h2{font-size:14px!important;font-weight:700!important;color:var(--bi3-dk)!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:var(--bi3-dk)!important;text-transform:uppercase!important;letter-spacing:.06em!important;margin-bottom:12px!important;}
  .lesson-objectives ul{list-style:none;padding:0;display:flex;flex-direction:column;gap:8px;}
  .lesson-objectives li{display:flex;align-items:flex-start;gap:10px;font-size:14px;color:#1e3a8a;line-height:1.5;}
  .lesson-objectives li::before{content:"\2713";color:var(--bi3);font-weight:700;flex-shrink:0;margin-top:1px;}
  .score-impact{background:#f0fdf4;border:1px solid #bbf7d0;border-radius:8px;padding:12px 18px;margin-bottom:28px;display:flex;align-items:center;gap:10px;font-size:14px;color:#14532d;}
  .score-impact strong{color:#14532d!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:#14532d!important;}

  /* HOOK */
  .hook-box{background:linear-gradient(135deg,#1e3a8a 0%,#1e40af 100%);border-radius:12px;padding:24px 28px;margin-bottom:32px;}
  .hook-label{font-size:11px;font-weight:700;letter-spacing:.1em;text-transform:uppercase;color:var(--bi3-lt)!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:var(--bi3-lt)!important;margin-bottom:8px;}
  .hook-box p{font-size:15px!important;color:#bfdbfe!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:#bfdbfe!important;line-height:1.7!important;margin-bottom:0!important;}

  /* LESSON SECTIONS */
  .lesson-section{margin-bottom:40px;}
  .lesson-section h2{font-family:"DM Serif Display",serif!important;font-size:24px!important;color:var(--navy)!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:var(--navy)!important;margin-bottom:14px!important;padding-bottom:10px!important;border-bottom:2px solid var(--bi3-bg)!important;}
  .lesson-section h3{font-size:17px!important;font-weight:700!important;color:var(--navy)!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:var(--navy)!important;margin-top:24px!important;margin-bottom:10px!important;}
  .lesson-section p{font-size:15px;color:#374151;line-height:1.8;margin-bottom:14px;}
  .lesson-section ul,.lesson-section ol{padding-left:20px;margin-bottom:14px;}
  .lesson-section li{font-size:15px;color:#374151;line-height:1.7;margin-bottom:6px;}
  .lesson-section code{background:#eef2ff;color:#1e3a8a!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:#1e3a8a!important;padding:1px 6px;border-radius:5px;font-size:13px;}

  /* DUAL CODE PANEL */
  .code-panel-wrap{margin:20px 0;border-radius:12px;overflow:hidden;border:1px solid #e2e8f0;}
  .code-panel-tabs{display:flex;background:#1e293b;}
  .code-tab{padding:8px 16px;font-size:12px;font-weight:700;cursor:pointer;border:none;background:transparent;letter-spacing:.04em;transition:background .15s;font-family:inherit;}
  .code-tab.py{color:#93c5fd!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:#93c5fd!important;}
  .code-tab.pseudo{color:#c4b5fd!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:#c4b5fd!important;}
  .code-tab.active{background:rgba(255,255,255,.15)!important;}
  .code-tab-label{font-size:10px;opacity:.6;margin-left:4px;font-weight:400;}
  .code-pane{background:#0f172a;padding:18px 20px;overflow-x:auto;height:0;overflow:hidden;padding:0;}
  .code-pane.active{height:auto;overflow-x:auto;padding:18px 20px;}
  .code-pane pre{font-family:monospace;font-size:13px;line-height:1.8;margin:0;white-space:pre-wrap;word-break:break-word;max-width:100%;color:#e2e8f0!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:#e2e8f0!important;}
  .py-kw{color:#93c5fd!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:#93c5fd!important;font-weight:700;}
  .py-fn{color:#6ee7b7!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:#6ee7b7!important;}
  .py-num{color:#fde68a!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:#fde68a!important;}
  .py-str{color:#f9a8d4!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:#f9a8d4!important;}
  .py-comment{color:#475569!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:#475569!important;font-style:italic;}
  .py-var{color:#e2e8f0!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:#e2e8f0!important;}
  .py-op{color:#94a3b8!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:#94a3b8!important;}
  .ps-kw{color:#c4b5fd!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:#c4b5fd!important;font-weight:700;}
  .ps-op{color:#f9a8d4!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:#f9a8d4!important;}
  .ps-num{color:#fde68a!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:#fde68a!important;}
  .ps-str{color:#86efac!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:#86efac!important;}
  .ps-comment{color:#475569!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:#475569!important;font-style:italic;}
  .ps-var{color:#e2e8f0!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:#e2e8f0!important;}

  /* CALLOUTS */
  .callout-exam{background:#fffbeb;border:1px solid #fcd34d;border-left:4px solid var(--amber);border-radius:0 8px 8px 0;padding:16px 20px;margin:20px 0;}
  .callout-exam-label{font-size:11px;font-weight:700;letter-spacing:.08em;text-transform:uppercase;color:var(--amber)!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:var(--amber)!important;margin-bottom:6px;}
  .callout-exam p{font-size:14px!important;color:#78350f!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:#78350f!important;margin-bottom:0!important;line-height:1.6!important;}
  .callout-trap{background:#fef2f2;border:1px solid #fca5a5;border-left:4px solid var(--red);border-radius:0 8px 8px 0;padding:16px 20px;margin:20px 0;}
  .callout-trap-label{font-size:11px;font-weight:700;letter-spacing:.08em;text-transform:uppercase;color:var(--red)!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:var(--red)!important;margin-bottom:6px;}
  .callout-trap p{font-size:14px!important;color:#7f1d1d!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:#7f1d1d!important;margin-bottom:0!important;line-height:1.6!important;}

  /* MINI EXERCISES */
  .mini-ex{background:#fff;border:1px solid #bfdbfe;border-radius:12px;padding:20px 24px;margin:24px 0;}
  .mini-ex-label{display:flex;align-items:center;gap:8px;font-size:11px;font-weight:700;letter-spacing:.08em;text-transform:uppercase;color:var(--bi3-dk)!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:var(--bi3-dk)!important;margin-bottom:12px;}
  .mini-ex-q{font-size:15px;font-weight:600;color:var(--navy)!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:var(--navy)!important;margin-bottom:14px;line-height:1.5;}
  .mini-ex-code{background:#0f172a;border-radius:8px;padding:14px 16px;font-family:monospace;font-size:13px;line-height:1.8;margin-bottom:14px;overflow-x:auto;white-space:pre;display:block;}
  .mini-opts{display:flex;flex-direction:column;gap:7px;margin-bottom:10px;}
  .mini-opt{display:flex;align-items:center;gap:10px;padding:10px 14px;border:2px solid #e2e8f0;border-radius:8px;cursor:pointer;font-size:14px;font-family:monospace;color:#374151!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:#374151!important;background:#f8fafc;text-align:left;width:100%;transition:border-color .15s;}
  .mini-opt:hover{border-color:var(--bi3-lt);background:var(--bi3-bg);}
  .mini-opt.correct{border-color:var(--green)!important;background:#f0fdf4!important;color:#14532d!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:#14532d!important;}
  .mini-opt.incorrect{border-color:var(--red)!important;background:#fef2f2!important;color:#7f1d1d!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:#7f1d1d!important;}
  .mini-opt.reveal{border-color:var(--green)!important;background:#f0fdf4!important;}
  .mini-opt-letter{font-weight:700;color:var(--bi3)!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:var(--bi3)!important;min-width:18px;font-family:inherit;}
  .mini-opt.correct .mini-opt-letter{color:#14532d!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:#14532d!important;}
  .mini-opt.incorrect .mini-opt-letter{color:#7f1d1d!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:#7f1d1d!important;}
  .mini-fib-row{display:flex;gap:8px;align-items:center;flex-wrap:wrap;margin-bottom:10px;}
  .mini-fib-input{padding:8px 12px;border:2px solid #e2e8f0;border-radius:8px;font-family:monospace;font-size:14px;width:130px;outline:none;color:var(--navy)!important;background:#f8fafc;}
  .mini-fib-input:focus{border-color:var(--bi3-lt);}
  .mini-fib-input.correct{border-color:var(--green);background:#f0fdf4;}
  .mini-fib-input.incorrect{border-color:var(--red);background:#fef2f2;}
  .mini-fib-btn{padding:8px 18px;background:var(--bi3);border:none;border-radius:8px;color:#fff!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:#fff!important;font-size:13px;font-weight:700;cursor:pointer;font-family:inherit;}
  .mini-fb{font-size:13px;font-weight:500;padding:8px 12px;border-radius:7px;margin-top:6px;display:none;line-height:1.5;}
  .mini-fb.c{background:#f0fdf4;color:var(--green)!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:var(--green)!important;display:block;}
  .mini-fb.w{background:#fef2f2;color:var(--red)!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:var(--red)!important;display:block;}

  /* VOCAB */
  .vocab-table{width:100%;border-collapse:collapse;margin-bottom:24px;font-size:14px;}
  .vocab-table thead tr{background:var(--bi3);}
  .vocab-table thead th{padding:10px 16px;text-align:left;font-weight:600;color:#fff!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:#fff!important;font-size:13px;}
  .vocab-table tbody tr:nth-child(even){background:var(--bi3-bg);}
  .vocab-table tbody tr:nth-child(odd){background:#fff;}
  .vocab-table tbody td{padding:10px 16px;border-bottom:1px solid #bfdbfe;color:#374151;vertical-align:top;line-height:1.5;}
  .vocab-table tbody td:first-child{font-weight:700;color:var(--bi3-dk)!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:var(--bi3-dk)!important;white-space:nowrap;}

  /* CPT CONNECTION */
  .cpt-connection{background:#fefce8;border:1px solid #fde68a;border-left:4px solid #f59e0b;border-radius:0 10px 10px 0;padding:20px 24px;margin:28px 0;}
  .cpt-connection-label{font-size:11px;font-weight:700;letter-spacing:.08em;text-transform:uppercase;color:#92400e!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:#92400e!important;margin-bottom:8px;}
  .cpt-connection h3{font-size:16px!important;font-weight:700!important;color:#78350f!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:#78350f!important;margin:16px 0 8px!important;}
  .cpt-connection p{font-size:14px!important;color:#78350f!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:#78350f!important;line-height:1.7!important;margin-bottom:12px!important;}
  .cpt-connection a{color:#b45309!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:#b45309!important;font-weight:600;text-decoration:underline;}
  .cpt-connection code{background:#fef3c7;color:#78350f!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:#78350f!important;padding:1px 6px;border-radius:5px;font-size:13px;}
  .cpt-stems{list-style:none;padding:0;margin:0 0 8px;display:flex;flex-direction:column;gap:8px;}
  .cpt-stems li{background:#fffef5;border:1px solid #fde68a;border-radius:8px;padding:10px 14px;font-size:13px!important;color:#78350f!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:#78350f!important;line-height:1.6;}
  .cpt-code{background:#0f172a;border-radius:8px;padding:14px 16px;font-family:monospace;font-size:13px;line-height:1.8;margin:6px 0 12px;overflow-x:auto;white-space:pre;display:block;color:#e2e8f0!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:#e2e8f0!important;}

  /* EMAIL */
  .email-capture{background:linear-gradient(135deg,#1e3a8a 0%,#1e40af 100%);border-radius:12px;padding:24px 28px;margin-bottom:36px;display:flex;align-items:center;gap:24px;flex-wrap:wrap;}
  .email-capture-text{flex:1;min-width:200px;}
  .email-capture-eyebrow{font-size:11px;font-weight:700;letter-spacing:.1em;text-transform:uppercase;color:var(--bi3-lt)!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:var(--bi3-lt)!important;margin-bottom:4px;}
  .email-capture h3{font-size:16px!important;font-weight:700!important;color:#fff!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:#fff!important;margin-bottom:4px!important;}
  .email-capture p{font-size:13px!important;color:#94a3b8!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:#94a3b8!important;margin-bottom:0!important;line-height:1.5!important;}
  .email-capture-form{display:flex;gap:8px;flex-wrap:wrap;flex-shrink:0;}
  .email-capture-input{padding:10px 14px;border-radius:8px;border:1px solid rgba(255,255,255,.2);background:rgba(255,255,255,.1);color:#fff!important;font-size:14px;font-family:inherit;min-width:180px;outline:none;}
  .email-capture-btn{padding:10px 20px!important;background:var(--bi3)!important;color:#fff!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:#fff!important;border:none!important;border-radius:8px!important;font-size:14px!important;font-weight:600!important;cursor:pointer!important;font-family:inherit!important;}
  .email-capture-success{display:none;font-size:14px;color:#93c5fd!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:#93c5fd!important;font-weight:600;padding:10px 0;}

  /* MCQ */
  .mcq-section{background:#fff;border:1px solid #e2e8f0;border-radius:14px;padding:28px;margin-bottom:40px;}
  .mcq-section-header{display:flex;align-items:center;gap:12px;margin-bottom:24px;padding-bottom:16px;border-bottom:2px solid var(--bi3-bg);}
  .mcq-section-icon{width:40px;height:40px;border-radius:10px;background:var(--bi3-bg);display:flex;align-items:center;justify-content:center;font-size:18px;flex-shrink:0;}
  .mcq-section-title{font-family:"DM Serif Display",serif;font-size:20px;color:var(--navy)!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:var(--navy)!important;}
  .mcq-section-sub{font-size:13px;color:var(--slate);}
  .mcq-item{margin-bottom:28px;padding-bottom:28px;border-bottom:1px solid #f1f5f9;}
  .mcq-item:last-child{border-bottom:none;margin-bottom:0;padding-bottom:0;}
  .mcq-q-num{font-size:11px;font-weight:700;letter-spacing:.08em;text-transform:uppercase;color:var(--slate);margin-bottom:8px;}
  .diff-tag{display:inline-block;font-size:10px;font-weight:700;letter-spacing:.06em;text-transform:uppercase;padding:2px 8px;border-radius:100px;margin-left:8px;background:#fef2f2;color:#b91c1c!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:#b91c1c!important;border:1px solid #fca5a5;}
  .mcq-q-text{font-size:15px!important;font-weight:600!important;color:#0f1f3d!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:#0f1f3d!important;line-height:1.6!important;margin-bottom:12px!important;}
  .predict-note{font-size:12px;font-style:italic;color:#64748b!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:#64748b!important;margin-bottom:12px;}
  .mcq-code{background:#0f172a;border-radius:8px;padding:12px 14px;margin:10px 0 14px;font-family:monospace;font-size:13px;line-height:1.75;color:#e2e8f0!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:#e2e8f0!important;white-space:pre;overflow-x:auto;display:block;}
  .mcq-code .k{color:#93c5fd!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:#93c5fd!important;}
  .mcq-code .s{color:#f9a8d4!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:#f9a8d4!important;}
  .mcq-code .n{color:#fde68a!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:#fde68a!important;}
  .mcq-code .c{color:#64748b!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:#64748b!important;font-style:italic;}
  .mcq-roman{list-style:none;padding:0;margin:10px 0 14px;display:flex;flex-direction:column;gap:6px;}
  .mcq-roman li{font-family:monospace;font-size:13px;color:#1e293b!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:#1e293b!important;background:#f1f5f9;border-radius:6px;padding:8px 12px;}
  .mcq-roman li strong{color:var(--bi3-dk)!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:var(--bi3-dk)!important;font-family:"DM Sans",sans-serif;margin-right:8px;}
  .mcq-options{display:flex;flex-direction:column;gap:8px;margin-bottom:12px;}
  .mcq-option{display:flex!important;align-items:flex-start!important;gap:12px!important;padding:11px 14px!important;border:2px solid #e2e8f0!important;border-radius:8px!important;cursor:pointer!important;background:#f8fafc!important;font-size:14px!important;color:#374151!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:#374151!important;line-height:1.5!important;text-align:left!important;width:100%!important;font-family:inherit!important;}
  .mcq-option:hover{border-color:var(--bi3-lt)!important;background:var(--bi3-bg)!important;}
  .mcq-option.correct{border-color:var(--green)!important;background:#f0fdf4!important;color:#14532d!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:#14532d!important;}
  .mcq-option.incorrect{border-color:var(--red)!important;background:#fef2f2!important;color:#7f1d1d!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:#7f1d1d!important;}
  .mcq-option.revealed-correct{border-color:var(--green)!important;background:#f0fdf4!important;}
  .mcq-option-letter{font-weight:700!important;color:var(--bi3)!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:var(--bi3)!important;flex-shrink:0!important;min-width:18px!important;}
  .mcq-option.correct .mcq-option-letter{color:#14532d!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:#14532d!important;}
  .mcq-option.incorrect .mcq-option-letter{color:#7f1d1d!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:#7f1d1d!important;}
  .mcq-feedback{display:none!important;padding:12px 16px!important;border-radius:8px!important;font-size:14px!important;line-height:1.6!important;margin-top:8px!important;}
  .mcq-feedback.show{display:block!important;}
  .mcq-feedback.correct-fb{background:#f0fdf4!important;color:#14532d!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:#14532d!important;border:1px solid #bbf7d0!important;}
  .mcq-feedback.incorrect-fb{background:#fef2f2!important;color:#7f1d1d!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:#7f1d1d!important;border:1px solid #fecaca!important;}

  /* GAME */
  .game-section{background:linear-gradient(135deg,#1e3a8a 0%,#1e40af 100%);border-radius:14px;padding:28px;margin-bottom:40px;}

    <div class="lesson-objectives">
      <h2>After this lesson, you will be able to:</h2>
      <ul>
        <li><span>Define fault tolerance as a system's ability to keep working when one or more components fail</span></li>
        <li><span>Explain redundancy as having multiple paths or copies so a failure does not stop the system</span></li>
        <li><span>Identify a single point of failure in a described network and explain why it is dangerous</span></li>
        <li><span>Explain why the Internet is fault tolerant because of redundant routing</span></li>
        <li><span>Describe the tradeoff between more redundancy and higher cost and resource use</span></li>
      </ul>
    </div>
    <div class="score-impact">📈 <span>Big Idea 4 (Computing Systems and Networks) is 11 to 15 percent of the AP CSP exam, and fault tolerance is one of its most reliably tested ideas. Questions about redundancy, single points of failure, and rerouting are quick points once you can read a network diagram, so this lesson is high value for the effort.</span>
</div>
    <div class="hook-box">
      <div class="hook-label">💡 Think about this first</div>
      <p>A small company runs its entire website through a single router in the closet. It is fast and cheap and works fine, until the day that one router dies and the whole site goes dark for everyone at once. A rival company spends a little more and wires every server to two separate routers. When one of theirs fails, customers never even notice. Both networks had a failure. Why did only one of them go down, and what did the second company buy with that extra wiring?</p>
    </div>
    <div class="lesson-section">
      <h2>What Fault Tolerance Actually Means</h2>
      <p><strong>Fault tolerance</strong> is the ability of a system to keep working, possibly at reduced performance, even when one or more of its components fail. A fault-tolerant system does not promise that nothing ever breaks. It promises that when something breaks, the whole system does not stop. The web page still loads, the packet still arrives, the service stays up, just maybe a little slower while the broken part is worked around.</p>
      <p>The mechanism that makes this possible is <strong>redundancy</strong>: having more than one path or more than one copy of a component, so that if one fails, another can take over. A network with only one cable between two points has no redundancy. A network with two independent cables between those same points is redundant, because losing one cable still leaves a working path. Redundancy is what you build in ahead of time so that fault tolerance is what you get when a failure actually happens.</p>
      <table class="vocab-table">
        <tr>
<th>Term</th>
<th>What it means</th>
</tr>
        <tr>
<td><strong>Redundancy</strong></td>
<td>Having multiple paths or copies of a component so the system can still function if one part fails.</td>
</tr>
        <tr>
<td><strong>Fault tolerance</strong></td>
<td>The ability of a system to keep working, possibly at reduced performance, when one or more components fail.</td>
</tr>
        <tr>
<td><strong>Single point of failure</strong></td>
<td>A component whose failure alone stops the entire system, because there is no backup path or copy for it.</td>
</tr>
      </table>
      <div class="callout-exam">
        <div class="callout-exam-label">🎯 What the exam rewards</div>
        <p>When a question asks why a system is fault tolerant, the credited answer is almost always <strong>redundancy: there is more than one path or copy, so a failure can be worked around</strong>. Fault tolerance is the outcome; redundancy is the reason.</p>
      </div>
    </div>

    <div class="lesson-section">
      <h2>Single Points of Failure</h2>
      <p>A <strong>single point of failure</strong> is a component whose failure, all by itself, brings down the whole system. If every request in a network has to pass through one router, one cable, or one server, then that one thing is a single point of failure: the moment it dies, everything that depends on it stops. Redundancy is precisely the tool for removing single points of failure. When you add a second path around a component, that component is no longer the only way through, so its failure no longer takes down the system.</p>
      <p>To spot a single point of failure in a described network, look for a component that <strong>every path must go through</strong>. If cutting one node or one link disconnects part of the network from the rest, that node or link is a single point of failure. If you can cut any one component and traffic still has another route, then there is no single point of failure at that spot.</p>
      <div class="callout-trap">
        <div class="callout-trap-label">⚠ Common trap</div>
        <p>Redundancy is <strong>not</strong> the same as making one path faster. Upgrading your single router to a faster model, or buying more bandwidth on your one cable, improves performance but adds zero fault tolerance: that faster router is still a single point of failure, and when it dies the system still goes fully down. Fault tolerance comes from having <strong>another</strong> path, not a better single path.</p>
      </div>
      <div class="mini-ex">
        <div class="mini-ex-label">Quick check</div>
        <div class="mini-ex-q">In a network, computers A and B both connect only to router R, and R is the only device connected to the Internet. Which component is a single point of failure?</div>
        <div class="mini-opts" id="mc-fault-1-opts">
          <button class="mini-opt" onclick="miniMCQ('mc-fault-1','A','C','mc-fault-1-fb')"><span class="mini-opt-letter">A</span> Computer A only</button>

          <button class="mini-opt" onclick="miniMCQ('mc-fault-1','C','C','mc-fault-1-fb')"><span class="mini-opt-letter">C</span> Router R, since all Internet traffic must pass through it</button>

        </div>
        <div class="mini-fb" id="mc-fault-1-fb"></div>
      </div>
    </div>

    <div class="lesson-section">
      <h2>Why the Internet Keeps Working: Redundant Routing</h2>
      <p>The Internet is a huge, fault-tolerant network, and the reason is <strong>redundant routing</strong>. Devices on the Internet are connected by many paths, not one. When you send data, it is broken into packets, and each packet is routed hop by hop from one router to the next toward its destination. If a router or a connection along the way <strong>fails</strong>, the routers around it can send packets along a <strong>different available path</strong>. The data still gets through; it just takes another route.</p>
      <p>This is why no single broken cable or dead router takes down the whole Internet. Because there are multiple paths between most points, the failure of any one path can be worked around. In general, <strong>connecting nodes with more than one path increases fault tolerance</strong>, and a network where every pair of important nodes has at least two independent paths has no single point of failure between them.</p>
      <ul>
        <li>
<strong>One path</strong> between two nodes: if that path fails, they are cut off. Not fault tolerant.</li>
        <li>
<strong>Two or more independent paths</strong> between two nodes: if one fails, traffic reroutes over another. Fault tolerant.</li>
      </ul>
      <div class="mini-ex">
        <div class="mini-ex-label">Quick check</div>
        <div class="mini-ex-q">A router on the Internet suddenly stops working. Users on both sides of it still reach each other, just over a slightly longer route. Which idea best explains why the network kept working?</div>
        <div class="mini-opts" id="mc-fault-2-opts">
          <button class="mini-opt" onclick="miniMCQ('mc-fault-2','A','B','mc-fault-2-fb')"><span class="mini-opt-letter">A</span> The failed router repaired itself instantly</button>
          <button class="mini-opt" onclick="miniMCQ('mc-fault-2','B','B','mc-fault-2-fb')"><span class="mini-opt-letter">B</span> Redundant routing let packets travel along another available path</button>
          <button class="mini-opt" onclick="miniMCQ('mc-fault-2','C','B','mc-fault-2-fb')"><span class="mini-opt-letter">C</span> The remaining routers ran at a faster clock speed to compensate</button>
          <button class="mini-opt" onclick="miniMCQ('mc-fault-2','D','B','mc-fault-2-fb')"><span class="mini-opt-letter">D</span> The packets were deleted and the users resent them by hand</button>
        </div>
        <div class="mini-fb" id="mc-fault-2-fb"></div>
      </div>
    </div>

    <div class="lesson-section">
      <h2>The Tradeoff: Redundancy Is Not Free</h2>
      <p>If redundancy is so good, why not build infinite backups everywhere? Because <strong>redundancy costs money and resources</strong>. Every extra path means extra cables, extra routers, extra servers, extra electricity, and extra maintenance. A second data center that mostly sits idle waiting for the first one to fail is expensive to run. So designers face a <strong>tradeoff</strong>: more redundancy generally means more fault tolerance, but also higher cost and more resources used.</p>
      <p>The right amount of redundancy depends on how important reliability is. A hospital network or a bank cannot tolerate downtime, so they pay for heavy redundancy. A hobby blog might accept the risk of a single server to save money. The exam wants you to recognize both directions of this relationship: adding redundant components increases fault tolerance, and it also increases cost.</p>
    </div>
    <div class="lesson-section">
      <h2>How Topic 4.2 Shows Up on the MCQ Exam</h2>
      <p>Fault tolerance questions on the multiple-choice section usually come in a few predictable shapes, and knowing them turns these into fast points. The most common is the <strong>network diagram or description</strong> where you must identify a <strong>single point of failure</strong>: look for the one component that every path passes through, the one whose removal disconnects part of the network. A close cousin asks <strong>which change would make a network more fault tolerant</strong>, and the answer is almost always the one that <strong>adds an additional path or a redundant component</strong> between nodes, not the one that upgrades a single link.</p>
      <p>The trap the exam loves is confusing <strong>redundancy with speed</strong>. Answers that make one path faster, add more bandwidth to a single cable, or use a more powerful single server improve performance but do <strong>not</strong> add fault tolerance, because a single point of failure remains. Remember the exact framework claim: the Internet is fault tolerant <strong>because of redundant routing</strong>, and connecting nodes with more than one path increases fault tolerance. Watch for stem words like <strong>MOST</strong>, <strong>LEAST</strong>, and <strong>EXCEPT</strong> that flip which option you should pick.</p>
    </div>

<button class="mcq-option" onclick="checkMCQ('q3','C','C','q3-fb-C')"><span class="mcq-option-letter">C</span> Switch S is a single point of failure, because if it fails all three computers are cut off</button>
<button class="mcq-option" onclick="checkMCQ('q3','D','C','q3-fb-D')"><span class="mcq-option-letter">D</span> Only the company network beyond S is a single point of failure</button>
</div>
<div id="q3-fb-A" class="mcq-feedback incorrect-fb">Incorrect. If computer X fails, Y and Z still reach the network through S. One computer is not what all traffic depends on.</div>
<div id="q3-fb-B" class="mcq-feedback incorrect-fb">Incorrect. Having several computers does not remove a single point of failure. All of them still depend on the one switch S.</div>
<div id="q3-fb-C" class="mcq-feedback correct-fb">Correct. Every connection from X, Y, and Z to the rest of the network passes through switch S, so S's failure alone disconnects all of them. That is a single point of failure.</div>
<div id="q3-fb-D" class="mcq-feedback incorrect-fb">Incorrect. The described bottleneck that every computer depends on is switch S, not the network beyond it.</div>

      <div class="mcq-item" data-activity="quiz" data-item="q4">
        <div class="mcq-q-num">Question 4 of 6<span class="diff-tag">Two true one false</span>
</div>
        <div class="predict-note">Decide which statements are true before matching to an option.</div>
        <div class="mcq-q-text"><p>Consider these claims about redundancy and fault tolerance:</p></div>
        <ul class="mcq-roman">
          <li>
<strong>I.</strong> Adding redundant paths between nodes can increase a network's fault tolerance.</li>
          <li>
<strong>II.</strong> The Internet is fault tolerant largely because packets can be rerouted along alternate paths when a router or connection fails.</li>
          <li>
<strong>III.</strong> Redundancy is free, so a well-designed network should always add as much of it as possible.</li>
        </ul>
        <div class="mcq-options" id="q4-options">
<button class="mcq-option" onclick="checkMCQ('q4','A','D','q4-fb-A')"><span class="mcq-option-letter">A</span> I only</button>
<button class="mcq-option" onclick="checkMCQ('q4','B','D','q4-fb-B')"><span class="mcq-option-letter">B</span> II only</button>
<button class="mcq-option" onclick="checkMCQ('q4','C','D','q4-fb-C')"><span class="mcq-option-letter">C</span> I, II, and III</button>
<button class="mcq-option" onclick="checkMCQ('q4','D','D','q4-fb-D')"><span class="mcq-option-letter">D</span> I and II only</button>
</div>
<div id="q4-fb-A" class="mcq-feedback incorrect-fb">Incorrect. Statement II is also true. Rerouting along alternate paths is exactly why the Internet tolerates failures.</div>
<div id="q4-fb-B" class="mcq-feedback incorrect-fb">Incorrect. Statement I is also true. Adding redundant paths is a core way to increase fault tolerance.</div>
<div id="q4-fb-C" class="mcq-feedback incorrect-fb">Incorrect. Statement III is false. Redundancy is not free; it adds cost and resource use, which is the tradeoff the framework describes.</div>
<div id="q4-fb-D" class="mcq-feedback correct-fb">Correct. I and II are true. III is false because redundancy costs money and resources, so there is a tradeoff rather than unlimited backups.</div>

      <div class="mcq-item" data-activity="quiz" data-item="q5">
        <div class="mcq-q-num">Question 5 of 6<span class="diff-tag">Tradeoff</span>
</div>
        <div class="predict-note">Predict what extra redundancy costs before reading the choices.</div>
        <div class="mcq-q-text"><p>A streaming company decides to run its service from three geographically separate data centers instead of one, so the service stays up if a whole data center goes offline. Which statement best describes the consequence of this decision?</p></div>
        <div class="mcq-options" id="q5-options">
          <button class="mcq-option" onclick="checkMCQ('q5','A','A','q5-fb-A')"><span class="mcq-option-letter">A</span> It increases fault tolerance but also increases the cost and resources required to run the service</button>
          <button class="mcq-option" onclick="checkMCQ('q5','B','A','q5-fb-B')"><span class="mcq-option-letter">B</span> It decreases fault tolerance because more data centers means more things that can break</button>
          <button class="mcq-option" onclick="checkMCQ('q5','C','A','q5-fb-C')"><span class="mcq-option-letter">C</span> It has no effect on fault tolerance, since the service already worked with one data center</button>
          <button class="mcq-option" onclick="checkMCQ('q5','D','A','q5-fb-D')"><span class="mcq-option-letter">D</span> It increases fault tolerance at no additional cost, because the extra centers are free to operate</button>
        </div>
        <div id="q5-fb-A" class="mcq-feedback correct-fb">Correct. Multiple independent data centers add redundancy, so the loss of one does not stop the service, but running three centers costs more money and resources. That is the tradeoff.</div>
        <div id="q5-fb-B" class="mcq-feedback incorrect-fb">Incorrect. More independent copies increase fault tolerance, because the service survives losing one. The relevant downside is cost, not reduced tolerance.</div>
        <div id="q5-fb-C" class="mcq-feedback incorrect-fb">Incorrect. Redundant data centers do change fault tolerance: the service can now survive a failure that would previously have taken it fully offline.</div>
        <div id="q5-fb-D" class="mcq-feedback incorrect-fb">Incorrect. Additional data centers are not free. They add hardware, electricity, and maintenance costs, which is the tradeoff for the extra fault tolerance.</div>
      </div>

        <div class="mcq-q-num">Question 6 of 6<span class="diff-tag">Reroute reasoning</span>
</div>
        <div class="predict-note">Predict why the message still arrived before you look.</div>
        <div class="mcq-q-text"><p>A message is sent across the Internet from one city to another. Partway through the transmission, a router on the original route fails, yet the complete message still arrives at its destination. Which of the following best explains this outcome?</p></div>
        <div class="mcq-options" id="q6-options">
<button class="mcq-option" onclick="checkMCQ('q6','A','A','q6-fb-A')"><span class="mcq-option-letter">A</span> Because the network has redundant paths, the remaining routers forwarded the packets along a different available route to the destination</button>
<button class="mcq-option" onclick="checkMCQ('q6','B','A','q6-fb-B')"><span class="mcq-option-letter">B</span> The failed router must not have actually been on the path the message used</button>
<button class="mcq-option" onclick="checkMCQ('q6','C','A','q6-fb-C')"><span class="mcq-option-letter">C</span> The message arrived only because it happened to be sent before the router failed and none of it needed the router afterward</button>
<button class="mcq-option" onclick="checkMCQ('q6','D','A','q6-fb-D')"><span class="mcq-option-letter">D</span> The destination computer rebuilt the missing part of the message on its own without receiving it</button>
</div>
<div id="q6-fb-A" class="mcq-feedback correct-fb">Correct. Redundant routing means that when a router fails, neighboring routers can forward packets along another available path, so the full message still reaches the destination.</div>
<div id="q6-fb-B" class="mcq-feedback incorrect-fb">Incorrect. The scenario states the failed router was on the original route. The message still arrived because of rerouting, not because the router was uninvolved.</div>
<div id="q6-fb-C" class="mcq-feedback incorrect-fb">Incorrect. The failure happened partway through, so later packets did need a route around the dead router. Redundant paths, not timing luck, explain the delivery.</div>
<div id="q6-fb-D" class="mcq-feedback incorrect-fb">Incorrect. A destination cannot invent data it never received. The missing packets arrived over an alternate path made possible by redundancy.</div>
      </div>

<script>
(function(){
  "use strict";
  var SVGNS="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg";
  var root=document.getElementById("rr-game");
  var svg=document.getElementById("rr-svg");
  var elLevel=document.getElementById("rr-level");
  var elMode=document.getElementById("rr-mode");
  var elCuts=document.getElementById("rr-cuts");
  var elScore=document.getElementById("rr-score");
  var elPrompt=document.getElementById("rr-prompt");
  var elStatus=document.getElementById("rr-status");
  var elReset=document.getElementById("rr-reset");
  var elNext=document.getElementById("rr-next");

  // ----- Level definitions (positions on a 640x380 canvas) -----
  var LEVELS=[
    {
      mode:"survivor",
      nodes:{A:[60,190],C:[230,80],D:[230,300],E:[410,80],F:[410,300],B:[580,190]},
      edges:[["A","C"],["A","D"],["C","E"],["D","F"],["E","B"],["F","B"],["C","D"],["E","F"]]
    },
    {
      mode:"attacker",
      nodes:{A:[60,190],C:[210,80],D:[210,300],E:[350,190],F:[490,80],G:[490,300],B:[600,190]},
      edges:[["A","C"],["A","D"],["C","E"],["D","E"],["E","F"],["E","G"],["F","B"],["G","B"]]
    },
    {
      mode:"survivor",
      nodes:{A:[60,190],C:[210,70],D:[210,190],E:[210,310],F:[440,70],G:[440,190],H:[440,310],B:[600,190]},
      edges:[["A","C"],["A","D"],["A","E"],["C","F"],["D","G"],["E","H"],["F","B"],["G","B"],["H","B"],["C","D"],["G","H"]]
    },
    {
      mode:"attacker",
      nodes:{A:[60,190],C:[200,70],D:[200,190],E:[200,310],F:[430,70],G:[430,190],H:[430,310],B:[600,190]},
      edges:[["A","C"],["A","D"],["A","E"],["C","F"],["D","G"],["E","H"],["F","B"],["G","B"],["H","B"],["C","D"],["D","E"],["F","G"],["G","H"]]
    }
  ];

  var levelIdx=0, score=0;
  var L=null;          // current level compiled data
  var cut=[];          // boolean per edge index
  var completed=false; // scored this level already
  var edgeEls=[];      // {line, hit}
  var nodeIds=[];      // ordered id list
  var idToIdx={};
  var minCutVal=0;

  // ----- graph algorithms -----
  function computeMinCut(n, edges, s, t){
    var cap=[],i;
    for(i=0;i<n;i++){cap.push(new Array(n).fill(0));}
    edges.forEach(function(e){cap[e.u][e.v]++;cap[e.v][e.u]++;});
    var flow=0;
    while(true){
      var par=new Array(n).fill(-1); par[s]=s; var q=[s], v;
      while(q.length){var u=q.shift(); for(v=0;v<n;v++){ if(par[v]===-1 && cap[u][v]>0){par[v]=u;q.push(v);} }}
      if(par[t]===-1) break;
      var b=Infinity;
      for(v=t; v!==s; v=par[v]){ b=Math.min(b,cap[par[v]][v]); }
      for(v=t; v!==s; v=par[v]){ cap[par[v]][v]-=b; cap[v][par[v]]+=b; }
      flow+=b;
    }
    return flow;
  }

  function findPath(){
    var N=nodeIds.length;
    var par=new Array(N).fill(-1), pe=new Array(N).fill(-1);
    var s=idToIdx.A, t=idToIdx.B;
    par[s]=s; var q=[s];
    while(q.length){
      var u=q.shift();
      if(u===t) break;
      L.adj[u].forEach(function(a){
        if(par[a.to]===-1 && !cut[a.ei]){ par[a.to]=u; pe[a.to]=a.ei; q.push(a.to); }
      });
    }
    if(par[t]===-1) return null;
    var nodes=[], eds=[], v=t;
    while(v!==s){ nodes.push(v); eds.push(pe[v]); v=par[v]; }
    nodes.push(s); nodes.reverse(); eds.reverse();
    return {nodes:nodes, edges:eds};
  }

  // ----- rendering -----
  function nodeColor(id){
    if(id==="A") return "#16a34a";
    if(id==="B") return "#7c3aed";
    return "#1a56db";
  }

  function renderLevel(){
    while(svg.firstChild) svg.removeChild(svg.firstChild);
    edgeEls=[];

    // edges first (under nodes)
    L.edges.forEach(function(e, ei){
      var p1=L.nodes[nodeIds[e.u]], p2=L.nodes[nodeIds[e.v]];
      var line=document.createElementNS(SVGNS,"line");
      line.setAttribute("x1",p1[0]); line.setAttribute("y1",p1[1]);
      line.setAttribute("x2",p2[0]); line.setAttribute("y2",p2[1]);
      line.setAttribute("stroke","#1a56db");
      line.setAttribute("stroke-width","5");
      line.setAttribute("stroke-linecap","round");
      svg.appendChild(line);

      var hit=document.createElementNS(SVGNS,"line");
      hit.setAttribute("x1",p1[0]); hit.setAttribute("y1",p1[1]);
      hit.setAttribute("x2",p2[0]); hit.setAttribute("y2",p2[1]);
      hit.setAttribute("stroke","transparent");
      hit.setAttribute("stroke-width","22");
      hit.setAttribute("stroke-linecap","round");
      hit.style.cursor="pointer";
      hit.addEventListener("click",(function(k){return function(){toggleEdge(k);};})(ei));
      svg.appendChild(hit);

      edgeEls.push({line:line, hit:hit});
    });

    // nodes on top
    nodeIds.forEach(function(id){
      var p=L.nodes[id];
      var c=document.createElementNS(SVGNS,"circle");
      c.setAttribute("cx",p[0]); c.setAttribute("cy",p[1]); c.setAttribute("r","22");
      c.setAttribute("fill",nodeColor(id));
      c.setAttribute("stroke","#ffffff"); c.setAttribute("stroke-width","3");
      svg.appendChild(c);
      var t=document.createElementNS(SVGNS,"text");
      t.setAttribute("x",p[0]); t.setAttribute("y",p[1]);
      t.setAttribute("text-anchor","middle");
      t.setAttribute("dominant-baseline","central");
      t.setAttribute("font-family","'DM Sans',sans-serif");
      t.setAttribute("font-size","16"); t.setAttribute("font-weight","700");
      t.setAttribute("fill","#ffffff");
      t.textContent=id;
      svg.appendChild(t);
    });
  }

  function paintEdges(pathEdges){
    var hi={};
    if(pathEdges){ pathEdges.forEach(function(ei){hi[ei]=true;}); }
    edgeEls.forEach(function(o, ei){
      var ln=o.line;
      if(cut[ei]){
        ln.setAttribute("stroke","#dc2626");
        ln.setAttribute("stroke-width","3");
        ln.setAttribute("stroke-dasharray","4 7");
      }else if(hi[ei]){
        ln.setAttribute("stroke","#16a34a");
        ln.setAttribute("stroke-width","7");
        ln.removeAttribute("stroke-dasharray");
      }else{
        ln.setAttribute("stroke","#1a56db");
        ln.setAttribute("stroke-width","5");
        ln.removeAttribute("stroke-dasharray");
      }
    });
  }

  // ----- game flow -----
  function pathString(nodes){
    return nodes.map(function(i){return nodeIds[i];}).join(" → ");
  }
  function cutCount(){
    var n=0; cut.forEach(function(b){if(b)n++;}); return n;
  }
  function setStatus(cls, html){
    elStatus.className="rr-status"+(cls?(" "+cls):"");
    elStatus.innerHTML=html;
  }

  function update(){
    var path=findPath();
    var connected=!!path;
    paintEdges(connected?path.edges:null);
    var cc=cutCount();
    elCuts.textContent="Cuts: "+cc;

    if(L.mode==="survivor"){
      if(cc===0){
        setStatus("", "Tap any link to cut it. A fault-tolerant network should still route A to B.");
      }else if(connected){
        setStatus("ok", "Still connected  -  the network rerouted.<br>Surviving path: <b>"+pathString(path.nodes)+"</b>. That is redundancy in action.");
        if(!completed){
          completed=true; score+=100; elScore.textContent="Score: "+score;
          setStatus("ok", "Redundancy proven! Cut "+cc+" link"+(cc>1?"s":"")+" and A still reaches B via <b>"+pathString(path.nodes)+"</b>.<br>Redundant paths make this network fault tolerant. +100");
          enableNext();
        }
      }else{
        setStatus("bad", "DISCONNECTED  -  you severed every path from A to B. With no redundant route left, this part of the network goes dark. Restore a link to reconnect.");
      }
    }else{ // attacker / min-cut
      if(!connected){
        if(!completed){
          completed=true;
          var pts, msg;
          if(cc===minCutVal){
            pts=200;
            msg="Perfect min-cut! You severed A from B using the true minimum of <b>"+minCutVal+"</b> link"+(minCutVal>1?"s":"")+". Every redundant path is gone. +200";
          }else{
            var extra=cc-minCutVal;
            pts=Math.max(60, 200-40*extra);
            msg="DISCONNECTED with "+cc+" cuts, but the minimum was only <b>"+minCutVal+"</b> ("+extra+" wasted). Fewer, smarter cuts sever the network faster. +"+pts;
          }
          score+=pts; elScore.textContent="Score: "+score;
          setStatus("bad", msg);
          enableNext();
        }else{
          setStatus("bad", "DISCONNECTED  -  no path from A to B.");
        }
      }else{

  function loadLevel(idx){
    levelIdx=idx;
    var def=LEVELS[idx];
    nodeIds=Object.keys(def.nodes);
    idToIdx={}; nodeIds.forEach(function(id,i){idToIdx[id]=i;});
    var edges=def.edges.map(function(p){return {u:idToIdx[p[0]], v:idToIdx[p[1]]};});
    var adj=nodeIds.map(function(){return [];});
    edges.forEach(function(e,ei){ adj[e.u].push({to:e.v,ei:ei}); adj[e.v].push({to:e.u,ei:ei}); });
    L={nodes:def.nodes, edges:edges, adj:adj, mode:def.mode};
    cut=new Array(edges.length).fill(false);
    completed=false;
    minCutVal=computeMinCut(nodeIds.length, edges, idToIdx.A, idToIdx.B);

    elLevel.textContent="Level "+(idx+1)+" / "+LEVELS.length;
    elMode.textContent=(def.mode==="survivor")?"Survivor":"Attacker";
    elNext.disabled=true;
    elNext.textContent=(idx>=LEVELS.length-1)?"Finish \u2691":"Next \u2192";

    if(def.mode==="survivor"){
      elPrompt.innerHTML="<b>Survivor:</b> a network is fault tolerant if it survives any single failure. Cut a link and prove A can still reach B through a redundant path.";

    elPrompt.innerHTML="<b>You've got it.</b> The Internet is fault tolerant because redundant paths connect its nodes.";
    setStatus("win", "A network keeps routing as long as ANY path survives  -  it only fails when EVERY path between two points is severed. That is why engineers build redundancy into the Internet. Press Play again to run it back.");
    elCuts.textContent="Cuts: 0";
    elReset.disabled=true;
    elNext.disabled=false;
    elNext.textContent="Play again \u21bb";

    levelIdx=LEVELS.length; // sentinel for restart
    document.dispatchEvent(new CustomEvent('apcsGameScore',{detail:{value:score}}));
  }

  elReset.addEventListener("click", function(){
    if(!L) return;
    cut=new Array(L.edges.length).fill(false);
    update();
  });
  elNext.addEventListener("click", function(){
    if(levelIdx>=LEVELS.length){ // restart from win
      score=0; elScore.textContent="Score: 0"; elReset.disabled=false;
      loadLevel(0); return;
    }
    if(elNext.disabled) return;
    nextLevel();
  });

  loadLevel(0);
})();

      <h2>Frequently Asked Questions</h2>
      <div class="faq-item">
        <button class="faq-q" onclick="toggleFAQ(this)">What is the difference between redundancy and fault tolerance?<i class="faq-icon">+</i></button>
        <div class="faq-a">Redundancy is the design feature: having multiple paths or copies of a component. Fault tolerance is the result: because of that redundancy, the system keeps working when a component fails. You build in redundancy so that you get fault tolerance when a failure happens.</div>
      </div>
      <div class="faq-item">
        <button class="faq-q" onclick="toggleFAQ(this)">Why is the Internet considered fault tolerant?<i class="faq-icon">+</i></button>
        <div class="faq-a">Because it uses redundant routing. Devices are connected by many paths, and data is sent as packets that are routed hop by hop. If a router or connection fails, the surrounding routers can send packets along a different available path, so the data still gets through.</div>
      </div>
      <div class="faq-item">
        <button class="faq-q" onclick="toggleFAQ(this)">How do I find a single point of failure in a network diagram?<i class="faq-icon">+</i></button>
        <div class="faq-a">Look for a component that every path has to pass through. If removing one node or one link disconnects part of the network from the rest, that component is a single point of failure. If any single component can be removed and traffic still has another route, there is no single point of failure there.</div>
      </div>
      <div class="faq-item">
        <button class="faq-q" onclick="toggleFAQ(this)">Does adding more bandwidth or a faster router make a network more fault tolerant?<i class="faq-icon">+</i></button>
        <div class="faq-a">No. Making a single path faster improves performance but adds no fault tolerance, because that path is still a single point of failure. Fault tolerance comes from adding another independent path or a redundant component, not from upgrading one path.</div>
      </div>
      <div class="faq-item">
        <button class="faq-q" onclick="toggleFAQ(this)">If redundancy is so useful, why not add as much as possible?<i class="faq-icon">+</i></button>
        <div class="faq-a">Because redundancy costs money and resources. Every extra path or backup means more cables, routers, servers, power, and maintenance. Designers weigh how much reliability they need against the added cost, which is the tradeoff the exam expects you to recognize.</div>
      </div>

  /* CPT CONNECTION */

    <div class="score-impact">📈 <span>Big Idea 4 (Computer Systems and Networks) is 11 to 15 percent of the AP CSP exam, and 4.3 questions are some of the most predictable points on it. Learn the formula and the limit and these become fast, reliable points.</span>
