  .lesson-section h3{font-size:17px!important;font-weight:700!important;color:var(--navy)!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:var(--navy)!important;margin-top:24px!important;margin-bottom:10px!important;}
  .lesson-section p{font-size:15px;color:#374151;line-height:1.8;margin-bottom:14px;}
  .lesson-section ul,.lesson-section ol{padding-left:20px;margin-bottom:14px;}
  .lesson-section li{font-size:15px;color:#374151;line-height:1.7;margin-bottom:6px;}
  .lesson-section code{background:#eef2ff;color:#1e3a8a!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:#1e3a8a!important;padding:1px 6px;border-radius:5px;font-size:13px;}

  /* DUAL CODE PANEL */
  .code-panel-wrap{margin:20px 0;border-radius:12px;overflow:hidden;border:1px solid #e2e8f0;}
  .code-panel-tabs{display:flex;background:#1e293b;}
  .code-tab{padding:8px 16px;font-size:12px;font-weight:700;cursor:pointer;border:none;background:transparent;letter-spacing:.04em;transition:background .15s;font-family:inherit;}
  .code-tab.py{color:#93c5fd!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:#93c5fd!important;}
  .code-tab.pseudo{color:#c4b5fd!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:#c4b5fd!important;}
  .code-tab.active{background:rgba(255,255,255,.15)!important;}
  .code-tab-label{font-size:10px;opacity:.6;margin-left:4px;font-weight:400;}
  .code-pane{background:#0f172a;padding:18px 20px;overflow-x:auto;height:0;overflow:hidden;padding:0;}
  .code-pane.active{height:auto;overflow-x:auto;padding:18px 20px;}
  .code-pane pre{font-family:monospace;font-size:13px;line-height:1.8;margin:0;white-space:pre-wrap;word-break:break-word;max-width:100%;color:#e2e8f0!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:#e2e8f0!important;}
  .py-kw{color:#93c5fd!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:#93c5fd!important;font-weight:700;}
  .py-fn{color:#6ee7b7!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:#6ee7b7!important;}
  .py-num{color:#fde68a!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:#fde68a!important;}
  .py-str{color:#f9a8d4!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:#f9a8d4!important;}
  .py-comment{color:#475569!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:#475569!important;font-style:italic;}
  .py-var{color:#e2e8f0!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:#e2e8f0!important;}
  .py-op{color:#94a3b8!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:#94a3b8!important;}
  .ps-kw{color:#c4b5fd!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:#c4b5fd!important;font-weight:700;}
  .ps-op{color:#f9a8d4!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:#f9a8d4!important;}
  .ps-num{color:#fde68a!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:#fde68a!important;}
  .ps-str{color:#86efac!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:#86efac!important;}
  .ps-comment{color:#475569!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:#475569!important;font-style:italic;}
  .ps-var{color:#e2e8f0!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:#e2e8f0!important;}

  /* CALLOUTS */
  .callout-exam{background:#fffbeb;border:1px solid #fcd34d;border-left:4px solid var(--amber);border-radius:0 8px 8px 0;padding:16px 20px;margin:20px 0;}
  .callout-exam-label{font-size:11px;font-weight:700;letter-spacing:.08em;text-transform:uppercase;color:var(--amber)!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:var(--amber)!important;margin-bottom:6px;}
  .callout-exam p{font-size:14px!important;color:#78350f!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:#78350f!important;margin-bottom:0!important;line-height:1.6!important;}
  .callout-trap{background:#fef2f2;border:1px solid #fca5a5;border-left:4px solid var(--red);border-radius:0 8px 8px 0;padding:16px 20px;margin:20px 0;}
  .callout-trap-label{font-size:11px;font-weight:700;letter-spacing:.08em;text-transform:uppercase;color:var(--red)!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:var(--red)!important;margin-bottom:6px;}
  .callout-trap p{font-size:14px!important;color:#7f1d1d!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:#7f1d1d!important;margin-bottom:0!important;line-height:1.6!important;}

  /* MINI EXERCISES */
  .mini-ex{background:#fff;border:1px solid #bfdbfe;border-radius:12px;padding:20px 24px;margin:24px 0;}
  .mini-ex-label{display:flex;align-items:center;gap:8px;font-size:11px;font-weight:700;letter-spacing:.08em;text-transform:uppercase;color:var(--bi3-dk)!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:var(--bi3-dk)!important;margin-bottom:12px;}
  .mini-ex-q{font-size:15px;font-weight:600;color:var(--navy)!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:var(--navy)!important;margin-bottom:14px;line-height:1.5;}
  .mini-ex-code{background:#0f172a;border-radius:8px;padding:14px 16px;font-family:monospace;font-size:13px;line-height:1.8;margin-bottom:14px;overflow-x:auto;white-space:pre;display:block;}
  .mini-opts{display:flex;flex-direction:column;gap:7px;margin-bottom:10px;}
  .mini-opt{display:flex;align-items:center;gap:10px;padding:10px 14px;border:2px solid #e2e8f0;border-radius:8px;cursor:pointer;font-size:14px;font-family:monospace;color:#374151!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:#374151!important;background:#f8fafc;text-align:left;width:100%;transition:border-color .15s;}
  .mini-opt:hover{border-color:var(--bi3-lt);background:var(--bi3-bg);}
  .mini-opt.correct{border-color:var(--green)!important;background:#f0fdf4!important;color:#14532d!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:#14532d!important;}
  .mini-opt.incorrect{border-color:var(--red)!important;background:#fef2f2!important;color:#7f1d1d!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:#7f1d1d!important;}
  .mini-opt.reveal{border-color:var(--green)!important;background:#f0fdf4!important;}
  .mini-opt-letter{font-weight:700;color:var(--bi3)!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:var(--bi3)!important;min-width:18px;font-family:inherit;}
  .mini-opt.correct .mini-opt-letter{color:#14532d!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:#14532d!important;}
  .mini-opt.incorrect .mini-opt-letter{color:#7f1d1d!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:#7f1d1d!important;}
  .mini-fib-row{display:flex;gap:8px;align-items:center;flex-wrap:wrap;margin-bottom:10px;}
  .mini-fib-input{padding:8px 12px;border:2px solid #e2e8f0;border-radius:8px;font-family:monospace;font-size:14px;width:130px;outline:none;color:var(--navy)!important;background:#f8fafc;}
  .mini-fib-input:focus{border-color:var(--bi3-lt);}
  .mini-fib-input.correct{border-color:var(--green);background:#f0fdf4;}
  .mini-fib-input.incorrect{border-color:var(--red);background:#fef2f2;}
  .mini-fib-btn{padding:8px 18px;background:var(--bi3);border:none;border-radius:8px;color:#fff!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:#fff!important;font-size:13px;font-weight:700;cursor:pointer;font-family:inherit;}
  .mini-fb{font-size:13px;font-weight:500;padding:8px 12px;border-radius:7px;margin-top:6px;display:none;line-height:1.5;}
  .mini-fb.c{background:#f0fdf4;color:var(--green)!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:var(--green)!important;display:block;}
  .mini-fb.w{background:#fef2f2;color:var(--red)!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:var(--red)!important;display:block;}

  /* VOCAB */
  .vocab-table{width:100%;border-collapse:collapse;margin-bottom:24px;font-size:14px;}
  .vocab-table thead tr{background:var(--bi3);}
  .vocab-table thead th{padding:10px 16px;text-align:left;font-weight:600;color:#fff!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:#fff!important;font-size:13px;}
  .vocab-table tbody tr:nth-child(even){background:var(--bi3-bg);}
  .vocab-table tbody tr:nth-child(odd){background:#fff;}
  .vocab-table tbody td{padding:10px 16px;border-bottom:1px solid #bfdbfe;color:#374151;vertical-align:top;line-height:1.5;}
  .vocab-table tbody td:first-child{font-weight:700;color:var(--bi3-dk)!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:var(--bi3-dk)!important;white-space:nowrap;}

  /* CPT CONNECTION */
  .cpt-connection{background:#fefce8;border:1px solid #fde68a;border-left:4px solid #f59e0b;border-radius:0 10px 10px 0;padding:20px 24px;margin:28px 0;}
  .cpt-connection-label{font-size:11px;font-weight:700;letter-spacing:.08em;text-transform:uppercase;color:#92400e!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:#92400e!important;margin-bottom:8px;}
  .cpt-connection h3{font-size:16px!important;font-weight:700!important;color:#78350f!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:#78350f!important;margin:16px 0 8px!important;}
  .cpt-connection p{font-size:14px!important;color:#78350f!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:#78350f!important;line-height:1.7!important;margin-bottom:12px!important;}
  .cpt-connection a{color:#b45309!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:#b45309!important;font-weight:600;text-decoration:underline;}
  .cpt-connection code{background:#fef3c7;color:#78350f!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:#78350f!important;padding:1px 6px;border-radius:5px;font-size:13px;}
  .cpt-stems{list-style:none;padding:0;margin:0 0 8px;display:flex;flex-direction:column;gap:8px;}
  .cpt-stems li{background:#fffef5;border:1px solid #fde68a;border-radius:8px;padding:10px 14px;font-size:13px!important;color:#78350f!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:#78350f!important;line-height:1.6;}
  .cpt-code{background:#0f172a;border-radius:8px;padding:14px 16px;font-family:monospace;font-size:13px;line-height:1.8;margin:6px 0 12px;overflow-x:auto;white-space:pre;display:block;color:#e2e8f0!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:#e2e8f0!important;}

  /* EMAIL */
  .email-capture{background:linear-gradient(135deg,#1e3a8a 0%,#1e40af 100%);border-radius:12px;padding:24px 28px;margin-bottom:36px;display:flex;align-items:center;gap:24px;flex-wrap:wrap;}
  .email-capture-text{flex:1;min-width:200px;}
  .email-capture-eyebrow{font-size:11px;font-weight:700;letter-spacing:.1em;text-transform:uppercase;color:var(--bi3-lt)!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:var(--bi3-lt)!important;margin-bottom:4px;}
  .email-capture h3{font-size:16px!important;font-weight:700!important;color:#fff!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:#fff!important;margin-bottom:4px!important;}
  .email-capture p{font-size:13px!important;color:#94a3b8!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:#94a3b8!important;margin-bottom:0!important;line-height:1.5!important;}
  .email-capture-form{display:flex;gap:8px;flex-wrap:wrap;flex-shrink:0;}
  .email-capture-input{padding:10px 14px;border-radius:8px;border:1px solid rgba(255,255,255,.2);background:rgba(255,255,255,.1);color:#fff!important;font-size:14px;font-family:inherit;min-width:180px;outline:none;}
  .email-capture-btn{padding:10px 20px!important;background:var(--bi3)!important;color:#fff!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:#fff!important;border:none!important;border-radius:8px!important;font-size:14px!important;font-weight:600!important;cursor:pointer!important;font-family:inherit!important;}
  .email-capture-success{display:none;font-size:14px;color:#93c5fd!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:#93c5fd!important;font-weight:600;padding:10px 0;}

  /* MCQ */
  .mcq-section{background:#fff;border:1px solid #e2e8f0;border-radius:14px;padding:28px;margin-bottom:40px;}
  .mcq-section-header{display:flex;align-items:center;gap:12px;margin-bottom:24px;padding-bottom:16px;border-bottom:2px solid var(--bi3-bg);}
  .mcq-section-icon{width:40px;height:40px;border-radius:10px;background:var(--bi3-bg);display:flex;align-items:center;justify-content:center;font-size:18px;flex-shrink:0;}
  .mcq-section-title{font-family:"DM Serif Display",serif;font-size:20px;color:var(--navy)!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:var(--navy)!important;}
  .mcq-section-sub{font-size:13px;color:var(--slate);}
  .mcq-item{margin-bottom:28px;padding-bottom:28px;border-bottom:1px solid #f1f5f9;}
  .mcq-item:last-child{border-bottom:none;margin-bottom:0;padding-bottom:0;}
  .mcq-q-num{font-size:11px;font-weight:700;letter-spacing:.08em;text-transform:uppercase;color:var(--slate);margin-bottom:8px;}
  .diff-tag{display:inline-block;font-size:10px;font-weight:700;letter-spacing:.06em;text-transform:uppercase;padding:2px 8px;border-radius:100px;margin-left:8px;background:#fef2f2;color:#b91c1c!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:#b91c1c!important;border:1px solid #fca5a5;}
  .mcq-q-text{font-size:15px!important;font-weight:600!important;color:#0f1f3d!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:#0f1f3d!important;line-height:1.6!important;margin-bottom:12px!important;}
  .predict-note{font-size:12px;font-style:italic;color:#64748b!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:#64748b!important;margin-bottom:12px;}
  .mcq-code{background:#0f172a;border-radius:8px;padding:12px 14px;margin:10px 0 14px;font-family:monospace;font-size:13px;line-height:1.75;color:#e2e8f0!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:#e2e8f0!important;white-space:pre;overflow-x:auto;display:block;}
  .mcq-code .k{color:#93c5fd!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:#93c5fd!important;}
  .mcq-code .s{color:#f9a8d4!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:#f9a8d4!important;}
  .mcq-code .n{color:#fde68a!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:#fde68a!important;}
  .mcq-code .c{color:#64748b!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:#64748b!important;font-style:italic;}
  .mcq-roman{list-style:none;padding:0;margin:10px 0 14px;display:flex;flex-direction:column;gap:6px;}
  .mcq-roman li{font-family:monospace;font-size:13px;color:#1e293b!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:#1e293b!important;background:#f1f5f9;border-radius:6px;padding:8px 12px;}
  .mcq-roman li strong{color:var(--bi3-dk)!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:var(--bi3-dk)!important;font-family:"DM Sans",sans-serif;margin-right:8px;}
  .mcq-options{display:flex;flex-direction:column;gap:8px;margin-bottom:12px;}
  .mcq-option{display:flex!important;align-items:flex-start!important;gap:12px!important;padding:11px 14px!important;border:2px solid #e2e8f0!important;border-radius:8px!important;cursor:pointer!important;background:#f8fafc!important;font-size:14px!important;color:#374151!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:#374151!important;line-height:1.5!important;text-align:left!important;width:100%!important;font-family:inherit!important;}
  .mcq-option:hover{border-color:var(--bi3-lt)!important;background:var(--bi3-bg)!important;}
  .mcq-option.correct{border-color:var(--green)!important;background:#f0fdf4!important;color:#14532d!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:#14532d!important;}
  .mcq-option.incorrect{border-color:var(--red)!important;background:#fef2f2!important;color:#7f1d1d!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:#7f1d1d!important;}
  .mcq-option.revealed-correct{border-color:var(--green)!important;background:#f0fdf4!important;}
  .mcq-option-letter{font-weight:700!important;color:var(--bi3)!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:var(--bi3)!important;flex-shrink:0!important;min-width:18px!important;}
  .mcq-option.correct .mcq-option-letter{color:#14532d!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:#14532d!important;}
  .mcq-option.incorrect .mcq-option-letter{color:#7f1d1d!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:#7f1d1d!important;}
  .mcq-feedback{display:none!important;padding:12px 16px!important;border-radius:8px!important;font-size:14px!important;line-height:1.6!important;margin-top:8px!important;}
  .mcq-feedback.show{display:block!important;}
  .mcq-feedback.correct-fb{background:#f0fdf4!important;color:#14532d!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:#14532d!important;border:1px solid #bbf7d0!important;}
  .mcq-feedback.incorrect-fb{background:#fef2f2!important;color:#7f1d1d!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:#7f1d1d!important;border:1px solid #fecaca!important;}

  /* GAME */
  .game-section{background:linear-gradient(135deg,#1e3a8a 0%,#1e40af 100%);border-radius:14px;padding:28px;margin-bottom:40px;}
  .game-badge{display:inline-block;background:rgba(147,197,253,.15);border:1px solid rgba(147,197,253,.35);color:var(--bi3-lt)!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:var(--bi3-lt)!important;font-size:11px;font-weight:700;letter-spacing:.1em;text-transform:uppercase;padding:5px 14px;border-radius:100px;margin-bottom:10px;}
  .game-title{font-family:"DM Serif Display",serif!important;font-size:24px!important;color:#fff!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:#fff!important;margin-bottom:4px!important;}
  .game-sub{font-size:13px!important;color:#94a3b8!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:#94a3b8!important;margin-bottom:20px!important;}
  .vt-score-bar{display:flex;justify-content:space-between;background:rgba(255,255,255,.06);border-radius:10px;padding:12px 20px;margin-bottom:20px;flex-wrap:wrap;gap:8px;}
  .vt-stat{text-align:center;}
  .vt-stat-val{font-size:20px;font-weight:800;color:#fff!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:#fff!important;line-height:1;}
  .vt-stat-lbl{font-size:10px;color:#94a3b8!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:#94a3b8!important;margin-top:2px;}
  .vt-code-card{background:rgba(255,255,255,.06);border:1px solid rgba(255,255,255,.1);border-radius:12px;padding:18px 20px;margin-bottom:16px;}
  .vt-code-label{font-size:11px;font-weight:700;letter-spacing:.06em;text-transform:uppercase;color:var(--bi3-lt)!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:var(--bi3-lt)!important;margin-bottom:10px;}
  .vt-code-lines{font-family:monospace;font-size:14px;line-height:2;color:#e2e8f0!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:#e2e8f0!important;}
  .vt-line{display:block;padding:2px 8px;border-radius:4px;white-space:pre;}
  .vt-line.hl{background:rgba(147,197,253,.2);color:#93c5fd!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:#93c5fd!important;}
  .vt-question{font-size:15px;font-weight:600;color:#e2e8f0!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:#e2e8f0!important;margin-bottom:14px;}
  .vt-options{display:grid;grid-template-columns:1fr 1fr;gap:8px;margin-bottom:14px;}
  .vt-btn{padding:12px;border-radius:9px;border:2px solid rgba(255,255,255,.15);background:rgba(255,255,255,.06);cursor:pointer;font-size:15px;font-weight:700;color:#e2e8f0!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:#e2e8f0!important;font-family:monospace;transition:all .15s;}
  .vt-btn:hover{border-color:var(--bi3-lt);background:rgba(26,86,219,.2);}
  .vt-btn.c{border-color:#4ade80;background:rgba(74,222,128,.15);color:#4ade80!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:#4ade80!important;}
  .vt-btn.w{border-color:#f87171;background:rgba(248,113,113,.15);color:#f87171!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:#f87171!important;}
  .vt-btn.rv{border-color:#4ade80;background:rgba(74,222,128,.08);}
  .vt-fb{padding:10px 14px;border-radius:8px;font-size:13px;font-weight:500;margin-bottom:12px;display:none;line-height:1.5;}
  .vt-fb.c{background:rgba(74,222,128,.1);color:#4ade80!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:#4ade80!important;display:block;}
  .vt-fb.w{background:rgba(248,113,113,.1);color:#f87171!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:#f87171!important;display:block;}
  .vt-next{display:none;width:100%;padding:12px;background:rgba(255,255,255,.1);border:2px solid rgba(255,255,255,.2);border-radius:8px;color:#fff!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:#fff!important;font-size:14px;font-weight:600;cursor:pointer;font-family:inherit;}

  .vt-results{display:none;text-align:center;padding:20px;}
  .vt-results.show{display:block;}
  .vt-res-score{font-family:"DM Serif Display",serif;font-size:52px;color:#fff!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:#fff!important;line-height:1;}

  .vt-restart{background:rgba(255,255,255,.1);color:#fff!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:#fff!important;border:2px solid rgba(255,255,255,.2);border-radius:8px;padding:11px 24px;font-size:14px;font-weight:600;cursor:pointer;font-family:inherit;}

  /* CODE EDITOR (Pyodide live) */
  .code-editor-section{background:#0f172a;border-radius:14px;padding:28px;margin-bottom:40px;}
  .code-editor-badge{display:inline-block;background:rgba(147,197,253,.15);border:1px solid rgba(147,197,253,.35);color:var(--bi3-lt)!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:var(--bi3-lt)!important;font-size:11px;font-weight:700;letter-spacing:.1em;text-transform:uppercase;padding:5px 14px;border-radius:100px;margin-bottom:10px;}
  .code-editor-title{font-family:"DM Serif Display",serif!important;font-size:22px!important;color:#fff!important;-webkit-text-fill-color:#fff!important;margin-bottom:4px!important;}

    <div class="lesson-objectives">
      <h2>After this lesson, you will be able to:</h2>
      <ul>
        <li><span>Define a computing innovation and identify examples that are physical, non-physical software, and non-physical concepts</span></li>
        <li><span>Explain that a single computing innovation can have both beneficial and harmful effects</span></li>
        <li><span>Explain how the same effect can be seen as beneficial by some people and harmful by others</span></li>
        <li><span>Distinguish the intended purpose of an innovation from its unintended consequences</span></li>
        <li><span>Analyze the effects of an innovation on society, economy, and culture depending on how it is used</span></li>
      </ul>
    </div>
    <div class="score-impact">📈 <span>Big Idea 5 (Impact of Computing) is 5 to 10 percent of the AP CSP exam, and 5.1 is the foundation for the whole unit. The exact idea that an innovation is not purely good or purely bad also shows up in the written reasoning you do about impacts, so this lesson earns points in more than one place.</span>
</div>
    <div class="hook-box">
      <div class="hook-label">💡 Think about this first</div>
      <p>A navigation app quietly reroutes thousands of drivers off a jammed highway and onto a quiet residential street. Commuters save twenty minutes and love it. The families who live on that street now have traffic racing past their front yards all day and hate it. Nobody who built the app planned for that street. Is the app's effect beneficial or harmful, and who gets to decide?</p>
    </div>
    <div class="lesson-section">
      <h2>What Counts as a Computing Innovation</h2>
      <p>People create <strong>computing innovations</strong>, and every question in Big Idea 5 starts with knowing what that phrase means. A <strong>computing innovation</strong> is anything that includes a program as an integral part of its function. That is the whole test: if a program is essential to how it works, it qualifies. Computing innovations come in three shapes:</p>
      <ul>
        <li>A <strong>physical</strong> innovation, such as a self-driving car or a fitness tracker, where hardware runs a program.</li>
        <li>A <strong>non-physical software</strong> innovation, such as a photo-editing app or an operating system.</li>
        <li>A <strong>non-physical concept</strong>, such as e-commerce or online transaction systems, which are built on programs but are not a single object.</li>
      </ul>
      <p>A printed book is not a computing innovation, because no program is integral to it. An e-reader is, because a program is essential to how it works. Getting this definition right is the first thing the exam checks.</p>
      <div class="callout-exam">
        <div class="callout-exam-label">🎯 What the exam rewards</div>
        <p>When a question asks whether something is a computing innovation, the deciding factor is always the same: <strong>is a program an integral part of it?</strong> Do not get distracted by whether it is physical or not. Both a smartwatch and a search engine qualify because a program is essential to each.</p>
      </div>
    </div>

    <div class="lesson-section">
      <h2>Effects Are Both Beneficial and Harmful</h2>
      <p>The central claim of 5.1 is short and heavily tested: the effects of a computing innovation can be <strong>both beneficial and harmful</strong>. The framework does not sort innovations into a good pile and a bad pile. A single innovation almost always does some good and some harm at the same time, and a mature answer names both sides.</p>
      <p>Even sharper: a <strong>single effect</strong> can be viewed as beneficial by some people and harmful by others, or even by the same person. A recommendation system that keeps showing you more of what you like is convenient when it surfaces a song you love and troubling when it narrows what you ever see. The effect did not change. The point of view did.</p>
      <table class="vocab-table">
        <tr>
<th>Innovation</th>
<th>Beneficial view</th>
<th>Harmful view</th>
</tr>
        <tr>
<td><strong>Facial recognition</strong></td>
<td>Unlocks your phone instantly and helps reunite missing people with their families.</td>
<td>Enables tracking of people without their knowledge and can misidentify some groups more often.</td>
</tr>
      </table>
      <p>Notice that the table does not declare a winner. The exam wants you to hold both columns at once, because that is how impact actually works.</p>
      <div class="mini-ex">
        <div class="mini-ex-label">Quick check</div>
        <div class="mini-ex-q">Social media lets a small business reach customers worldwide for free, and it also spreads a rumor about that same business faster than it can respond. This best illustrates that:</div>
        <div class="mini-opts" id="mc-effects-1-opts">

          <button class="mini-opt" onclick="miniMCQ('mc-effects-1','C','C','mc-effects-1-fb')"><span class="mini-opt-letter">C</span> A single innovation can produce both beneficial and harmful effects</button>

        </div>
        <div class="mini-fb" id="mc-effects-1-fb"></div>
      </div>
    </div>

    <div class="lesson-section">
      <h2>Intended Purpose vs Unintended Consequences</h2>
      <p>Every innovation is built with an <strong>intended purpose</strong>, the reason its creators made it. But not every effect is <strong>anticipated</strong>. Innovations also produce <strong>unintended consequences</strong>, effects the creators did not plan for. Crucially, an unintended consequence can be positive or negative, not just bad.</p>
      <ul>
        <li>GPS was intended for military navigation. An unintended, and largely positive, consequence is that it now powers ride-sharing, delivery, and everyday maps.</li>
        <li>A social feed intended to help friends stay in touch produced the unintended consequence that some users compare themselves to others and feel worse.</li>
      </ul>
      <p>On the exam, watch for the word <strong>unintended</strong>. It signals an effect outside the original purpose, and it does not tell you whether that effect is good or bad. You have to judge each one on its own.</p>
      <div class="callout-trap">
        <div class="callout-trap-label">⚠ Common trap</div>
        <p>Two traps live here. First, assuming an innovation is <strong>purely good or purely bad</strong>. It rarely is, so an answer that names only one side is usually incomplete. Second, assuming <strong>unintended means harmful</strong>. An unintended consequence can be a happy surprise. GPS reaching civilians was unplanned and hugely beneficial.</p>
      </div>
      <div class="mini-ex">
        <div class="mini-ex-label">Quick check</div>
        <div class="mini-ex-q">A study app is built so students can review flashcards on their phones. Teachers later notice students also use it to quietly message each other during class. The messaging use is best described as:</div>
        <div class="mini-opts" id="mc-effects-2-opts">
          <button class="mini-opt" onclick="miniMCQ('mc-effects-2','A','B','mc-effects-2-fb')"><span class="mini-opt-letter">A</span> The intended purpose of the app</button>
          <button class="mini-opt" onclick="miniMCQ('mc-effects-2','B','B','mc-effects-2-fb')"><span class="mini-opt-letter">B</span> An unintended consequence of the app</button>
          <button class="mini-opt" onclick="miniMCQ('mc-effects-2','C','B','mc-effects-2-fb')"><span class="mini-opt-letter">C</span> Proof the app is not a computing innovation</button>
          <button class="mini-opt" onclick="miniMCQ('mc-effects-2','D','B','mc-effects-2-fb')"><span class="mini-opt-letter">D</span> A beneficial effect the creators planned</button>
        </div>
        <div class="mini-fb" id="mc-effects-2-fb"></div>
      </div>
    </div>

    <div class="lesson-section">
      <h2>Effects Depend on Context and Use</h2>
      <p>The same innovation lands differently depending on <strong>context</strong> and on <strong>how people use it</strong>. Its effects ripple through <strong>society, economy, and culture</strong> all at once. A translation app breaks down language barriers for a traveler (a cultural benefit), can put some human translators out of work (an economic harm), and reshapes how strangers across the world communicate (a social change). None of these cancels the others out.</p>
      <p>This is why the exam asks you to reason about effects rather than memorize a verdict. The right analysis identifies <em>who</em> is affected, <em>how</em>, and whether the effect was intended, and it accepts that the answer can point in more than one direction at the same time.</p>
    </div>
    <div class="lesson-section">
      <h2>How 5.1 Is Tested, and Where Impact Shows Up in Writing</h2>
      <p>On the multiple-choice exam, 5.1 questions usually hand you a scenario about a real-sounding innovation and ask you to reason about its effects. Expect to be asked to identify whether something is a <strong>computing innovation</strong>, to name <strong>both</strong> a beneficial and a harmful effect, to tell an <strong>intended purpose</strong> from an <strong>unintended consequence</strong>, and to recognize when a single effect is seen differently by different people. The strongest answers avoid declaring an innovation purely good or purely bad.</p>
      <p>This thinking is not only for the MCQ. Reasoning about the impact of a computing innovation, weighing benefits against harms and considering data and context, is exactly the Explore-style analysis the course trains, and that same reasoning about effects appears when you write about the impact of an innovation. Practicing evenhanded, two-sided impact analysis here builds the habit you use in written responses.</p>
    </div>

  function next(){

    idx += 1;
    if(idx >= deck.length){ endGame(); return; }

    els.fscore.textContent = 'You scored ' + score + ' points';

  Array.prototype.forEach.call(btns, function(b){

  });
  els.next.addEventListener('click', next);
  $('ts-again').addEventListener('click', start);

  start();
})();

        <div class="faq-a">The intended purpose is the reason creators built the innovation. An unintended consequence is an effect they did not plan for. Importantly, an unintended consequence can be positive or negative, so 'unintended' does not mean 'harmful.'</div>

  <div class="lesson-main">

    <div class="lesson-objectives">
      <h2>After this lesson, you will be able to:</h2>
      <ul>
        <li><span>Explain that computing innovations can reflect existing human biases, usually unintentionally</span></li>
        <li><span>Identify the two main places bias enters a system: the data and the algorithm or design</span></li>
        <li><span>Explain why bias can exist even when no one intended it and can be hard to detect until use</span></li>
        <li><span>Locate the source of bias in a scenario as coming from the data or from the design</span></li>
        <li><span>Describe how programmers can reduce bias with representative data and testing with diverse users</span></li>
      </ul>
    </div>
    <div class="score-impact">📈 <span>Big Idea 5 (Impact of Computing) is 5 to 8 percent of the AP CSP exam, and bias questions appear almost every year. They are quick concept points if you can tell where the bias entered and remember that bias does not require bad intent.</span>
</div>
    <div class="hook-box">
      <div class="hook-label">💡 Think about this first</div>
      <p>A company builds a resume-screening tool and trains it on ten years of its own past hiring decisions. The team writes careful, neutral code and never once tries to favor any group. A year later the tool is quietly ranking certain qualified applicants lower than others. Nobody wrote a rule to do that, so where did the bias actually come from, and how could a program end up biased when no one meant for it to be?</p>
    </div>
    <div class="lesson-section">
      <h2>Computing Reflects Human Bias</h2>
      <p>A <strong>computing innovation</strong> is anything that includes a program as an integral part, from a phone app to a machine-learning model. The AP CSP framework makes a claim you will be tested on: computing innovations can <strong>reflect existing human biases</strong>, sometimes on purpose but <strong>more often unintentionally</strong>. A program is built by people and trained on data produced by people, so any assumptions or imbalances baked into those people and that data can carry straight into the finished system.</p>
      <p>The key word is <strong>unintentional</strong>. Bias in computing does not mean someone was malicious. Most biased systems are built by well-meaning teams who never wrote a single unfair rule. The bias slips in through the material they used and the choices they made about how the program should work, and it often stays invisible until real users start hitting it.</p>
      <div class="callout-exam">
        <div class="callout-exam-label">🎯 What the exam rewards</div>
        <p>When a question describes a system that ends up treating some group unfairly, the strongest answer usually identifies <strong>where the bias entered</strong> (the data or the design) and notes that it can happen <strong>without anyone intending it</strong>. "The programmers were dishonest" is almost never the credited answer.</p>
      </div>
    </div>

    <div class="lesson-section">
      <h2>Two Places Bias Enters: Data and Algorithm</h2>
      <p>Bias can be embedded at two main points in a computing system, and the exam expects you to tell them apart.</p>
      <ul>
        <li>
<strong>Bias in the data</strong> happens when the information used to build or train the system does not fairly represent everyone it will affect. A face-recognition model trained mostly on photos of one group will work worse for the groups that were underrepresented in the photos.</li>
        <li>
<strong>Bias in the algorithm or design</strong> happens through the choices built into how the program works: which inputs it considers, what it ignores, and how heavily it weights each factor. If a loan model weights a factor that happens to track with one group, the design itself can produce a biased result even on balanced data.</li>
      </ul>
      <table class="vocab-table">
        <tr>
<th>Source of bias</th>
<th>What it means</th>
<th>Example</th>
</tr>
        <tr>
<td><strong>Bias in the DATA</strong></td>
<td>The training or sample data is not representative of all users the system will affect.</td>
<td>An image classifier trained on photos of mostly one skin tone misidentifies people with other skin tones.</td>
</tr>
        <tr>
<td><strong>Bias in the ALGORITHM / design</strong></td>
<td>The choices about which inputs matter and how factors are weighted advantage or disadvantage some group.</td>
<td>A hiring model is designed to rank candidates by how closely they resemble past hires, so it keeps repeating the old pattern.</td>
</tr>
      </table>
      <p>Sometimes both are present at once, but on the exam you should be ready to point to the <strong>primary</strong> source a scenario is describing.</p>
      <div class="mini-ex">
        <div class="mini-ex-label">Quick check</div>
        <div class="mini-ex-q">A map app gives poor directions in rural areas because very few rural roads were included in the map information it was built from. This bias comes primarily from the:</div>
        <div class="mini-opts" id="mc-bias-1-opts">
          <button class="mini-opt" onclick="miniMCQ('mc-bias-1','A','B','mc-bias-1-fb')"><span class="mini-opt-letter">A</span> Speed of the app</button>
          <button class="mini-opt" onclick="miniMCQ('mc-bias-1','B','B','mc-bias-1-fb')"><span class="mini-opt-letter">B</span> Data the app was built from</button>
          <button class="mini-opt" onclick="miniMCQ('mc-bias-1','C','B','mc-bias-1-fb')"><span class="mini-opt-letter">C</span> Color of the interface</button>
          <button class="mini-opt" onclick="miniMCQ('mc-bias-1','D','B','mc-bias-1-fb')"><span class="mini-opt-letter">D</span> Number of downloads</button>
        </div>
        <div class="mini-fb" id="mc-bias-1-fb"></div>
      </div>
    </div>

    <div class="lesson-section">
      <h2>Unintended and Hard to Detect</h2>
      <p>Because bias usually arrives through imbalanced data or design choices rather than a deliberate rule, it can be <strong>present even when no one intended it</strong>, and it is often <strong>difficult to detect</strong> until the system is actually used by a wide range of people. A team testing only on users like themselves may see the program work perfectly and conclude it is fair, while a group they did not test with runs into failures. This is why real-world testing with diverse users matters so much: it surfaces bias that a small, similar test group would never reveal.</p>
      <div class="callout-trap">
        <div class="callout-trap-label">⚠ Common trap</div>
        <p>Bias in computing does <strong>NOT</strong> require bad intent. A very common wrong answer says a system can only be biased if its creators were prejudiced or trying to discriminate. The framework is explicit that bias is most often <strong>unintentional</strong>, entering through unrepresentative data or design choices. A team that meant well can still ship a biased system.</p>
      </div>
      <div class="mini-ex">
        <div class="mini-ex-label">Quick check</div>
        <div class="mini-ex-q">A team builds a photo tool and never intends to favor anyone, but it performs worse for some users. Which statement is correct?</div>
        <div class="mini-opts" id="mc-bias-2-opts">
          <button class="mini-opt" onclick="miniMCQ('mc-bias-2','A','C','mc-bias-2-fb')"><span class="mini-opt-letter">A</span> The tool cannot be biased because no one intended it</button>
          <button class="mini-opt" onclick="miniMCQ('mc-bias-2','B','C','mc-bias-2-fb')"><span class="mini-opt-letter">B</span> Bias only exists if a programmer wrote an unfair rule on purpose</button>
          <button class="mini-opt" onclick="miniMCQ('mc-bias-2','C','C','mc-bias-2-fb')"><span class="mini-opt-letter">C</span> The tool can still be biased, since bias is often unintentional</button>
          <button class="mini-opt" onclick="miniMCQ('mc-bias-2','D','C','mc-bias-2-fb')"><span class="mini-opt-letter">D</span> Intent is the only thing that determines whether bias exists</button>
        </div>
        <div class="mini-fb" id="mc-bias-2-fb"></div>
      </div>
    </div>

    <div class="lesson-section">
      <h2>Reducing Bias</h2>
      <p>The framework does not just describe bias, it expects designers to try to <strong>reduce</strong> it. Programmers and designers should take deliberate steps:</p>
      <ul>
        <li>Use <strong>representative data</strong> that reflects the full range of people the system will affect, not just the easiest group to collect.</li>
        <li>
<strong>Test with diverse users</strong> so failures that hurt a specific group show up before release, not after.</li>
        <li>Review the design to ask <strong>who could be disadvantaged</strong> by which inputs are used and how factors are weighted.</li>
      </ul>
      <p>Bias can rarely be reduced to zero, and adding more data alone is not a guaranteed fix if that data is itself skewed. The point is that bias is something teams are responsible for <strong>looking for and reducing</strong>, not a fact of nature they can ignore.</p>
    </div>
    <div class="lesson-section">
      <h2>How This Shows Up on the Exam</h2>
      <p>Topic 5.3 is tested almost entirely on the <strong>multiple-choice section</strong>, and the questions follow a small number of patterns. Most common is a short scenario in which a system produces an unfair or lopsided result, and you must <strong>identify the source of the bias</strong>: did it enter through the <strong>data</strong> (unrepresentative training or sample data) or through the <strong>algorithm and design</strong> (which inputs are used and how they are weighted)? A second frequent pattern checks whether you understand that <strong>bias can be unintentional</strong>, so answers that insist the creators must have been malicious are distractors, not the key. You may also see a question about <strong>reducing</strong> bias, where the credited answer involves representative data and testing with diverse users rather than simply removing a feature or adding more of the same skewed data. Read for who is affected and where the bias came from, and these become reliable points.</p>

        <div class="mcq-q-text"><p>A hospital builds a model to flag patients who need extra care. It is trained on records from the past, when one neighborhood rarely received such care.           <button class="mcq-option" onclick="checkMCQ('q1','D','A','q1-fb-D')"><span class="mcq-option-letter">D</span> Through the number of patients using the system</button>
        </div>
        <div id="q1-fb-A" class="mcq-feedback correct-fb">Correct. The model learned from historical records that under-served one neighborhood, so the bias entered through unrepresentative training data.</div>
        <div id="q1-fb-B" class="mcq-feedback incorrect-fb">Incorrect. Nothing indicates a deliberate exclusion rule. The framework stresses that such bias is usually unintentional and here it came from the data.</div>
        <div id="q1-fb-C" class="mcq-feedback incorrect-fb">Incorrect. Processing speed does not determine which patients are flagged; the historical data does.</div>
        <div id="q1-fb-D" class="mcq-feedback incorrect-fb">Incorrect. The number of users does not create the biased recommendation. The past pattern in the training data does.</div>

        <div class="mcq-q-text"><p>A design team builds a voice-command feature and genuinely tries to make it work for everyone. After release, speakers with certain accents find it frequently misunderstands them. Which statement best describes this situation?</p></div>
        <div class="mcq-options" id="q2-options">
          <button class="mcq-option" onclick="checkMCQ('q2','A','B','q2-fb-A')"><span class="mcq-option-letter">A</span> The feature is not biased, because the team did not intend any unfairness</button>
          <button class="mcq-option" onclick="checkMCQ('q2','B','B','q2-fb-B')"><span class="mcq-option-letter">B</span> The feature shows unintended bias, which is common and can be hard to detect before real use</button>
          <button class="mcq-option" onclick="checkMCQ('q2','C','B','q2-fb-C')"><span class="mcq-option-letter">C</span> The feature can only be called biased if the team admits they were prejudiced</button>
          <button class="mcq-option" onclick="checkMCQ('q2','D','B','q2-fb-D')"><span class="mcq-option-letter">D</span> The feature is unbiased as long as it works for most users</button>
        </div>
        <div id="q2-fb-A" class="mcq-feedback incorrect-fb">Incorrect. Lack of intent does not make a system unbiased. The framework says bias is most often unintentional.</div>
        <div id="q2-fb-B" class="mcq-feedback correct-fb">Correct. Bias can be present without intent and is often undetected until diverse users try the system, exactly as described here.</div>
        <div id="q2-fb-C" class="mcq-feedback incorrect-fb">Incorrect. An admission of prejudice is not required. Unintended bias still counts as bias.</div>
        <div id="q2-fb-D" class="mcq-feedback incorrect-fb">Incorrect. Working for most users does not erase bias against a specific group; that is the bias being described.</div>

<strong>I.</strong> Bias can enter through data that is not representative of all users.</li>
          <li>
<strong>II.</strong> Bias can enter through design choices about which inputs are used and how they are weighted.</li>
          <li>
<strong>III.</strong> A computing innovation can only be biased if its creators intended to discriminate.</li>
        </ul>
        <div class="mcq-options" id="q3-options">

      <div class="mcq-item" data-activity="quiz" data-item="q4">

</div>
        <div class="predict-note">Predict the action most likely to reduce bias first.</div>
        <div class="mcq-q-text"><p>A team learns that their image classifier performs poorly for a group that was scarcely present in its training photos. Which action would most directly reduce the bias?</p></div>
        <div class="mcq-options" id="q4-options">
<button class="mcq-option" onclick="checkMCQ('q4','A','D','q4-fb-A')"><span class="mcq-option-letter">A</span> Make the classifier run faster so it returns results sooner</button>
<button class="mcq-option" onclick="checkMCQ('q4','B','D','q4-fb-B')"><span class="mcq-option-letter">B</span> Hide the accuracy results so users do not notice the failures</button>
<button class="mcq-option" onclick="checkMCQ('q4','C','D','q4-fb-C')"><span class="mcq-option-letter">C</span> Add more photos of the group that was already well represented</button>
<button class="mcq-option" onclick="checkMCQ('q4','D','D','q4-fb-D')"><span class="mcq-option-letter">D</span> Add more photos of the underrepresented group so the training data better represents all users, and retest with diverse users</button>
</div>
<div id="q4-fb-A" class="mcq-feedback incorrect-fb">Incorrect. Speed does not change accuracy for the underrepresented group; the data imbalance remains.</div>
<div id="q4-fb-B" class="mcq-feedback incorrect-fb">Incorrect. Hiding results conceals the bias rather than reducing it, and the system stays biased.</div>
<div id="q4-fb-C" class="mcq-feedback incorrect-fb">Incorrect. Adding more of the already-represented group deepens the imbalance instead of correcting it.</div>
<div id="q4-fb-D" class="mcq-feedback correct-fb">Correct. More representative data plus testing with diverse users targets the actual cause, unrepresentative training data.</div>
      </div>
      <div class="mcq-item" data-activity="quiz" data-item="q5">

</div>
        <div class="predict-note">Predict whether this is a data problem or a design problem.</div>
        <div class="mcq-q-text"><p>Two teams each ship a biased app. Team X used a balanced dataset but designed the ranking to weight a factor that happens to favor one group.         <div class="mcq-options" id="q5-options">
<button class="mcq-option" onclick="checkMCQ('q5','A','C','q5-fb-A')"><span class="mcq-option-letter">A</span> Both teams have bias that came from the data</button>
<button class="mcq-option" onclick="checkMCQ('q5','B','C','q5-fb-B')"><span class="mcq-option-letter">B</span> Both teams have bias that came from the algorithm design</button>
<button class="mcq-option" onclick="checkMCQ('q5','C','C','q5-fb-C')"><span class="mcq-option-letter">C</span> Team X has bias from the algorithm design, and Team Y has bias from the data</button>

</div>
<div id="q5-fb-A" class="mcq-feedback incorrect-fb">Incorrect. Team X used balanced data; its bias came from a design choice, not the data.</div>
<div id="q5-fb-B" class="mcq-feedback incorrect-fb">Incorrect. Team Y used neutral logic; its bias came from unrepresentative data, not the design.</div>
<div id="q5-fb-C" class="mcq-feedback correct-fb">Correct. Team X's bias is in the weighting design, while Team Y's is in the unrepresentative training data.</div>
<div id="q5-fb-D" class="mcq-feedback incorrect-fb">Incorrect. The two are reversed. Team X is a design problem and Team Y is a data problem.</div>
      </div>
      <div class="mcq-item" data-activity="quiz" data-item="q6">
        <div class="mcq-q-num">Question 6 of 6<span class="diff-tag">Application</span>
</div>
        <div class="predict-note">Predict the most accurate takeaway before reading options.</div>
        <div class="mcq-q-text"><p>After a widely used screening tool is found to disadvantage a group, the developers say they are surprised because they never wrote any rule targeting that group and tested the tool before release.         <div class="mcq-options" id="q6-options">
<button class="mcq-option" onclick="checkMCQ('q6','A','C','q6-fb-A')"><span class="mcq-option-letter">A</span> The tool must actually be fair, since no targeting rule was written</button>
<button class="mcq-option" onclick="checkMCQ('q6','B','C','q6-fb-B')"><span class="mcq-option-letter">B</span> The developers clearly intended to discriminate and are not being honest</button>
<button class="mcq-option" onclick="checkMCQ('q6','C','C','q6-fb-C')"><span class="mcq-option-letter">C</span> Bias can enter unintentionally through data or design and can go undetected when testing does not include diverse users</button>
<button class="mcq-option" onclick="checkMCQ('q6','D','C','q6-fb-D')"><span class="mcq-option-letter">D</span> The tool would be unbiased if it simply ran on faster hardware</button>
</div>
<div id="q6-fb-A" class="mcq-feedback incorrect-fb">Incorrect. The absence of a targeting rule does not make the tool fair; unintended bias still disadvantages the group.</div>
<div id="q6-fb-B" class="mcq-feedback incorrect-fb">Incorrect. Nothing supports an accusation of intent, and the framework emphasizes that bias is usually unintentional.</div>
<div id="q6-fb-C" class="mcq-feedback correct-fb">Correct. The framework holds that bias is often unintentional, entering through data or design, and can escape detection when testing lacks diverse users.</div>
<div id="q6-fb-D" class="mcq-feedback incorrect-fb">Incorrect. Hardware speed does not address a bias rooted in data or design.</div>

      fb:"Choosing spending as a proxy for need bakes past unequal access into the score -- a design decision, not a data-entry error."
    },
    {
      tag:"Voice assistant",
      text:"A voice assistant is trained mostly on speakers with one regional accent. It transcribes them well but frequently misunderstands users with other accents, who then stop using it.",
      q:"Pick the single most accurate statement.",
      opts:[
        "Biased data collection produced uneven performance, which can worsen as fewer diverse users contribute data",
        "Accents are objectively harder and no dataset could help",
        "The assistant is choosing to ignore certain people",
        "This is a hardware microphone defect, not bias"
      ],
      correct:0,
      fb:"Narrow data collection creates unequal accuracy; if excluded users leave, future data stays narrow -- bias can be amplified over time."
    }
  ];

  var TOTAL = SCN.length;
  var idx=0, score=0, streak=0, answered=false;

  var $=function(id){ return document.getElementById(id); };
  var body=$('stb-body');
  $('stb-total').textContent=TOTAL;

  function updateBar(){
    $('stb-round').textContent=Math.min(idx+1,TOTAL);
    $('stb-score').textContent=score;
    $('stb-streak').textContent=streak;
    $('stb-prog').style.width=(idx/TOTAL*100)+'%';
  }

  function renderRound(){
    answered=false;
    updateBar();
    var s=SCN[idx];
    var html='';
    html+='<span class="stb-tag">'+s.tag+'</span>';
    html+='<div class="stb-scn">'+s.text+'</div>';
    html+='<p class="stb-q">'+s.q+'</p>';
    html+='<div class="stb-opts" id="stb-opts"></div>';
    html+='<div class="stb-fb" id="stb-fb"></div>';
    html+='<button class="stb-next" id="stb-next">Next round →</button>';
    body.innerHTML=html;
    var opts=$('stb-opts');
    s.opts.forEach(function(txt,i){
      var b=document.createElement('button');
      b.className='stb-opt';
      b.type='button';
      b.innerHTML=txt;
      b.onclick=function(){ choose(i,b); };
      opts.appendChild(b);
    });
    $('stb-next').onclick=next;
  }

  function choose(i,btn){
    if(answered) return;
    answered=true;
    var s=SCN[idx];
    var buttons=body.querySelectorAll('.stb-opt');
    Array.prototype.forEach.call(buttons,function(b){ b.disabled=true; });
    var fb=$('stb-fb');
    if(i===s.correct){
      btn.classList.add('right');
      streak++;
      var gain=10+Math.min(streak,5)*2;
      score+=gain;
      fb.className='stb-fb show ok';
      fb.innerHTML='<b>Correct (+'+gain+').</b> '+s.fb;
    } else {
      btn.classList.add('wrong');
      buttons[s.correct].classList.add('right');
      streak=0;
      fb.className='stb-fb show no';
      fb.innerHTML='<b>Not quite.</b> '+s.fb;
    }
    updateBar();
    var nb=$('stb-next');
    nb.innerHTML=(idx>=TOTAL-1)?'See results →':'Next round →';
    nb.className='stb-next show';
  }

  function next(){
    idx++;
    if(idx>=TOTAL){ endGame(); return; }
    renderRound();
  }

  function endGame(){
    $('stb-prog').style.width='100%';
    $('stb-round').textContent=TOTAL;
    $('stb-score').textContent=score;
    var max=SCN.reduce(function(a){ return a+20; },0);
    var pct=score/max;
    var msg;
    if(pct>=0.85) msg="Outstanding. You can trace bias to its source -- data, labeling, design, or a feedback loop -- and explain how systems amplify it.";
    else if(pct>=0.5) msg="Solid work. Remember: bias often enters unintentionally through unrepresentative data or design choices, then gets amplified at scale.";
    else msg="Keep going. The key idea: computing bias usually comes from the data or the design, not a computer 'deciding' to be unfair -- and it can grow through feedback loops.";
    body.innerHTML=
      '<div class="stb-end">'+
        '<h3>🎯 Run complete!</h3>'+
        '<div class="stb-score-big">'+score+'</div>'+
        '<p>'+msg+'</p>'+
        '<button class="stb-again" id="stb-again" type="button">↻ Play again</button>'+
      '</div>';
    $('stb-again').onclick=reset;
    document.dispatchEvent(new CustomEvent('apcsGameScore',{detail:{value:score}}));
  }

  function reset(){
    idx=0; score=0; streak=0;
    renderRound();
  }

  renderRound();
})();
</script>

      <h2>Frequently Asked Questions</h2>
      <div class="faq-item">
        <button class="faq-q" onclick="toggleFAQ(this)">Does bias in computing mean the programmers were being unfair on purpose?<i class="faq-icon">+</i></button>
        <div class="faq-a">No. The AP CSP framework says bias in computing is most often unintentional. It usually enters through data that does not represent all users or through design choices about which inputs matter, not through a deliberate unfair rule. A well-meaning team can still build a biased system.</div>
      </div>
      <div class="faq-item">
        <button class="faq-q" onclick="toggleFAQ(this)">What are the two main places bias can enter a computing system?<i class="faq-icon">+</i></button>
        <div class="faq-a">The data and the algorithm or design. Bias in the data comes from training or sample data that is not representative of everyone the system affects. Bias in the design comes from choices about which inputs are considered and how heavily each factor is weighted.</div>
      </div>
      <div class="faq-item">
        <button class="faq-q" onclick="toggleFAQ(this)">Why is bias sometimes hard to detect?<i class="faq-icon">+</i></button>
        <div class="faq-a">Because it often does not appear until the system is used by a wide range of people. A team that tests only on users like themselves may see the program work perfectly, while a group they never tested with runs into failures. Testing with diverse users is what surfaces the problem.</div>
      </div>
      <div class="faq-item">
        <button class="faq-q" onclick="toggleFAQ(this)">How can programmers reduce bias?<i class="faq-icon">+</i></button>
        <div class="faq-a">Use data that represents the full range of affected users, test the system with diverse users so group-specific failures appear before release, and review the design to ask who could be disadvantaged by which inputs are used and how they are weighted. Bias can rarely be removed completely, but it can be reduced.</div>
      </div>
      <div class="faq-item">
        <button class="faq-q" onclick="toggleFAQ(this)">If a system works well for most users, is it still biased?<i class="faq-icon">+</i></button>
        <div class="faq-a">It can be. Working for a majority does not erase unfair results for a specific group. If the system consistently performs worse for one group because of its data or design, that is bias even if most users are served well.</div>

  <div class="lesson-main">

    <div class="lesson-objectives">
      <h2>After this lesson, you will be able to:</h2>
      <ul>
        <li><span>Define crowdsourcing as obtaining input, ideas, content, labor, or funding from a large group of people</span></li>
        <li><span>Explain how the Internet and computing give crowdsourcing the reach, speed, and scale a small team cannot match</span></li>
        <li><span>Identify examples of crowdsourcing, including citizen science, crowdfunding, and collaborative content</span></li>
        <li><span>Distinguish crowdsourcing from ordinary small-group collaboration</span></li>
        <li><span>Describe the benefits and the quality and coordination concerns of crowdsourced work</span></li>
      </ul>
    </div>
    <div class="score-impact">📈 <span>Big Idea 5 (Impact of Computing) is 21 to 26 percent of the AP CSP exam, the single largest slice. Crowdsourcing questions are fast, definition-driven points: if you can recognize the crowd, what it provides, and the role of the Internet in enabling it, you bank these reliably.</span>
</div>
    <div class="hook-box">
      <div class="hook-label">💡 Think about this first</div>
      <p>A museum has ten thousand old handwritten weather logs it wants turned into a searchable database, but its staff of three would need years to type them all in. Instead it posts scans online and asks the public to transcribe a page or two each. Within weeks the whole archive is done by strangers who never met. What made that possible, and what is this approach actually called?</p>
    </div>
    <div class="lesson-section">
      <h2>What Crowdsourcing Is</h2>
      <p><strong>Crowdsourcing</strong> is the practice of obtaining input, ideas, content, labor, or funding from a <strong>large group of people</strong>, often through the Internet, to accomplish a task or solve a problem. The key word is <em>large</em>. Instead of a small, fixed team doing all the work, a task is opened up to a big, often open crowd, and each contributor supplies a small piece. Add those pieces together and you get a result no small group could have produced as quickly, if at all.</p>
      <p>The crowd can provide different things depending on the project. Sometimes it provides <strong>labor</strong> (people transcribing documents or classifying images), sometimes <strong>data</strong> (volunteers reporting bird sightings or road conditions), sometimes <strong>ideas or content</strong> (writing entries, submitting designs), and sometimes <strong>money</strong> (many small donations funding a project). Naming exactly what the crowd contributes is a favorite exam move.</p>
      <div class="callout-exam">
        <div class="callout-exam-label">🎯 What the exam rewards</div>
        <p>When a scenario is crowdsourcing, the exam wants you to point to two things: a <strong>large group of people each contributing a small part</strong>, and the fact that <strong>the Internet or computing is what makes gathering those contributions at scale possible</strong>. If you can name both, you can answer almost any 5.4 question.</p>
      </div>
    </div>

    <div class="lesson-section">
      <h2>Why Computing Makes It Work</h2>
      <p>Crowdsourcing is an old idea, but the Internet transformed it. Computing gives a crowdsourced project three things a small team cannot match on its own:</p>
      <ul>
        <li>
<strong>Reach.</strong> A request posted online can be seen by millions of people across the world, so the potential pool of contributors is enormous.</li>
        <li>
<strong>Speed.</strong> Thousands of people can work in parallel at the same moment, so a task that would take one team years can finish in days.</li>
        <li>
<strong>Scale.</strong> Software collects, combines, and stores every small contribution automatically, so the size of the crowd is not limited by how much a coordinator can manually track.</li>
      </ul>
      <p>Take those away and crowdsourcing shrinks back to whoever you can reach in person. That is why the framework ties crowdsourcing so tightly to computing: the Internet is not a minor detail of these examples, it is the <strong>enabling technology</strong> that gives the crowd its reach, speed, and scale.</p>
      <div class="mini-ex">
        <div class="mini-ex-label">Quick check</div>
        <div class="mini-ex-q">A wildlife group asks people everywhere to photograph frogs in their area and upload the pictures with a location, building a nationwide map of where each species lives. What is the crowd primarily providing?</div>
        <div class="mini-opts" id="mc-crowd-1-opts">
          <button class="mini-opt" onclick="miniMCQ('mc-crowd-1','A','B','mc-crowd-1-fb')"><span class="mini-opt-letter">A</span> Funding for the project</button>
          <button class="mini-opt" onclick="miniMCQ('mc-crowd-1','B','B','mc-crowd-1-fb')"><span class="mini-opt-letter">B</span> Data, in the form of observations the group could not gather alone</button>
          <button class="mini-opt" onclick="miniMCQ('mc-crowd-1','C','B','mc-crowd-1-fb')"><span class="mini-opt-letter">C</span> Finished software for the map</button>
          <button class="mini-opt" onclick="miniMCQ('mc-crowd-1','D','B','mc-crowd-1-fb')"><span class="mini-opt-letter">D</span> Legal ownership of the species</button>
        </div>
        <div class="mini-fb" id="mc-crowd-1-fb"></div>
      </div>
    </div>

    <div class="lesson-section">
      <h2>The Main Kinds of Crowdsourcing</h2>
      <p>The exam expects you to recognize a few recurring flavors of crowdsourcing by their example, not by memorizing a definition word for word:</p>
      <table class="vocab-table">
        <tr>
<th>Type</th>
<th>What the crowd provides</th>
<th>Example</th>
</tr>
        <tr>
<td><strong>Citizen science</strong></td>
<td>Data and labor: ordinary volunteers collect or classify observations</td>
<td>People worldwide count backyard birds or tag galaxies in telescope images so scientists can study far more data than a lab could gather alone.</td>
</tr>
        <tr>
<td><strong>Crowdfunding</strong></td>
<td>Money: many small contributions add up to fund a project</td>
<td>An inventor raises money for a new gadget by collecting small pledges from thousands of online backers instead of one big investor.</td>
</tr>
        <tr>
<td><strong>Collaborative content</strong></td>
<td>Ideas and content: the public writes, edits, or reviews shared material</td>
<td>A public reference site where volunteers write and correct entries, or product ratings where many buyers each leave a review.</td>
</tr>
      </table>
      <p>Notice they differ only in <strong>what the crowd supplies</strong> (data, money, or content) while sharing the same core: a large, open group each doing a little, gathered through the Internet.</p>
      <div class="callout-trap">
        <div class="callout-trap-label">⚠ Common trap</div>
        <p>Crowdsourcing is <strong>not</strong> just any group working together. A five-person class project or a company's normal design team is collaboration, but it is not crowdsourcing, because the group is small and closed. Crowdsourcing draws on a <strong>large, often open group, usually reached through the Internet</strong>. If the scenario has a small fixed team, it is collaboration, not crowdsourcing.</p>
      </div>
    </div>

    <div class="lesson-section">
      <h2>Benefits and Concerns</h2>
      <p>The upside of crowdsourcing is harnessing the <strong>knowledge, effort, or money of many people</strong> to do something no small team could. A crowd can label millions of images, spot a rare event happening somewhere in the world, or fund a project that no single backer would risk on.</p>
      <p>But scale brings problems the exam also expects you to know. <strong>Quality and accuracy</strong> vary because contributions come from strangers with mixed expertise, so crowdsourced data or content usually needs verification. <strong>Coordination</strong> is hard when thousands of people work loosely on the same task. And <strong>attribution</strong> gets murky: when a crowd builds something together, deciding who gets credit or ownership is not obvious. Good crowdsourcing platforms design for these problems with review steps, guidelines, and reputation systems.</p>
      <div class="mini-ex">
        <div class="mini-ex-label">Quick check</div>
        <div class="mini-ex-q">A startup's five employees meet each week to design their app together. A rival instead posts its design online and invites thousands of users worldwide to submit and vote on ideas. Which situation is crowdsourcing, and why?</div>
        <div class="mini-opts" id="mc-crowd-2-opts">
          <button class="mini-opt" onclick="miniMCQ('mc-crowd-2','A','C','mc-crowd-2-fb')"><span class="mini-opt-letter">A</span> The startup, because a team working together is what crowdsourcing means</button>
          <button class="mini-opt" onclick="miniMCQ('mc-crowd-2','B','C','mc-crowd-2-fb')"><span class="mini-opt-letter">B</span> Both, because any group solving a problem is crowdsourcing</button>
          <button class="mini-opt" onclick="miniMCQ('mc-crowd-2','C','C','mc-crowd-2-fb')"><span class="mini-opt-letter">C</span> The rival, because it gathers input from a large, open group through the Internet</button>
          <button class="mini-opt" onclick="miniMCQ('mc-crowd-2','D','C','mc-crowd-2-fb')"><span class="mini-opt-letter">D</span> Neither, because crowdsourcing requires paying the contributors</button>
        </div>
        <div class="mini-fb" id="mc-crowd-2-fb"></div>
      </div>
    </div>
    <div class="lesson-section">
      <h2>How 5.4 Is Tested on the Multiple-Choice Exam</h2>
      <p>Crowdsourcing shows up in the multiple-choice section as short scenario questions, and there is no free-response component specific to this topic. Two skills earn the points. First, <strong>recognizing crowdsourcing</strong>: given a scenario, decide whether it counts, and the test is whether a <strong>large, often open group</strong> is each contributing a small piece, as opposed to a small fixed team (which is ordinary collaboration). Second, <strong>identifying what makes it possible</strong>: questions frequently ask why the approach works, and the intended answer is that <strong>the Internet and computing provide the reach, speed, and scale</strong> to gather many contributions that a small team could not. Expect distractors that describe small-group collaboration, or that credit better hardware or faster coding instead of the crowd and the network. Know the flavors (citizen science, crowdfunding, collaborative content) so you can name what the crowd supplies, and you will clear these quickly.</p>
    </div>

      <div class="mcq-item" data-activity="quiz" data-item="q1">
        <div class="mcq-q-num">Question 1 of 6<span class="diff-tag">Definition</span>
</div>
        <div class="predict-note">Predict what makes something crowdsourcing before reading the options.</div>
        <div class="mcq-q-text"><p>Which of the following scenarios is the best example of crowdsourcing?</p></div>
        <div class="mcq-options" id="q1-options">
<button class="mcq-option" onclick="checkMCQ('q1','A','B','q1-fb-A')"><span class="mcq-option-letter">A</span> A team of five engineers at one company meets daily to design a bridge together</button>
<button class="mcq-option" onclick="checkMCQ('q1','B','B','q1-fb-B')"><span class="mcq-option-letter">B</span> An app invites millions of drivers to report traffic jams and road hazards, combining their reports into a live map</button>
<button class="mcq-option" onclick="checkMCQ('q1','C','B','q1-fb-C')"><span class="mcq-option-letter">C</span> A single scientist runs an experiment alone and publishes the results</button>
<button class="mcq-option" onclick="checkMCQ('q1','D','B','q1-fb-D')"><span class="mcq-option-letter">D</span> A manager assigns each of three employees a separate section of a report</button>
</div>
<div id="q1-fb-A" class="mcq-feedback incorrect-fb">Incorrect. Five engineers at one company is a small, closed team. That is collaboration, not crowdsourcing.</div>
<div id="q1-fb-B" class="mcq-feedback correct-fb">Correct. A large, open group of drivers each contributes a small report, and the Internet gathers those contributions at scale into a shared result. That is crowdsourcing.</div>
<div id="q1-fb-C" class="mcq-feedback incorrect-fb">Incorrect. One scientist working alone is the opposite of a crowd. Crowdsourcing needs input from a large group.</div>
<div id="q1-fb-D" class="mcq-feedback incorrect-fb">Incorrect. Dividing a report among three assigned employees is division of labor within a small team, not a large open crowd.</div>
      </div>
      <div class="mcq-item" data-activity="quiz" data-item="q2">
        <div class="mcq-q-num">Question 2 of 6<span class="diff-tag">Role of computing</span>
</div>
        <div class="predict-note">Name what the Internet contributes before you look.</div>
        <div class="mcq-q-text"><p>A charity used to raise money by mailing letters to a few hundred local residents. It now posts its campaign online, where anyone in the world can donate. Which best explains how computing changed what the charity can do?</p></div>
        <div class="mcq-options" id="q2-options">
<button class="mcq-option" onclick="checkMCQ('q2','A','D','q2-fb-A')"><span class="mcq-option-letter">A</span> Computing guarantees that every donation will be larger than before</button>
<button class="mcq-option" onclick="checkMCQ('q2','B','D','q2-fb-B')"><span class="mcq-option-letter">B</span> Computing removes the need for the charity to have any goal or plan</button>
<button class="mcq-option" onclick="checkMCQ('q2','C','D','q2-fb-C')"><span class="mcq-option-letter">C</span> Computing makes the donations more accurate by checking each donor's math</button>
<button class="mcq-option" onclick="checkMCQ('q2','D','D','q2-fb-D')"><span class="mcq-option-letter">D</span> Computing gives the campaign the reach and scale to gather many small contributions from a huge, dispersed group of people</button>
</div>
<div id="q2-fb-A" class="mcq-feedback incorrect-fb">Incorrect. Crowdsourcing does not guarantee larger individual donations. Its power is the number of contributors, not the size of each gift.</div>
<div id="q2-fb-B" class="mcq-feedback incorrect-fb">Incorrect. A crowdfunding campaign still needs a clear goal. Computing changes the reach, not the need for a plan.</div>
<div id="q2-fb-C" class="mcq-feedback incorrect-fb">Incorrect. Accuracy of arithmetic is not the issue. The change is scale and reach, letting the crowd grow far beyond a local mailing list.</div>
<div id="q2-fb-D" class="mcq-feedback correct-fb">Correct. The Internet gives the campaign reach and scale, letting it collect many small contributions from far more people than local mail ever could. That enabling role is the point of 5.4.</div>
      </div>
      <div class="mcq-item" data-activity="quiz" data-item="q3">
        <div class="mcq-q-num">Question 3 of 6<span class="diff-tag">Is it crowdsourcing</span>
</div>
        <div class="predict-note">Decide yes or no and your reason before matching an option.</div>
        <div class="mcq-q-text"><p>Four friends split the cost of a pizza and decide together which toppings to get. A student claims this is an example of crowdsourcing. Is the student correct?</p></div>
        <div class="mcq-options" id="q3-options">
<button class="mcq-option" onclick="checkMCQ('q3','A','B','q3-fb-A')"><span class="mcq-option-letter">A</span> Yes, because several people contributed money toward one goal</button>
<button class="mcq-option" onclick="checkMCQ('q3','B','B','q3-fb-B')"><span class="mcq-option-letter">B</span> No, because the group is small and closed rather than a large, open crowd reached through computing</button>
<button class="mcq-option" onclick="checkMCQ('q3','C','B','q3-fb-C')"><span class="mcq-option-letter">C</span> Yes, because the friends reached a decision together</button>
<button class="mcq-option" onclick="checkMCQ('q3','D','B','q3-fb-D')"><span class="mcq-option-letter">D</span> No, because crowdsourcing can only involve labor and never money</button>
</div>
<div id="q3-fb-A" class="mcq-feedback incorrect-fb">Incorrect. Pooling money among four friends is not crowdfunding. The defining feature of crowdsourcing is a large, open group, not just more than one contributor.</div>
<div id="q3-fb-B" class="mcq-feedback correct-fb">Correct. Four friends are a small, closed group, so this is ordinary collaboration. Crowdsourcing requires a large, often open crowd, typically reached through the Internet.</div>
<div id="q3-fb-C" class="mcq-feedback incorrect-fb">Incorrect. Reaching a decision together is collaboration. Crowdsourcing specifically draws on a large, often open group, usually via the Internet.</div>
<div id="q3-fb-D" class="mcq-feedback incorrect-fb">Incorrect. Crowdsourcing can involve money (crowdfunding). The real reason this is not crowdsourcing is that the group is small and closed.</div>
      </div>
      <div class="mcq-item" data-activity="quiz" data-item="q4">
        <div class="mcq-q-num">Question 4 of 6<span class="diff-tag">II and III style</span>
</div>
        <div class="predict-note">Judge each statement true or false before choosing.</div>
        <div class="mcq-q-text"><p>Consider these statements about crowdsourcing:</p></div>
        <ul class="mcq-roman">
          <li>
<strong>I.</strong> Crowdsourcing can only be used to raise money, never to gather data or labor.</li>
          <li>
<strong>II.</strong> The Internet gives crowdsourcing reach, speed, and scale that a small team could not achieve alone.</li>
          <li>
<strong>III.</strong> Because contributions come from a large, varied group of strangers, quality and accuracy can be a concern.</li>
        </ul>
        <div class="mcq-options" id="q4-options">
<button class="mcq-option" onclick="checkMCQ('q4','A','A','q4-fb-A')"><span class="mcq-option-letter">A</span> II and III only</button>
<button class="mcq-option" onclick="checkMCQ('q4','B','A','q4-fb-B')"><span class="mcq-option-letter">B</span> I and II only</button>
<button class="mcq-option" onclick="checkMCQ('q4','C','A','q4-fb-C')"><span class="mcq-option-letter">C</span> I and III only</button>
<button class="mcq-option" onclick="checkMCQ('q4','D','A','q4-fb-D')"><span class="mcq-option-letter">D</span> I, II, and III</button>
</div>
<div id="q4-fb-A" class="mcq-feedback correct-fb">Correct. II and III are both accurate: the Internet enables scale, and quality of mixed contributions is a real concern. I is false because crowdsourcing is not limited to money.</div>
<div id="q4-fb-B" class="mcq-feedback incorrect-fb">Incorrect. Statement I is false: crowdsourcing gathers data and labor too, not only money. So it cannot be part of the answer.</div>
<div id="q4-fb-C" class="mcq-feedback incorrect-fb">Incorrect. Statement I is false, so any choice that includes I is wrong, even though III is true.</div>
<div id="q4-fb-D" class="mcq-feedback incorrect-fb">Incorrect. Statement I is false, so all three cannot be correct.</div>
      </div>
      <div class="mcq-item" data-activity="quiz" data-item="q5">
        <div class="mcq-q-num">Question 5 of 6<span class="diff-tag">Identify the type</span>
</div>
        <div class="predict-note">Predict which flavor of crowdsourcing this is first.</div>
        <div class="mcq-q-text"><p>An astronomy project posts millions of telescope images online and asks volunteers around the world to classify the shape of each galaxy, producing labeled data that researchers analyze. Which term best describes this activity?</p></div>
        <div class="mcq-options" id="q5-options">
<button class="mcq-option" onclick="checkMCQ('q5','A','A','q5-fb-A')"><span class="mcq-option-letter">A</span> Citizen science</button>
<button class="mcq-option" onclick="checkMCQ('q5','B','A','q5-fb-B')"><span class="mcq-option-letter">B</span> Crowdfunding</button>
<button class="mcq-option" onclick="checkMCQ('q5','C','A','q5-fb-C')"><span class="mcq-option-letter">C</span> Pair programming</button>
<button class="mcq-option" onclick="checkMCQ('q5','D','A','q5-fb-D')"><span class="mcq-option-letter">D</span> Division of labor within a single research team</button>
</div>
<div id="q5-fb-A" class="mcq-feedback correct-fb">Correct. Volunteers collecting or classifying scientific data at scale is citizen science, a form of crowdsourcing where the crowd supplies data and labor.</div>
<div id="q5-fb-B" class="mcq-feedback incorrect-fb">Incorrect. No money is being raised. Crowdfunding is crowdsourcing money, and this scenario gathers classifications, not funds.</div>
<div id="q5-fb-C" class="mcq-feedback incorrect-fb">Incorrect. Pair programming is two people sharing one computer to write code. It has nothing to do with a global crowd labeling images.</div>
<div id="q5-fb-D" class="mcq-feedback incorrect-fb">Incorrect. A single research team dividing work is small and closed. Here the labeling is done by a large, open crowd of volunteers online.</div>
      </div>
      <div class="mcq-item" data-activity="quiz" data-item="q6">
        <div class="mcq-q-num">Question 6 of 6<span class="diff-tag">Concern</span>
</div>
        <div class="predict-note">Predict the most likely downside before reading the options.</div>
        <div class="mcq-q-text"><p>A travel site lets anyone post reviews and star ratings of hotels, and it shows the average rating for each hotel. Which of the following is the most significant concern a computer scientist would raise about this crowdsourced data?</p></div>
        <div class="mcq-options" id="q6-options">
<button class="mcq-option" onclick="checkMCQ('q6','A','D','q6-fb-A')"><span class="mcq-option-letter">A</span> The site cannot store more than a few reviews at once</button>
<button class="mcq-option" onclick="checkMCQ('q6','B','D','q6-fb-B')"><span class="mcq-option-letter">B</span> Averaging the ratings is mathematically impossible</button>
<button class="mcq-option" onclick="checkMCQ('q6','C','D','q6-fb-C')"><span class="mcq-option-letter">C</span> Using the Internet to collect reviews prevents the site from ever reaching a large audience</button>
<button class="mcq-option" onclick="checkMCQ('q6','D','D','q6-fb-D')"><span class="mcq-option-letter">D</span> The reviews come from many unverified strangers, so their quality and accuracy may vary and some may be fake or biased</button>
</div>
<div id="q6-fb-A" class="mcq-feedback incorrect-fb">Incorrect. Storage capacity is not the crowdsourcing concern here. Computing easily stores large numbers of reviews.</div>
<div id="q6-fb-B" class="mcq-feedback incorrect-fb">Incorrect. Averaging ratings is straightforward arithmetic. The real concern is the trustworthiness of the individual contributions.</div>
<div id="q6-fb-C" class="mcq-feedback incorrect-fb">Incorrect. The opposite is true: the Internet is exactly what lets the site reach a large audience. Reach is a benefit, not the concern.</div>
<div id="q6-fb-D" class="mcq-feedback correct-fb">Correct. Because contributions come from a large group of unverified strangers, quality and accuracy vary, and fake or biased reviews are a genuine risk. Verification is the core concern with crowdsourced content.</div>
      </div>
